dd-rwanda.p: In 1959 a Hutu uprising overthrew Rwanda's Tutsi monarchy, and over the next years thousands of Tutsi were killed and hundreds of thousands fled abroad. In 1990 their children's army, the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), invaded from Uganda. A 1993 peace deal collapsed when President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane was shot down on 6 April 1994.

steps: Belgium issued ID cards fixing people as Hutu or Tutsi.
After independence, Hutu governments persecuted Tutsis.
RTLM called Tutsis "cockroaches" to be exterminated.
The president’s plane is shot down; killings begin within hours.

dd-rwanda.p: Mostly Tutsis and moderate Hutus, while UN peacekeepers were ordered not to intervene.

Hutu extremists then killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in 100 days, while the UN withdrew most of its peacekeepers. The RPF won the war in July, and some 2 million Hutu fled abroad, most of them into Zaire. Rwanda's pursuit of the militias among them set off two Congo wars, from 1996 to 2003; the second drew in nine African countries.

Under Belgian rule the categories of Hutu and Tutsi hardened into fixed 'races' on identity cards, and Belgium governed through a Tutsi elite. After 1959 Hutu-led governments treated Tutsi as second-class citizens. The RPF invasion, economic crisis and a power-sharing deal that threatened Habyarimana's circle let extremists organise militias, import machetes and spread hate through radio. In Congo, a collapsing state, armed refugees and rich minerals turned Rwanda's war into a regional one.

dd-rwanda.q: What happened in Rwanda between April and July 1994?
a: A border war with Uganda over refugees
Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in 100 days
Belgium returned to restore colonial rule
A peaceful election ended the Tutsi monarchy
dd-rwanda.why: After the president's plane was shot down, extremist militias and soldiers killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, by UN estimates, until the RPF won the war.

dd-rwanda.p: On 6 April 1994 a plane carrying Rwanda's Hutu president was shot down over Kigali. Within hours Hutu extremist militias and soldiers began killing Tutsi and moderate Hutu, at roadblocks and in churches where victims had sought refuge. In about 100 days some 800,000 people were killed, by UN estimates. The Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front, which had invaded from Uganda in 1990, ended the genocide by taking the country, and some 2 million Hutu fled, mostly into Zaire, now DR Congo.

Genocide, April–July 1994

Rwanda's government counted over 1 million victims; the UN estimate is about 800,000, perhaps 70 percent of Rwanda's Tutsi. Between 250,000 and 500,000 women were raped, by UN estimates.

Its leaders grew up as Tutsi refugees here

Paul Kagame and other RPF leaders grew up as refugees in Uganda and fought in Yoweri Museveni's rebel army there before invading Rwanda in October 1990.

dd-rwanda.q: What did Rwanda's war lead to beyond its borders?
a: A lasting peace across the Great Lakes region
Belgium's return as colonial ruler of Congo
Two Congo wars, the second drawing in nine African countries
dd-rwanda.why: About 2 million Hutu fled, mostly to Zaire, among them armed militias; Rwanda's pursuit of them set off the Congo wars of 1996 to 2003.

dd-rwanda.p:
About 2 million people in camps, July 1994

The camps around Goma and Bukavu held ordinary civilians but also the soldiers and militiamen who had led the genocide, and they soon rearmed.

Hundreds of thousands fled east into Tanzania. The UN tribunal for Rwanda sat in Arusha, Tanzania, from 1994 to 2015 and convicted 62 people.

Hutu and Tutsi speak the same language, Kinyarwanda, share the same religion and lived side by side for centuries. Before colonial rule the labels were partly about status and cattle: Tutsi were often herders and the royal court was Tutsi, and people could sometimes move between groups. German and then Belgian colonisers, influenced by racial theories, treated Tutsi as a superior race from the north. In 1933 Belgium issued identity cards stating each person's group. In 1994 those cards decided who lived and died at roadblocks. Today Rwanda has dropped the labels from its cards and officially promotes a single Rwandan identity.

The killing was organised. Officials, soldiers and the Interahamwe militia, linked to the ruling party, used lists of names, and local leaders called on villagers to take part in 'work'. Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines had spent months calling Tutsi 'cockroaches'; during the killings it broadcast names and hiding places. Neighbours killed neighbours, mostly with machetes and clubs. Churches, schools and stadiums, where Tutsi had sheltered in earlier waves of violence, became sites of mass murder. Some Hutu risked their lives to hide Tutsi. At the Hôtel des Mille Collines in Kigali, manager Paul Rusesabagina sheltered over 1,200 people, a story told in the film 'Hotel Rwanda', though some survivors dispute his account.

In 1996 Rwanda and Uganda invaded Zaire to break up the Hutu militia camps and backed Laurent-Désiré Kabila, who toppled the dictator Mobutu in May 1997 and renamed the country DR Congo. When Kabila turned on his backers in 1998 they invaded again. Angola, Zimbabwe and Namibia sent troops to save him. Nine African countries and dozens of armed groups fought, often over gold, diamonds and coltan.

Zaire until 1997

A 2008 survey by the International Rescue Committee estimated 5.4 million excess deaths in 1998–2007, mostly from disease and hunger; other researchers think the toll was lower. A transitional government took office in 2003.

dd-rwanda.q: How did Belgian rule help harden the Hutu–Tutsi divide?
a: It moved Tutsi herders out of the country
It fixed Hutu and Tutsi as 'races' on identity cards
It gave the Hutu majority control of the royal court
dd-rwanda.why: Influenced by racial theories, Belgium issued identity cards stating each person's group in 1933; in 1994 those cards decided who lived at roadblocks.

dd-rwanda.p:
Rwanda said it was hunting the génocidaires. A UN panel in 2001 accused it, and Uganda, of plundering eastern Congo's minerals. Rwanda withdrew its troops after the 2002 Pretoria Accord.

Uganda backed its own rebel movements in the north-east. In 2005 the International Court of Justice found it had illegally occupied parts of Congo.

Angola intervened to protect Kinshasa and to deny bases to its own UNITA rebels. Its tanks and planes stopped a rebel advance on the capital in 1998.

Zimbabwe sent up to about 11,000 troops. Its generals and businessmen won mining and timber deals in return.

dd-rwanda.q: Where does the conflict that grew from 1994 stand in 2026?
a: Eastern Congo is at peace after the Washington Accords
Fighting goes on in eastern Congo, where M23 holds Goma and Bukavu
The UN now governs eastern Congo directly
dd-rwanda.why: M23, backed by Rwanda according to UN experts, took Goma and Bukavu in 2025; despite US- and Qatari-brokered deals, the war went on in October 2026.

dd-rwanda.p: UN commander Roméo Dallaire warned in January 1994 that militias were stockpiling weapons and drawing up lists, but was told not to raid the caches. After ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed on 7 April, the Security Council cut his force to 270. Western countries flew out their own citizens and left. US officials avoided the word 'genocide', which could have created a duty to act. France launched Opération Turquoise in June, saving some lives but also, critics say, letting the organisers escape to Zaire. President Clinton apologised in 1998, and in 2021 France's President Macron acknowledged France's 'responsibilities' while denying complicity.

The war never fully ended in eastern DR Congo, home to over 100 armed groups. In January 2025 the M23 rebels, backed by Rwanda according to UN experts and the US, seized Goma, then Bukavu. Rwanda denies directing M23 and cites the threat of Hutu militias. A US-brokered peace deal was signed in Washington in December 2025, and Qatar mediated talks with M23, but in October 2026 the rebels still held both cities.

M23 holds much of North and South Kivu

About 7 million people were displaced inside Congo in 2025, by UN counts. In October 2026 former president Joseph Kabila, sentenced to death in absentia in 2025, launched a new anti-government front with M23 in Goma.

Accused of backing M23 with troops

UN experts reported thousands of Rwandan troops in Congo. In March 2026 the US sanctioned Rwanda's army, which Rwanda called one-sided; Kigali says the Hutu FDLR militia, founded by génocidaires, threatens it.

dd-rwanda.q: How did the genocide's organisers turn neighbours against neighbours?
a: Lists of names, militias, and hate radio calling Tutsi 'cockroaches'
Foreign armies forced villagers to fight
The UN peacekeepers handed over Tutsi refugees
Churches called for war against Uganda
dd-rwanda.why: The killing was organised: officials and the Interahamwe used lists, and radio spread hate for months, then broadcast names and hiding places.

dd-rwanda.p:
Uganda against the ADF; Burundi alongside Congo's army

Since 2021 Uganda's army has fought the ADF, an Islamic State-linked militia, inside Congo. UN experts have also accused Uganda of tolerating support for M23, which it denies.

Burundi sent thousands of troops to fight alongside Congo's army against M23, which it sees as backed by its rival, Rwanda.

Over 100,000 suspects filled Rwanda's prisons after 1994, far too many for its courts. From 2002 to 2012 the country revived gacaca, village courts where elected local judges heard nearly 2 million cases, letting survivors learn how relatives died and perpetrators confess for lighter sentences. The UN tribunal in Arusha convicted 62 people, and in 1998 delivered the first genocide conviction by an international court. Rwanda abolished the death penalty in 2007. Each April the country mourns during Kwibuka, 'remember'. Women hold over 60 percent of the seats in its lower house of parliament, a world record, while rights groups say opposition politicians and journalists are jailed or silenced.

Under Paul Kagame, in charge since 1994 and president since 2000, Rwanda rebuilt fast and became one of Africa's most orderly economies, though critics and rights groups say dissent is harshly repressed. Eastern Congo has never known lasting peace: the M23 rebels, backed by Rwanda according to UN experts, took Goma and Bukavu in 2025, and despite US- and Qatari-brokered deals the war went on in October 2026.

The world's failure in Rwanda led to the idea of the 'Responsibility to Protect' (2005) and international criminal courts. Rwanda has since rebuilt fast under Paul Kagame, though with little political freedom.

dd-ukraine.p: Ukraine became independent when the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, and in 1994 gave up its nuclear weapons in return for promises to respect its borders. In 2014 protests in Kyiv toppled a pro-Russian president; Russia then seized Crimea, and Russian-backed separatists took part of the Donbas. On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion.

l: A distinct nation with its own language
Holodomor famine (1932–33) as a crime against Ukrainians
r: Kyiv as the cradle of Russia

steps: Orange Revolution against a rigged election.
Maidan protests; Russia seizes Crimea and backs fighting in Donbas.
Grinding war along a long front line.

dd-ukraine.p: Ukraine held Kyiv, and that autumn retook much of the north-east and the city of Kherson. The war then became a grinding struggle of trenches, artillery and drones. In October 2026 Russia held about a fifth of Ukraine, and US-led talks had brought only brief truces, no lasting ceasefire.

a: Protests in Kyiv toppled a pro-Russian president
Russia annexed Crimea after a referendum
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union
dd-ukraine.why: Russia attacked from the north, east and south, partly from Belarus; it failed to take Kyiv, and the war became a long grinding struggle.

dd-ukraine.p: Russia's leaders saw Ukraine as part of Russia's historic sphere and called NATO's expansion towards it a threat; Vladimir Putin argued in 2021 that Russians and Ukrainians were 'one people'. Most Ukrainians wanted their own path, closer to Europe, especially after 2014. Ukraine and its Western backers call the war an unprovoked war of conquest; Russia calls it a defence against NATO and of Russian speakers, claims that most historians and international bodies reject.

Ukraine became independent in 1991 with its Soviet borders, Crimea included. From 1999 NATO took in former Soviet-bloc states, from Poland to the Baltic states: Russia called this a threat, the new members called it protection. In 2014, after protests in Kyiv toppled a pro-Russian president, Russia seized and annexed Crimea, and Russian-backed separatists took part of the Donbas. About 14,000 people died in that war by 2021.

dd-ukraine.q: Which change in Europe did the war bring about?
a: Europe became more dependent on Russian gas
Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and defence spending rose sharply
dd-ukraine.why: Neutral Finland and Sweden joined NATO, Europe sharply cut its reliance on Russian gas, and defence spending rose the most since the Cold War.

dd-ukraine.p:
Founded in 1949; West Germany joined in 1955, Spain in 1982

The US signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum and backed NATO's enlargement. After 2014 it sanctioned Russia and trained and armed Ukraine's army.

Britain also signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which gave Ukraine assurances but no promise of military defence.

Former communist states, including three ex-Soviet republics

Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004. Like other former Soviet-bloc states, it sought NATO membership as protection from Russia.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, Soviet republics until 1991, joined NATO in 2004, bringing the alliance to Russia's border.

The two sides tell very different stories. Russia's government says NATO broke a promise, made as Germany reunified in 1990, not to expand east, and that a Western-leaning Ukraine threatened Russia's security and its Russian speakers. It framed the 2022 invasion as a 'special military operation' to 'demilitarise and denazify' Ukraine. Western officials say no such promise was ever agreed, and that countries are free to choose their alliances. Ukraine's government and most scholars point to Putin's own words denying that Ukraine is a real nation, and to Russia's annexation of four regions it did not even fully hold, as evidence of a war for territory.

On 24 February 2022 Russia attacked from the north, east and south, partly from Belarus. It failed to take Kyiv and pulled back from the north by early April. Ukrainian counter-offensives freed most of Kharkiv region and the city of Kherson that autumn, but a 2023 offensive stalled. Since then Russia has advanced slowly and at great cost. In October 2026 it held about a fifth of Ukraine, and the fighting went on.

About a fifth occupied by Russia in October 2026

Ukraine's army has an estimated 125,000–150,000 dead (CSIS, mid-2026). The UN had verified over 16,000 civilian deaths by mid-2026 and says the true number is much higher. About 5.8 million Ukrainians lived abroad as refugees.

dd-ukraine.q: How did Russia's leaders see Ukraine and NATO's growth?
a: As part of Russia's historic sphere, with NATO's expansion a threat
As a fellow NATO member to be protected
As a neutral buffer they had no interest in
As a rival nuclear power threatening Moscow
dd-ukraine.why: Russia's leaders called NATO's expansion a threat, and Putin argued Russians and Ukrainians were 'one people'; most historians and international bodies reject Russia's claims about the war.

dd-ukraine.p: Russia called the war a 'special military operation'. CSIS estimated up to 450,000 Russian soldiers dead by mid-2026; Russia publishes no full figures. In September 2022 it claimed to annex four Ukrainian regions it did not fully control.

Let Russian forces attack from its land in 2022

Belarus let Russian troops invade from its territory in 2022 and later hosted Russian tactical nuclear weapons, but its own army has not fought in Ukraine.

dd-ukraine.q: How is this war changing warfare elsewhere?
a: It proved tanks make drones useless
Cheap drones, used at huge scale, are changing how armies fight
It ended the use of trenches and minefields
It showed that air power alone wins wars
dd-ukraine.why: Both sides build millions of drones a year; small FPV drones hunt soldiers and vehicles, and armies everywhere are learning from it.

dd-ukraine.p: After the fast-moving battles of 2022, the front hardened into hundreds of kilometres of trenches and minefields, like a First World War front watched from the sky. Cheap drones changed everything. Small first-person-view (FPV) drones, flown by operators wearing goggles, hunt soldiers and vehicles miles behind the lines, so that troops move in tiny groups and tanks hide under metal 'cope cages'. Both sides now build millions of drones a year. Russia fires waves of Shahed-type drones and missiles at cities and power stations, while Ukraine's long-range drones strike oil refineries deep inside Russia. In June 2025 Ukraine hit bombers at airbases across Russia using drones smuggled in on lorries.

Most of Europe, the United States, Japan and their allies sanctioned Russia and armed or funded Ukraine. Russia drew on Iranian drone designs, and in late 2024 North Korea sent thousands of troops to help it fight. Much of the world stayed neutral: China, India and Turkey became the biggest buyers of Russian oil, which kept its war economy going.
Ukraine depended on Western weapons and money but built a huge drone industry of its own, striking deep into Russia at refineries and airfields.
Sanctions cut Russia off from most Western trade and froze about $300 billion of its central bank reserves. It redirected oil exports to Asia and turned its economy towards arms production.

dd-ukraine.q: What turned Ukraine further away from Russia from 2014?
a: Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons
Russia seized Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas
Ukraine joined NATO and the EU
dd-ukraine.why: After protests toppled a pro-Russian president in 2014, Russia annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas, and most Ukrainians looked increasingly towards Europe.

dd-ukraine.p:
Weapons, drones or troops

Belarus served as a launch pad for the 2022 invasion and stayed Russia's closest ally.

Iran supplied Shahed attack drones from 2022. Russia later built its own version, the Geran-2, in large numbers.

For Ukrainians the war is part of daily life. Air-raid alerts sound on phones across the country, and people in Kyiv have spent nights in metro stations. Russian strikes on power stations brought rolling blackouts every winter since 2022, and cafés ran on generators. Most men aged 23 to 60 may not leave the country, so families have been split, with about 5.8 million Ukrainians living abroad as refugees and millions more displaced inside the country. Ukraine says nearly 20,000 children have been taken to Russia; in 2023 the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over these deportations, which Russia calls evacuations.

It is Europe's deadliest war since 1945, with hundreds of thousands of soldiers killed and millions of Ukrainians made refugees. It sharply cut Europe's reliance on Russian gas, brought Finland and Sweden into NATO and set off the biggest rise in European defence spending since the Cold War. Russia turned towards China, Iran and North Korea. Drone warfare, pioneered here at scale, is changing how armies everywhere fight.

dd-terror.p: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania. President George W. Bush declared a 'war on terror'. In October US-led forces invaded Afghanistan and toppled the Taliban, who had sheltered Osama bin Laden.

dd-terror.h: From 9/11 to the war on terror
steps: Founded by Osama bin Laden in 1988 from fighters in Afghanistan.
2003 invasion based on false claims of weapons of mass destruction.

dd-terror.p: In 2003 the US and Britain invaded Iraq, citing weapons of mass destruction that did not exist, and years of insurgency and sectarian war followed. Bin Laden was killed in Pakistan in 2011. From the chaos in Iraq and Syria rose the Islamic State, which held a 'caliphate' from 2014 to 2019. In August 2021 US troops left Afghanistan and the Taliban returned to power.

Al-Qaeda, founded by veterans of the 1980s war against the Soviets in Afghanistan, blamed the United States for its troops in Saudi Arabia, its support for Israel and for Arab rulers it called corrupt, and hoped attacks would draw America into a ruinous war. After 9/11, US leaders resolved to strike terrorists and the states that sheltered them before they could attack again, an approach that critics said led to overreach in Iraq.

dd-terror.q: What did the United States do in response to the 11 September attacks?
a: It declared a 'war on terror' and invaded Afghanistan
It invaded Saudi Arabia, home of most hijackers
It withdrew its troops from the Middle East
It asked the UN to try bin Laden in court
dd-terror.why: President Bush declared a 'war on terror', and in October 2001 US-led forces toppled the Taliban, who had sheltered Osama bin Laden.

dd-terror.p: On 11 September 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people in the United States. Al-Qaeda's leader, Osama bin Laden, was sheltered by the Taliban in Afghanistan. A US-led invasion toppled the Taliban within weeks, and a NATO-led force from about 50 countries later joined. Bin Laden was killed in Pakistan in 2011. In August 2021, as US troops left, the Taliban retook Kabul.
About 2,400 US service members died in Afghanistan, the longest war in US history. The US also spent over $2 trillion there, by the Costs of War project's estimate.

Among about 50 countries in the NATO-led mission

Britain sent the second-largest force, up to about 9,500 troops, mostly in Helmand province. 457 British service personnel died.

Canada fought in Kandahar province from 2006 to 2011, and 158 Canadian soldiers died.

dd-terror.q: How did the Islamic State come to rise?
a: It grew out of the Taliban government in Kabul
It was founded by Iraq's army after 2003
It began as a branch of Hezbollah
Al-Qaeda in Iraq survived and regrouped in Syria's civil war
dd-terror.why: Weakened by 2010, al-Qaeda in Iraq regrouped amid Syria's chaos and, as ISIS, seized Mosul in 2014 and declared a 'caliphate'.

dd-terror.p: The Costs of War project estimates about 176,000 people were killed directly in the war, including over 46,000 Afghan civilians. In 2021 the Taliban restored strict rule, barring girls from secondary school.

On a clear Tuesday morning 19 men, 15 of them Saudi citizens, hijacked four airliners with box cutters and knives. At 8:46 a.m. the first struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center; the second hit the South Tower 17 minutes later, as millions watched live on television. A third plane hit the Pentagon. On the fourth, passengers who had learned of the other attacks by phone stormed the cockpit, and it crashed in a Pennsylvania field, short of its probable target in Washington. Both towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 victims died, including 343 New York firefighters. The 9/11 Commission later found that US agencies had missed warning signs.

The war on terror raised hard questions about law and rights. From January 2002 the US held suspected militants at Guantanamo Bay in Cuba, outside normal courts; about 780 men passed through it, many never charged, and about 15 remained in 2026. The CIA held prisoners in secret 'black sites' and used 'enhanced interrogation', including waterboarding, which a 2014 Senate report found brutal and ineffective; President Obama said the US had 'tortured some folks', while former CIA officials defended the programme. Photos of abuse at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq in 2004 shocked the world. Supporters argued such measures helped prevent further attacks on the scale of 9/11, which did not happen.

In March 2003 the United States and Britain, with Australia and Poland, invaded Iraq, saying Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction; none were found. France, Germany and Russia opposed the war at the UN. Saddam fell within weeks, but an insurgency, al-Qaeda bombings and a sectarian civil war between Sunni and Shia followed. US troops left at the end of 2011.
About 4,400 US troops died in Iraq. A troop 'surge' in 2007 and a deal with Sunni tribes reduced the violence before the US withdrew in 2011.

dd-terror.q: What did al-Qaeda hope its attacks on America would achieve?
a: Draw the United States into a ruinous war
Win US support against the Soviets
Persuade the US to sell it weapons
dd-terror.why: Al-Qaeda blamed the US for its troops in Saudi Arabia and its support for Israel and Arab rulers, and hoped to draw America into a ruinous war.

dd-terror.p:
Sent combat troops in March 2003

Prime Minister Tony Blair backed the war despite huge protests. The 2016 Chilcot inquiry found that Britain went to war before peaceful options were exhausted, on flawed intelligence.

Australia sent about 2,000 personnel for the invasion, including special forces, ships and aircraft.

Some of the over 30 countries in the occupation force

Spain withdrew its troops in 2004, after al-Qaeda-inspired bombers killed 193 people on Madrid commuter trains.

dd-terror.q: Where did Afghanistan end up after twenty years of war?
a: Ruled again by the Taliban, still in power in 2026
dd-terror.why: As US troops left in August 2021, the Afghan army collapsed and the Taliban swept back into Kabul; they still ruled in 2026.

dd-terror.p: After the Iraq invasion, al-Qaeda in Iraq, led by Abu Musab al-Zarqawi, bombed Shia shrines and markets to provoke civil war. It was weakened by 2010, but survivors regrouped in Syria's civil war and, as the Islamic State, seized Mosul in 2014. ISIS ran its 'caliphate' like a state, with taxes, courts and schools, while carrying out mass executions, enslaving Yazidi women and spreading propaganda online that drew some 40,000 foreigners to join it. It inspired or directed attacks from Paris to Sri Lanka. A coalition of over 80 countries helped Iraqi and Kurdish-led forces destroy it by 2019.

dd-terror.h: The Islamic State at its height, 2015
dd-terror.p: Al-Qaeda in Iraq survived, and in Syria's civil war it was reborn as the Islamic State, or ISIS. In June 2014 it seized Mosul in Iraq and declared a 'caliphate' across Iraq and Syria, ruling millions of people by terror. Groups in Libya, Egypt, Nigeria and Afghanistan pledged loyalty. A US-led coalition and local forces destroyed the caliphate by March 2019, but ISIS cells survive.

Land held in Iraq and Syria, 2014–2019

ISIS swept across Sunni areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014, as the Iraqi army collapsed. Iraq declared victory in December 2017.

ISIS grew in the chaos of Syria's civil war, ruling the east from Raqqa. Kurdish-led forces, with US support, did most of the ground fighting against it.

dd-terror.q: What reason did the US and Britain give for invading Iraq in 2003?
a: Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction
The Islamic State had seized Mosul
dd-terror.why: They cited weapons of mass destruction, but none were found; critics said the war was overreach, and years of insurgency and sectarian war followed.

dd-terror.p:
Local groups that pledged loyalty to ISIS

ISIS held the coastal city of Sirte in 2015–16, amid Libya's civil war.

An ISIS affiliate fought Egypt's army in northern Sinai and claimed the 2015 bombing of a Russian airliner that killed 224 people.

In February 2020 the Trump administration signed a deal with the Taliban to withdraw US troops. President Biden completed the pullout in August 2021, as the Afghan army collapsed and the Taliban swept into Kabul; crowds clung to departing aircraft at the airport. Al-Qaeda's leader Ayman al-Zawahiri was killed by a US drone in Kabul in 2022. Neither al-Qaeda nor ISIS has struck the West on the scale of 9/11 since, but their affiliates have grown in Africa's Sahel and Somalia. The 9/11 accused at Guantanamo had still not been tried 25 years after the attacks; a military judge has set their trial for 2028.

The Costs of War project at Brown University estimates over 900,000 people were killed directly in the post-9/11 wars, and millions more died of indirect causes. The US spent about $8 trillion. Air travel brought new security checks, and governments gained wide surveillance powers. The Iraq war strengthened Iran, and ISIS's rise fed Syria's civil war and a refugee crisis that changed European politics. The Taliban still ruled Afghanistan in 2026.

The wars cost trillions of dollars and hundreds of thousands of lives. The Iraq war helped give rise to ISIS, and the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021. Airport security, surveillance and drone warfare all grew from this era.

dd-syria.p: In December 2010 a young Tunisian street vendor set himself on fire, and protests against ageing dictators spread across the Arab world. Tunisia's president fled in January 2011, Egypt's Hosni Mubarak resigned in February, and Libya's Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown and killed by October with NATO air support. In Syria, Bashar al-Assad met peaceful protests with bullets, and the country slid into civil war.

items: Backed by Turkey and Gulf states

dd-syria.p: The largest refugee crisis of its time, mostly to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Germany.

Russia, Iran and Hezbollah fought for him; Turkey, the Gulf states and the West backed rebels, and the Islamic State seized the east. Assad survived for 13 years, until a lightning rebel offensive took Damascus on 8 December 2024 and he fled to Moscow.

Across the region, young and fast-growing populations faced unemployment, corruption, rising food prices and police brutality under rulers who had held power for decades. Satellite television and social media let protests spread quickly. In Syria the Assad family's rule rested on the army and security services, many of whose leaders came from its Alawite minority, so the regime fought rather than fell, and the war became a sectarian and international proxy struggle.

dd-syria.q: How did Syria's 2011 uprising turn into civil war?
a: Assad resigned and rival parties fought over power
Assad met peaceful protests with bullets, and the country slid into war
Israel invaded and the army split
The Islamic State began the protests in Damascus
dd-syria.why: Security forces fired on protesters, starting in Daraa; some soldiers deserted to form the Free Syrian Army, and by 2012 it was full civil war.

dd-syria.p: In December 2010 a street vendor in Tunisia set himself on fire after officials confiscated his goods, and protests spread across the Arab world. Within about a year rulers fell in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen. In Bahrain the uprising was crushed with Saudi-led help, and in Syria peaceful protests met gunfire and turned into civil war. Elsewhere kings and presidents offered money or reforms.

Ben Ali, Mubarak, Gaddafi, Saleh

President Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011 after 23 years in power. Tunisia was long the Arab Spring's one democratic success, until President Kais Saied took sweeping powers in 2021.

Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011. The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the 2012 election, but the army removed him in July 2013, and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi became president.

Uprisings put down or turned to war

President Bashar al-Assad called the protesters foreign-backed terrorists and sent in the army. By 2012 armed rebellion had become full civil war.

Mainly Shia protesters demanded reform from the Sunni monarchy. Gulf troops helped crush the movement, and many activists were jailed.

dd-syria.q: What changed the course of the war in Assad's favour from 2015?
dd-syria.why: Russian air strikes from September 2015 helped Assad retake Aleppo in 2016 and most of the country by 2018.

dd-syria.p:
Rulers survived with reforms, jobs or cash

King Mohammed VI offered a new constitution, approved by referendum in July 2011, that gave parliament and the prime minister more power.

Algeria lifted a 19-year state of emergency and raised spending. Mass protests came later, in 2019, and forced out President Bouteflika.

In March 2011 security forces in the southern town of Daraa arrested and reportedly tortured a group of boys for spraying anti-government slogans on walls. Protests over their treatment spread, and soldiers fired on crowds. Some soldiers deserted rather than shoot, forming the Free Syrian Army. In 2011 an amnesty freed hundreds of jailed Islamist militants, which critics saw as deliberate. The government portrayed the uprising as terrorism, and over time hardline jihadist groups came to dominate the armed opposition. The government used barrel bombs, sieges that starved whole districts, and, according to UN and international investigators, chemical weapons, including sarin at Ghouta in 2013. A former military photographer codenamed 'Caesar' smuggled out tens of thousands of photographs of detainees who died in custody.

Syria became a battlefield for outside powers. Iran saw Assad as a vital ally and the land link to Hezbollah in Lebanon, and sent commanders and militias. Russia's air campaign from September 2015 turned the war, helping Assad retake Aleppo in 2016 and most of the country by 2018. The US first armed some rebels, then focused on destroying the Islamic State, working with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces. Turkey, which sees those Kurdish forces as part of the PKK, sent its own army across the border from 2016. Israel struck Iranian targets hundreds of times. By 2020 the front lines froze, and Syria's economy collapsed under war, sanctions and a drug trade in captagon pills.

dd-syria.h: Syria's war and the outside powers, 2011–2024
dd-syria.p: Syria's war drew in the world. Russia, Iran and Lebanon's Hezbollah fought for Assad. Turkey, the Gulf states and Western countries backed rebel groups, and a US-led coalition bombed the Islamic State. Over half of Syria's 22 million people were driven from their homes; more than 6 million fled abroad, many to Lebanon, Jordan and Turkey, and about a million reached Europe, mostly Germany.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based monitor, counted over 600,000 dead by 2025. In 2022 the UN estimated about 307,000 civilians killed in 2011–2021.

dd-syria.q: What drove protests across the Arab world in 2010–2011?
a: Unemployment, corruption, food prices and police brutality under long-ruling leaders
Anger at falling oil prices in Europe
A call from the United Nations for elections
A war between Tunisia and Egypt
dd-syria.why: Young, fast-growing populations faced joblessness and rising prices under rulers in power for decades, and satellite TV and social media spread the protests quickly.

dd-syria.p:
Air power, troops, militias and money

Russia began air strikes in September 2015, turning the war in Assad's favour. Its bases at Hmeimim and Tartus gave it a foothold on the Mediterranean.

Iran sent Revolutionary Guard officers and organised militias from Lebanon, Iraq, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Syria was its land bridge to Hezbollah.

Weapons, money and air strikes

The US armed some rebels, then from 2014 led a coalition of over 80 countries against the Islamic State, partnering with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).

Saudi Arabia and Qatar funded and armed rival rebel groups, many of them Islamist, especially in 2012–2015.

dd-syria.q: What was Syria's situation in 2026, after Assad's fall?
a: A settled democracy with all refugees home
Ruled again by Assad's family from Moscow
Al-Sharaa's government won sanctions relief, but the future remained uncertain
dd-syria.why: Ahmed al-Sharaa's government won sanctions relief and took over the north-east, but sectarian killings, Israeli troops in the south and ruined cities left much unsettled.

dd-syria.p: Under the nom de guerre Abu Mohammad al-Jolani, Ahmed al-Sharaa fought with al-Qaeda in Iraq, spent years in US detention, and in 2012 founded the Nusra Front, al-Qaeda's Syrian branch. In 2016 he broke with al-Qaeda, and his Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) went on to run Idlib as a strict but more pragmatic administration. In late 2024, with Russia distracted by Ukraine and Hezbollah weakened by war with Israel, HTS-led forces took Aleppo, Hama and Homs in days, and Assad's army melted away. As president, Sharaa swapped fatigues for suits and promised a state for all Syrians. Critics, including many Alawites, Druze and Kurds, doubt that promise, especially after the killings of 2025.

On 27 November 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham swept out of Idlib, and on 8 December Assad fled to Russia. The HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa became interim president. Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar backed the new government, and the United States lifted sanctions in 2025. Sectarian killings shook the coast and Suwayda in 2025. In January 2026 Damascus took Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and the oil fields from the Kurdish-led SDF, while Israel kept troops in the south.

Transitional government under Ahmed al-Sharaa

A March 2025 constitutional declaration set a five-year transition. By mid-2026 UNHCR counted over 1.7 million refugees and nearly 2 million displaced Syrians returned home, but much of the country lay in ruins.

Money, diplomacy and training

Turkey was HTS's main outside patron in Idlib and became the new government's closest ally, helping rebuild its army.

Saudi Arabia hosted Sharaa's first foreign trip in February 2025, paid off some of Syria's World Bank debt with Qatar, and promised investment.

dd-syria.q: Why did Assad's regime fight rather than fall like Egypt's or Tunisia's?
a: It had the support of most Syrian rebels
Western powers protected it from the start
Its army and security chiefs came largely from its Alawite minority
Syria had no army able to remove him
dd-syria.why: Many security chiefs came from the Assad family's Alawite minority, so the regime fought on, and the war became a sectarian and international proxy struggle.

dd-syria.p:
Holds a buffer zone in southern Syria

Israel seized the buffer zone after Assad fell, citing security, and bombed much of Syria's old army. It says it protects the Druze; Damascus calls its presence an occupation.

After Assad's fall, crowds opened prisons such as Sednaya, and families searched for some of the more than 100,000 people missing, by rights groups' counts. In 2025 the US and the EU lifted most sanctions, the UN dropped its sanctions on Sharaa, and Gulf states and Turkey offered aid and investment. In 2025 the World Bank put reconstruction costs at about $216 billion. By mid-2026 the UN refugee agency counted over 1.7 million refugees home from abroad, though millions remained abroad. In January 2026 a decree recognised Kurdish as a national language, and the government took much of the oil-rich north-east from the Kurdish-led SDF, which dissolved into the army in August. US-mediated talks with Israel over its forces in the south had produced no deal by October 2026.

Only Tunisia became a lasting democracy, and in 2021 its president took sweeping powers. Egypt's army returned in 2013, while Libya and Yemen fell into wars. Syria's war killed hundreds of thousands and drove millions abroad, helping fuel Europe's 2015 migrant crisis. Since Assad's fall, Ahmed al-Sharaa's government has won sanctions relief and taken over the Kurdish-run north-east, but sectarian killings, Israeli troops in the south and ruined cities left its future uncertain in 2026.

dd-syria.why: Rebels led by HTS took Damascus; Assad fled to Russia.

dd-humans.p: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa: fossils from Morocco are about 300,000 years old. For most of our history we shared the planet with other humans, Neanderthals in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans further east. Roughly 60,000–50,000 years ago small bands left Africa and spread fast, reaching Australia by at least 50,000 years ago and Europe by 45,000.

steps: Small groups leave Africa through Arabia.

items: Planning, stories and cooperation in large groups.
Hunting and sewn clothing for the cold.

dd-humans.q: Most non-Africans carry DNA from which other human species?

dd-humans.p: By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone. During the last Ice Age people crossed from Siberia into the Americas, reaching Chile by about 14,500 years ago. Then, from about 9500 BC, people in the Middle East, China, New Guinea and the Americas each began to farm.

Our species spread thanks to language, planning, long-distance trade and flexible tools, which let small groups adapt to deserts, rainforests and Arctic cold. Swings in climate opened and closed routes: low Ice Age seas joined Siberia to Alaska and Australia to New Guinea. Farming began as the climate warmed and steadied after about 10,000 BC, when wild cereals were plentiful and growing populations had fewer new lands to move into.

dd-humans.q: Where did our species, Homo sapiens, evolve?
a: In Africa, with the oldest fossils in Morocco
dd-humans.why: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa; fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are about 300,000 years old, and small bands later spread out across the world.

dd-humans.h: Who lived where, c. 100,000–50,000 years ago
dd-humans.p: Our species, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa: the oldest known fossils, about 300,000 years old, come from Morocco. We were not alone. Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia, from Spain to Uzbekistan and as far as Siberia, and their cousins the Denisovans across eastern Asia, from Siberia in Russia to China. On the island of Flores, in Indonesia, lived the tiny Homo floresiensis.

Our own species, across Africa

Ethiopia has some of the oldest Homo sapiens fossils, from Omo Kibish and Herto, and much older human ancestors, such as 'Lucy', about 3.2 million years old.

Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, dated to about 300,000 years ago, showed in 2017 that Homo sapiens was older, and more widespread in Africa, than once thought.

Europe and western Asia, c. 400,000–40,000 years ago

Neanderthals lived in Iberia until about 40,000 years ago or a little later. Gibraltar, at its southern tip, was one of their last known homes.

France has many Neanderthal sites, including burials such as La Chapelle-aux-Saints. Whether Neanderthals buried their dead on purpose is still debated, though most experts now think some did.

dd-humans.q: What did farming change for human societies?
a: It made early farmers taller and healthier
It ended disease by moving people away from animals
It kept populations small and stable
It fed many more people, leading to towns, cities and kings
dd-humans.why: Fields fed far more people than foraging; stored surplus could be taxed and fought over, opening the way to towns, cities, inequality and states.

dd-humans.p:
Known mostly from DNA and a handful of bones

Denisova Cave, in the Altai mountains, held both Neanderthals and Denisovans. One girl from there, 'Denny', had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.

A skull found in Harbin in 1933 was identified in 2025, from ancient proteins and DNA, as Denisovan. A Denisovan jaw was also found high on the Tibetan Plateau.

Neanderthals were not the brutish cavemen of old cartoons. They had brains as large as ours, made fine stone tools, controlled fire, hunted mammoths and bison, wore ochre and eagle talons, and cared for their sick. When modern humans arrived they met, and sometimes had children together: most people of non-African descent carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, and Papuans also carry about 4% from Denisovans. Some of these genes still matter, affecting immunity, skin and, in Tibetans, a Denisovan gene that helps with life at high altitude. Why Neanderthals vanished about 40,000 years ago is debated: competition, small and inbred populations, climate swings and absorption into our own species probably all played a part.

Long before writing, people made art. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone engraved a block of red ochre with criss-cross lines about 75,000 years ago. The oldest dated rock art is a hand stencil on Muna, an island off Sulawesi in Indonesia, at least 67,800 years old; its fingertips appear to have been reshaped to look like claws. In Europe, painters filled Chauvet Cave in France with lions, rhinos and horses about 36,000 years ago, and Lascaux about 17,000 years ago. Carved ivory figures, bone flutes and shell beads show people who sang, decorated themselves and traded over hundreds of kilometres. What the images meant to their makers remains a mystery.

dd-humans.h: Peopling the world, c. 70,000–15,000 years ago
dd-humans.p: Small groups of Homo sapiens had left Africa before, but the great spread began roughly 60,000–50,000 years ago. People followed coasts across Asia and crossed open sea to reach Australia by at least 50,000 years ago. They entered Europe by about 45,000 years ago. During the last Ice Age, sea levels were lower, and people walked from Siberia into Alaska, then down to Chile by about 14,500 years ago.

Southern Asia earlier, Siberia and Japan later

Islands such as Sulawesi were stepping stones to Australia. A hand stencil on Muna, off Sulawesi, is at least 67,800 years old.

Modern humans passed through South Asia on the coastal route. Stone tools from Jwalapuram, buried by a huge eruption 74,000 years ago, may be theirs or another species'.

dd-humans.q: What helped modern humans spread into so many different environments?
a: Farming, which they took with them from Africa
Language, planning, trade and flexible tools
Horses that let them travel fast
dd-humans.why: Language, planning, long-distance trade and adaptable tools let small groups cope with deserts, rainforests and Arctic cold.

dd-humans.h: Australia and New Guinea, by c. 50,000 years ago
dd-humans.p:
One landmass, called Sahul, when seas were low

People reached Australia by at least 50,000 years ago, and some researchers argue 65,000, crossing open sea from Indonesia. Aboriginal Australians have one of the longest continuous cultures on Earth.

New Guinea was joined to Australia when seas were low. Papuans carry about 4% Denisovan DNA, among the highest shares of any living people, though the Ayta Magbukon of the Philippines carry more.

Farming did not make life easier at first. Skeletons show that early farmers were often shorter than the hunter-gatherers before them, with worn joints from grinding grain, more tooth decay and signs of malnutrition, because they relied on a few crops. Living close together and beside their animals, they caught new diseases; measles and smallpox, for example, are thought to have evolved from animal infections over the following millennia. But a field fed many more mouths than the wild, so farming populations boomed. Surplus grain could be stored, taxed and fought over, and that opened the way to property, inequality, warfare and, eventually, kings and states.

dd-humans.q: What link to the Neanderthals do most people outside Africa carry today?
a: Half of their genes come from Neanderthals
dd-humans.why: Modern humans and Neanderthals sometimes had children together, so most people of non-African descent carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA.

dd-humans.p: As the Ice Age ended, people in several places tamed wild plants and animals, each on their own. Wheat, barley, sheep and goats came first, about 9500 BC, in the Fertile Crescent, from Turkey to Iraq. Rice and millet followed in China, taro and bananas in Papua New Guinea, maize and squash in Mexico, and potatoes and llamas in the Andes of Peru.

Wheat, barley, peas, lentils; sheep, goats, cattle, pigs

Goats were domesticated in the Zagros mountains of Iraq and Iran around 8000 BC. Farming later spread into the dry plains, where irrigation fed the first cities.

At Abu Hureyra on the Euphrates, hunter-gatherers became farmers over a few thousand years. Their bones show the strain of grinding grain all day.

Millet in the north, rice in the south

Foxtail and broomcorn millet were domesticated in the Yellow River valley, and rice along the Yangtze, from about 8000 BC. Pigs and later silkworms followed.

dd-humans.q: How did Ice Age conditions help people reach the Americas?
a: Low sea levels joined Siberia to Alaska
Warm seas let them sail across the Atlantic
Ice sheets made a bridge from Europe
Glaciers carved a canal through Canada
dd-humans.why: Low Ice Age seas exposed land between Siberia and Alaska, and people moved south, reaching Chile by about 14,500 years ago.

dd-humans.p:
Taro, bananas, sugar cane

New Guinea's highlanders invented farming on their own, one of the clearest independent centres. Kuk Swamp is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Much of this story was rewritten in the last 20 years by ancient DNA. In 2010 the Swedish geneticist Svante Pääbo and his team published a draft Neanderthal genome, proving that our ancestors had interbred with them. The same year, DNA from a single finger bone in Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed the Denisovans, a human group nobody had known existed. Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for this work. Proteins, which survive longer than DNA, have since identified Denisovan fossils in China and off Taiwan. New dating methods keep pushing dates back, so every figure in this chapter may change.

Farming fed far more people per square kilometre than hunting and gathering, so farmers multiplied and spread, pushing aside or absorbing foragers on most continents. Villages grew into towns and, by about 3500 BC, into the first cities, with kings, priests and writing. Every person alive today descends from those early Africans, and most people outside Africa still carry a little Neanderthal DNA.

All humans alive today share recent African ancestry and are genetically very similar: there is more variety inside Africa than between other continents. Farming, about 12,000 years ago, began the shift to villages, cities and states.

dd-languages.p: Around 4000–3000 BC herders on the steppes north of the Black Sea probably spoke the ancestor of the Indo-European languages, which their descendants carried across Europe and into Iran and India. Other families spread too: Bantu languages with farmers across central and southern Africa, Austronesian languages by canoe from Taiwan to Madagascar and Hawaii.

dd-languages.q: English and Hindi belong to which family?
dd-languages.why: They share an ancestor spoken about 6,000 years ago.

dd-languages.p: Later, empires and religions made a few languages dominant: Latin, then Arabic after 632, then from 1492 Spanish, Portuguese, English and French. Today about 7,000 languages survive, but just a few dozen are spoken by most people, and many small ones are disappearing.

Languages spread when their speakers grow in number or power. Farming and herding let populations expand into new land; conquerors, traders and missionaries brought their languages with them; and people switched to the language of jobs, schools, religion and government. Nation-states from the 1800s promoted one standard language, and modern media and cities speed the shift to big languages.

dd-languages.q: Who probably spoke the ancestor of the Indo-European languages?
a: Herders on the steppes north of the Black Sea
Traders in the ports of Phoenicia
dd-languages.why: Most scholars, backed by ancient DNA, place its speakers on the steppe around 4000–3000 BC; their descendants carried related languages across Europe and into Iran and India.

dd-languages.p: Most scholars think the ancestor of English, Hindi, Persian and Russian was spoken around 4000–3000 BC on the steppes of today's Ukraine and southern Russia, by herders who used horses and wagons. Their descendants carried related languages west into Europe and south-east to Iran and India. By 500 BC they were spoken from Ireland to the Ganges valley. Today almost half the world speaks one.

The Pontic-Caspian steppe, c. 4000–3000 BC

The leading theory places the Indo-European homeland on the steppe north of the Black Sea. Herders of the Yamnaya culture, c. 3300–2600 BC, are widely linked to the spread.

The southern Russian steppe, between the Volga and the Don, is part of the most widely accepted homeland. Ancient DNA shows steppe herders moved west into Europe around 3000–2500 BC.

Greek, Italic, Celtic, Germanic, Baltic, Slavic and others

Greek is the European branch with the longest written record, from Linear B tablets of about 1400 BC.

Celtic languages, including Irish, reached Ireland and Britain by the first millennium BC.

dd-languages.q: What does today's world language map still show?
a: That most countries speak their ancient languages unchanged
That languages spread evenly across continents
That Mandarin is spoken on every continent
Old migrations and empires, such as Spanish in Latin America
dd-languages.why: Spanish and Portuguese in Latin America, English and French across Africa, and Arabic from Morocco to Iraq trace earlier conquests and empires.

dd-languages.p:
Hittite and its relatives, the first written, c. 1900–1200 BC

The Hittites of central Anatolia wrote the first known Indo-European texts. Their branch died out, and Turkish, which arrived much later, belongs to a different family.

dd-languages.h: How we know languages are related
dd-languages.p: In 1786 William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, noticed that Sanskrit was strikingly similar to Greek and Latin and suggested they had 'sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists'. Linguists then found regular sound patterns linking words across languages: English father, Latin pater and Sanskrit pitṛ; English mother, Latin mater and Sanskrit mātṛ. Using such patterns they reconstructed parts of the lost parent language, Proto-Indo-European, including words for wheels and horses. Most scholars, backed since 2015 by ancient DNA, place its speakers on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, though some argue for earlier roots south of the Caucasus or in Anatolia.

A language rarely spreads because it is easier or better; it spreads because its speakers have power, wealth or numbers. Latin replaced Celtic tongues in Gaul and Spain under Roman rule and became French, Spanish, Portuguese and Italian. Arabic became the everyday language of North Africa and the Middle East over centuries after the Islamic conquests, while Persia kept Persian. Trade created common languages, or lingua francas, such as Swahili on the East African coast and Malay in Southeast Asian ports. In the 1800s and 1900s national schools, armies and radio pushed regional languages, from Breton in France to Indigenous languages in the Americas, toward the national standard.

Conquest, trade and religion spread a few languages across continents. Arabic moved out of Arabia with Islam after 632. From 1492 Spain and Portugal took their languages to the Americas and beyond, and Britain and France planted English and French on every continent. Darker colours show where it became most people's mother tongue, lighter colours where it is an official or main second language.

Spread with the Islamic conquests from 632

Arabic spread from Arabia with the Islamic conquests after 632. It replaced Aramaic, Coptic and Berber languages as the everyday tongue from Iraq to Morocco over several centuries.

Egyptians gradually switched from Coptic, the last stage of ancient Egyptian, to Arabic. Coptic survives only in church services.

dd-languages.q: Why does a language usually spread?
a: Because it is easier to learn than others
Because its speakers grow in number or power
dd-languages.why: A language rarely spreads because it is better; farming, conquest, trade and religion spread their speakers' tongues, and people switch to the language of jobs and government.

dd-languages.p:
From 1492

Spanish, or Castilian, spread across Spain during the Reconquista and to the Americas after 1492. Today it has about 500 million native speakers, second only to Mandarin.

Mexico has the most Spanish speakers of any country, about 130 million, though it still has 68 recognised Indigenous languages, such as Nahuatl and Maya.

From the 1400s

Portuguese colonisers and settlers made Brazil the world's largest Portuguese-speaking country, with over 200 million people.

Portuguese is Angola's official language and, especially in cities, increasingly the first language of young people.

dd-languages.q: What do revivals such as Hebrew and Māori show about endangered languages?
a: Only languages with alphabets can survive
Revived languages stay in prayer and study only
Endangered languages always die within a generation
dd-languages.why: About two in five languages are endangered, but Hebrew became an everyday tongue again, and Māori language nests brought new young speakers.

dd-languages.p: In 1600 English was spoken by perhaps 5 million people, almost all in Britain. British colonisation, then the economic and cultural power of the United States after 1945, made it the most widely spoken language on Earth, with about 1.5 billion speakers, most of whom learned it as a second language. It is the main language of science, aviation and the internet. Mandarin still has the most native speakers, about a billion, and Spanish, Hindi and Arabic each have hundreds of millions. Many linguists expect English to remain the main global language, though machine translation may reduce the need to learn it.

Ethnologue counts about 7,100–7,200 living languages, but most have few speakers and roughly two in five are endangered. About half are spoken in Asia and the Pacific, with over 800 in Papua New Guinea alone. Mandarin in China has the most native speakers, about a billion. Some languages have been brought back: Hebrew in Israel was revived as an everyday tongue, while most Indigenous languages of Australia are at risk.

The four countries with over 400 living languages each

Papua New Guinea has over 800 living languages, more than any other country, for about 10 million people. Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, is the common language.

Indonesia has about 700 languages. Indonesian, based on Malay, was chosen as the national language in 1928 and now unites the country.

Main examples

Hebrew was mainly a written and religious language for nearly 2,000 years. Revived as an everyday tongue from the 1880s, it is now the first language of millions of Israelis.

By the 1970s few young people spoke Māori. Language 'nests' for preschoolers began in 1982, and Māori became an official language in 1987.

dd-languages.q: What did nation-states from the 1800s do to languages within their borders?
a: Promoted one standard language, pushing regional ones aside
Gave every regional language official status
Banned the teaching of foreign languages
dd-languages.why: National schools, armies and radio pushed regional and Indigenous languages, from Breton in France to those of the Americas, toward the national standard.

dd-languages.p:
Most native languages endangered; main examples

Over 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken when Europeans arrived in 1788. About 120 are still spoken, but only about 12 are still learned by children as a first language.

Hundreds of Native American languages were spoken before European contact. Most surviving ones are endangered, after generations of boarding schools that punished children for speaking them.

When parents stop passing a language to their children, it can vanish within a few generations. Most endangered languages are Indigenous ones pushed aside by colonisation, boarding schools and the pull of bigger languages: in Australia only about 12 of over 250 original languages are still learned by children. Yet revivals happen. Hebrew, used for nearly 2,000 years mainly in prayer and study, became the everyday language of millions of Israelis within a century. Māori 'language nests' from 1982 and Welsh-medium schools have brought new young speakers, and communities now record elders and teach languages online.

The world's language map still traces old migrations and empires: Spanish and Portuguese in Latin America, English and French across Africa, Arabic from Morocco to Iraq. English became the global language of science, business and the internet. Linguists estimate that roughly two in five languages are endangered, mostly Indigenous languages with few young speakers, though revivals such as Hebrew and Māori show decline can be reversed.

dd-languages.s: About half of the world’s 7,000 languages may vanish by 2100.
dd-languages.why: Most have only a few thousand speakers.

dd-writing.p: Around 3300–3000 BC scribes in the cities of Mesopotamia began pressing signs into clay to keep track of grain, animals and workers. Egypt developed hieroglyphs at about the same time, China wrote on oracle bones by about 1250 BC, and Mesoamerican peoples created their own scripts centuries later. Sometime around 1900–1500 BC Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt invented a much simpler idea, the alphabet, with one sign per sound.

dd-writing.h: Writing was invented at least four times
items: Oracle bones; still in use as Chinese characters.

steps: A drawing of an ox means "ox".
Phoenicians use 22 letters for consonants, c. 1050 BC.
Greeks add vowels; Romans pass on the Latin alphabet.

dd-writing.q: Which people spread the first widely used alphabet?
dd-writing.why: Ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

dd-writing.p: Phoenician traders spread it, the Greeks added vowels and the Romans passed it to Europe. China invented paper and printing, and Gutenberg's press of the 1450s made books cheap in Europe. Today most adults in the world can read.

dd-writing.q: What were the first Mesopotamian scribes mostly writing down?
a: Accounts of grain, animals and workers
dd-writing.why: Writing began as bookkeeping: most early tablets from Uruk list rations, sheep, beer and workers; literature came much later.

dd-writing.p: Writing began as bookkeeping. As cities, temples and kings collected taxes and traded goods, they needed records that outlasted memory. Pictures for things slowly became signs for sounds, which let scribes write names, laws and stories. The alphabet spread because a few dozen letters were far easier to learn than hundreds of signs, and traders, empires and religions carried it with them.

Writing was invented independently at least three times. In Mesopotamia scribes pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform into clay from about 3300–3000 BC, and Egypt had hieroglyphs almost as early. In China characters appear on oracle bones by about 1250 BC, and in Mexico and Guatemala the Zapotec, Maya and their neighbours created scripts from about 600–300 BC. The script of the Indus valley, in Pakistan, is still unread.

dd-writing.q: What did printing and mass schooling change about reading?
a: Reading moved from a small elite to most adults
It ended the use of the alphabet
It kept reading for scribes and priests
dd-writing.why: For thousands of years reading belonged to scribes and priests; in 1820 one adult in eight could read, and today about 88% can.

dd-writing.p:
Mesopotamia from c. 3300 BC, later used across the Near East

Sumerian scribes first used pictures for accounts, then wedge-shaped signs for sounds and words. Cuneiform was used for about 3,000 years, for laws, letters and the Epic of Gilgamesh.

Cuneiform was written across Syria. At Ugarit, around 1400 BC, scribes even used a short cuneiform alphabet of 30 signs.

Egypt from c. 3200 BC

Egyptian hieroglyphs mixed pictures for words with signs for sounds. Scribes also used faster cursive scripts, hieratic and later demotic, for everyday writing.

The kingdom of Kush, in today's Sudan, used hieroglyphs and then its own Meroitic script, which can be read aloud but is still largely not understood.

c. 2600–1900 BC, still undeciphered

The Indus civilisation left over 4,000 short inscriptions, mostly on seals. Whether the signs record a language is still debated.

Indus cities such as Dholavira and Lothal lay in today's India. After the Indus script vanished, India seems to have had no writing until Brahmi appeared in the 200s BC.

The first writing was not poetry but paperwork. Most early tablets from Uruk list rations, sheep, beer and workers, with numbers and signs for things. Some scholars think clay tokens used for counting goods led to the idea. Only over centuries did scribes learn to write full sentences, and literature such as the Epic of Gilgamesh came much later. Learning cuneiform took years in a 'tablet house', where boys, and a few girls, copied signs and model texts. Many tablets survive only because clay hardens in fire: when enemies burned palace libraries, such as Ashurbanipal's at Nineveh, they baked thousands of texts for us to read.

Around 1900–1500 BC, Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai borrowed a few hieroglyphs to write single sounds: the first alphabet. Phoenician traders from Lebanon carried their version around the Mediterranean. The Greeks added vowels, the Romans in Italy adapted it, and Aramaic letters gave rise to Hebrew and Arabic. In the late 800s Slavic churchmen in Bulgaria shaped the script now called Cyrillic.

Proto-Sinaitic c. 1900–1500 BC, Phoenician c. 1050 BC

The Phoenician cities of Byblos, Tyre and Sidon used 22 letters, all consonants. Their trade spread the alphabet from Cyprus to Spain.

Hebrew was first written in a Phoenician-style script. After about 500 BC Jews adopted the Aramaic 'square' letters still used for Hebrew today.

dd-writing.q: Why did early cities and kings need writing?
a: To collect taxes and trade with records that outlasted memory
To teach every child to read
To print holy books for the public
dd-writing.why: As cities, temples and kings collected taxes and traded goods, they needed records that would outlast human memory.

dd-writing.p:
Vowels added c. 800 BC

The Greeks adapted Phoenician letters around 800 BC and turned some unneeded consonants into vowels, making the first full alphabet. Alpha and beta gave the alphabet its name.

Cyprus, where Phoenician and Greek settlers lived side by side, was one of the likely places where Greeks learned the alphabet.

Roman letters, via the Etruscans, from c. 600s BC

The Etruscans borrowed Greek letters, and the Romans took them from the Etruscans. The Roman Empire then carried the Latin alphabet across western Europe.

dd-writing.q: What do the world's scripts today still trace?
a: The order in which languages were invented
dd-writing.why: Latin letters spread with European empires, Arabic script with Islam and Cyrillic with Slavic churchmen and later the Soviet Union.

dd-writing.p: Many scripts were forgotten and had to be decoded. The Rosetta Stone, found by French soldiers in Egypt in 1799, repeated one decree in Greek and Egyptian, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion used it to show that hieroglyphs mixed signs for sounds and ideas. Cuneiform was cracked in the mid-1800s with the help of a three-language royal inscription at Behistun in Iran. In 1952 Michael Ventris showed that Linear B from Crete recorded an early form of Greek, and from the 1950s Yuri Knorozov and others unlocked Maya glyphs. The Indus script and Easter Island's rongorongo remain unread.

Today the Latin alphabet is the most widely used script, carried abroad by European empires and adopted by countries such as Turkey and Vietnam. Cyrillic is used in Russia and its neighbours, Arabic script from Morocco to Pakistan, and Chinese characters in China and, with kana, Japan. Most scripts of India and Southeast Asia descend from Brahmi. Korea, Greece and Israel keep scripts of their own.

Main script of most countries

Somali got an official Latin alphabet only in 1972. Before that, Arabic and other scripts had been tried.

Uzbekistan officially moved from Cyrillic to Latin letters in 1993, though Cyrillic is still widely seen. Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan also switched.

Russia, Slavic and Central Asian neighbours, Mongolia

Russia uses a Cyrillic alphabet reformed by Peter the Great in 1708 and again in 1918. The Soviet Union spread Cyrillic to many languages of Central Asia and Siberia.

Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters. Cyrillic is the official script, but Latin is common in daily life.

dd-writing.q: Why did the alphabet spread so widely?
a: It was invented by the Roman emperors
It used pictures that everyone recognised
A few dozen letters were far easier to learn than hundreds of signs
It was the only script that could be carved
dd-writing.why: One sign per sound meant a few dozen letters; Phoenician traders, then Greeks, Romans, empires and religions carried it far.

dd-writing.p:
Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Pashto and others

Persian uses the Arabic script with four added letters for sounds that Arabic lacks.

Urdu, Pakistan's national language, is written in an elegant hanging Arabic style called Nastaliq.

China invented paper by the 100s BC and woodblock printing by the 700s; the oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, dates from 868. Bi Sheng made movable clay type in the 1040s, and Korea printed a book with metal type, the Jikji, in 1377. In Europe, Gutenberg's press of about 1455 had far fewer letters to manage, and by 1500 presses in over 200 towns had turned out millions of books, helping spread the Reformation and science. In 1820 only about one adult in eight in the world could read; mass schooling, and now phones, changed that.

Writing made history possible: laws, contracts, holy books, science and literature could be kept and shared across centuries. For thousands of years reading belonged to a small elite of scribes and priests, but printing and then mass schooling changed that. Today about 88% of adults can read, according to UNESCO, though some 740 million still cannot. The scripts on the map still trace old empires and faiths.

dd-money.p: Money began as a way of keeping accounts: by about 3000 BC Mesopotamian temples recorded debts in barley and silver weighed in shekels. Around 630 BC the kingdom of Lydia stamped the first coins, and coins soon spread across Greece, Persia, India and China. China's Song dynasty issued the first government paper money in the 1020s.

steps: Swapping goods: hard without a "double coincidence of wants".
Lydia, c. 600 BC: standard weight, stamped by a king.
China, c. 1000: notes backed by trust.
Today most money is just numbers in banks.

a: A general rise in prices, so money buys less
A rise in the stock market
dd-money.why: Central banks aim for about 2% a year.

dd-money.p: Italian, then Dutch and English, bankers built modern banking, shares and national debts, while American silver became the first global currency. In the 1800s most major currencies were tied to gold, but in 1971 the last link was cut. Today almost all money is digital, and its value rests on trust in the governments and central banks that issue it.

dd-money.q: What is today's money mostly, and what gives it value?
a: Gold coins, valued by their weight
Paper notes, each backed by silver
Digital money, valued through trust in governments and central banks
Cryptocurrency, valued by the cost of mining it
dd-money.why: Almost all money is now digital, numbers in bank accounts, and its value rests on trust in the governments and central banks that issue it.

dd-money.p: Money solves practical problems. It lets people compare the value of very different things, store wealth and settle debts with strangers. Rulers had their own reasons: coins and paper money made it easier to pay soldiers and collect taxes, and the right to issue money was a source of profit and power. Each new form, from coins to banknotes to cards and phones, spread because it made trade cheaper, faster or safer.

In Mesopotamia, from about 3000 BC, temples and palaces kept accounts in barley and in silver weighed in shekels. The first coins, stamped lumps of electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, appeared in Lydia in western Turkey around 630–600 BC and spread to Greece and Persia. India and China developed their own metal coins at about the same time, apparently independently.

dd-money.q: What happened when governments printed far too much paper money?
a: Prices fell and goods became cheaper
Banks closed and switched to barter
Trust collapsed, and prices soared, as in Germany in 1923
dd-money.why: A note is worth something only if people trust others will accept it; in 1923 a dollar cost about 4.2 trillion marks.

dd-money.p:
Mesopotamia, from c. 3000 BC

Mesopotamians used silver, weighed out in shekels of about 8 grams, to value goods and settle debts, and barley to pay wages. Loans with interest were common.

Northern Syria was part of the same trading world, and hoards of cut silver pieces, valued by weight, have been found across the Levant.

Lydia c. 630 BC, then Greece and Persia

Greek cities took up coins quickly, and by 500 BC there were hundreds of local mints. Coins helped pay soldiers, rowers and public works.

Lydia's kings, at Sardis, issued the first known coins around 630–600 BC. The earliest found were buried at the temple of Artemis at Ephesus.

India, from c. 500 BC

Silver 'punch-marked' coins, stamped with symbols such as suns and animals, circulated in the Ganges kingdoms by about the 5th century BC.

Textbooks long taught that before money people bartered, swapping a cow for some shoes, until money was invented to make trade easier. Anthropologists have found little evidence of any society that ran mainly on barter. In small communities people more often gave and owed, keeping track of favours and debts, and barter mostly happened between strangers. Money also took many surprising forms. Cowrie shells served as money from China to West Africa. On the Pacific island of Yap, giant stone discs called rai, some taller than a person, were quarried on Palau and changed owners without being moved: everyone simply knew who owned which stone.

China's Song dynasty issued the first government paper money in the 1020s. In Italy, bankers in Florence, Venice and Genoa spread bills of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping. From 1545 silver from Potosí, in Bolivia, and from Mexico flooded the world as Spanish 'pieces of eight', and much of it ended up in China. The Netherlands and England then built public banks, stock markets and national debts.

Paper money from the 1020s

Paper money spread under the Song and Mongol Yuan, and Marco Polo marvelled at it. Over-printing caused inflation, and the Ming dynasty largely gave up paper notes by the 1400s, turning to silver.

dd-money.q: What practical problem does money solve for ordinary people?
a: It removes the need for any debts
It lets them compare values, store wealth and settle debts with strangers
It guarantees that prices never rise
It replaces the need for trade
dd-money.why: Money lets people compare the value of very different things, store wealth and settle debts with strangers.

dd-money.p:
Banking and bookkeeping, 1200s–1400s

Italian merchant bankers moved money across Europe with bills of exchange instead of chests of coins. Luca Pacioli described double-entry bookkeeping in print in 1494.

Mines in the Americas, coins minted for the world

Spain minted American silver into the 'piece of eight', or Spanish dollar, which became the first global currency, used from the Americas to China.

Potosí's silver mountain, the Cerro Rico, produced vast amounts of silver from 1545. The mines were worked largely by Indigenous people forced to serve under the mita labour draft.

dd-money.q: What does the dollar's role as the world's main currency give the United States?
a: A link between its money and gold
dd-money.why: The dollar is over half of world reserves and on one side of almost 90% of currency trades, giving the US unusual financial power.

dd-money.p: A banknote is worth something only because people trust that others will accept it. Marco Polo, visiting Kublai Khan's China in the late 1200s, was amazed that people traded gold and pearls for printed paper. When governments print too much, that trust collapses. In Germany in November 1923 a US dollar cost about 4.2 trillion marks, and people were paid twice a day to spend wages before prices rose. In Hungary in 1946 prices doubled roughly every 15 hours, the worst inflation on record, and in 2009 Zimbabwe issued a 100 trillion dollar note. Most central banks today aim for steady inflation of about 2% a year.

Most money is now numbers in bank accounts, backed by trust in governments rather than gold. The US dollar is the world's main currency, used in most foreign-exchange trades and adopted by countries such as Ecuador. Twenty-one EU countries share the euro, Bulgaria the newest in 2026. Phone payments boomed, from Kenya's M-Pesa to India's UPI and Brazil's Pix.

The US, its territories and countries that adopted it

The dollar makes up over half of the world's foreign-exchange reserves and is on one side of almost 90% of currency trades. In 1971 President Nixon ended its link to gold.

Ecuador replaced its sucre with the US dollar in 2000, after a banking crisis and runaway inflation.

21 EU members, plus a few small states and neighbours

Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, becoming the euro area's 21st member.

Germany gave up the Deutschmark for the euro. Euro notes and coins replaced national money in 12 countries on 1 January 2002.

dd-money.q: Why did rulers want to issue coins and paper money?
a: To pay soldiers and collect taxes more easily, and for profit and power
To stop merchants from trading abroad
To replace barter, which every society relied on
Because banks refused to lend to them
dd-money.why: Coins and notes made it easier to pay soldiers and collect taxes, and the right to issue money brought rulers profit and power.

dd-money.p:
Where mobile payments took over everyday spending

M-Pesa, launched in 2007, let Kenyans send money by text message on basic phones. It is now used by most adults in the country.

India's UPI, launched in 2016, lets people pay instantly by scanning a QR code. It handled about 24.5 billion payments in August 2026 alone.

dd-money.h: The rise and fall of gold
dd-money.p: Britain tied the pound to gold in the early 1800s, and by the 1870s Germany, France, the United States and others had followed. Under this gold standard, notes could be swapped for a fixed weight of gold, which kept prices stable but limited how much money could be created. It broke down during the First World War and the Great Depression, when countries that left gold early recovered faster. In 1944, at Bretton Woods, the Allies tied their currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce. As dollars piled up abroad, President Nixon ended that link on 15 August 1971, and paper money has floated on trust ever since.

Money shaped the modern world. Banks, stock markets and cheap government borrowing helped the Dutch and British build trading empires and fund industrial growth. Central banks now steer whole economies by setting interest rates, and their mistakes can bring inflation or depression. The US dollar's role as the world's main currency gives the United States unusual financial power, and new digital forms, from phone payments to cryptocurrencies, are changing how billions of people pay.
