c. 630 BC
Lydia, in today's Turkey, strikes the first coins
Song China issues the first government paper money
The Bank of England is founded to fund war with France
President Nixon ends the dollar's link to gold
Bitcoin, the first cryptocurrency, is launched

dd-democracy.p: Around 508 BC Athens let its male citizens vote directly on laws, and Rome ran a republic with elected officials until its emperors took over. After centuries of kings, assemblies such as Iceland's Althing and England's Parliament slowly limited royal power.

items: Leaders are not above the law.
The majority can’t do anything it likes.

dd-democracy.q: Which was the first country where women won the vote nationally?

dd-democracy.p: The American and French revolutions of 1776 and 1789 declared that power comes from the people, and over the next 150 years the vote spread from men of property to all men and then to women. Democracy collapsed across much of Europe in the 1920s and 1930s, then spread in waves after 1945 and again after 1974, reaching most of the world by 2000.

Rulers who needed taxes and soldiers had to bargain with the people who paid and fought, and assemblies grew out of that bargain. Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke argued that government needs the consent of the governed. Printing, trade, cities and mass schooling created citizens who demanded a say, and workers, women and colonised peoples campaigned for decades to win it. Wars, economic crises and coups explain the retreats.

dd-democracy.q: What was new about Athens around 508 BC?
a: Its king shared power with a Senate
Its male citizens voted directly on laws
All its residents, including women and slaves, could vote
It elected representatives to a parliament
dd-democracy.why: Athens became the first known democracy: adult male citizens voted directly in the Assembly, while women, slaves and foreigners had no say.

dd-democracy.p: Around 508 BC the city of Athens in Greece gave its male citizens the power to vote on laws: the first known democracy. Rome ran a republic with elected officials for nearly 500 years. In 930 Iceland founded the Althing, an assembly of free men. In England, Magna Carta in 1215 put the king under the law, and in 1689 Parliament won lasting power over the Crown.

Democracy from about 508 to 322 BC

Athens was a democracy for most of the years 508–322 BC. Adult male citizens voted directly, but women, slaves and foreigners, the majority of residents, had no say.

509–27 BC: elected officials and a Senate

Rome's Republic elected two consuls each year and had a powerful Senate, but the rich dominated it. It ended when Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC.

dd-democracy.q: How did the vote change between the late 1700s and the mid-1900s?
a: It narrowed to men of property
It passed from parliaments to kings
It spread from men of property to all men, then women
dd-democracy.why: After campaigns by workers and women, the vote widened; New Zealand let women vote nationally first, in 1893.

dd-democracy.p:
An assembly of free men from AD 930

Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, made laws and settled disputes for the whole island. It is often called the world's oldest surviving parliament.

Athenian democracy was direct: there were no elected representatives in the modern sense. Adult male citizens, perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 men, could attend the Assembly on the Pnyx hill, about 40 times a year, and vote by show of hands on laws, taxes and war. A Council of 500, chosen by lot each year, prepared its business, and most officials were also picked by lottery, since Athenians thought elections favoured the rich. Juries of hundreds of citizens decided court cases. Once a year citizens could vote to exile a powerful politician for ten years by scratching his name on pottery shards, called ostracism. Women, slaves and foreign residents, the majority of people, could not vote.

Magna Carta is often hailed as the birth of English liberty, but in 1215 it was a peace deal between King John and rebel barons, mostly about their own rights and taxes. It failed: within weeks the Pope annulled it at John's request, and civil war resumed. Reissued in revised form in 1216, 1217 and 1225, it became a symbol. Its most famous clause promised that no free man would be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land. Centuries later, English lawyers and American revolutionaries cited it against royal power. Only three of its clauses are still law in England and Wales.

The American Revolution of 1776 and the French Revolution of 1789 spread the idea that power comes from the people. At first, though, the vote went mostly to men, often only those with property. Women won it first in New Zealand in 1893, then Australia, Finland and Norway. After World War I a wave followed, including Britain, Germany and the United States.

The first countries to give women the national vote

In 1893 New Zealand gave women, including Māori women, the vote after a petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures.

Australian women won the federal vote in 1902, but most Aboriginal people were shut out of it until 1962.

dd-democracy.q: How did assemblies such as Parliament come to limit kings?
a: Rulers needing taxes and soldiers bargained with those who paid and fought
Kings gave up power after reading Locke
The Pope ordered kings to share power
dd-democracy.why: Assemblies grew out of the bargain between rulers needing taxes and soldiers and the people who paid and fought, slowly limiting royal power.

dd-democracy.p:
Main examples, some at first with age or other limits

Russia's Provisional Government gave women the vote in 1917, but the Bolsheviks soon dissolved the elected assembly and ruled as a single party.

Most Canadian women won the federal vote in 1918, but many people of Asian origin and First Nations people were excluded for decades longer.

In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to let women vote, after a petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures. Finland went further in 1906, letting women stand for parliament, and elected 19 of them the next year. In Britain the suffragettes of Emmeline Pankhurst smashed windows and went on hunger strike; women over 30 won the vote in 1918. American women won it through the 19th Amendment in 1920, French women in 1944, and Swiss women in national elections only in 1971. Saudi Arabian women first voted, in local elections, in 2015.

dd-democracy.q: What has happened to democracy worldwide since about 2010?
a: It has declined in many countries, and autocracies again outnumber democracies
Every country has become a liberal democracy
Elections have been abolished almost everywhere
It has spread faster than ever before
dd-democracy.why: By V-Dem's count, at the end of 2025 there were 92 autocracies and 87 democracies; yet voters still remove governments peacefully, as in Hungary in 2026.

dd-democracy.p: The V-Dem Institute in Sweden rates every country each year. By its count, at the end of 2025 there were 87 democracies and 92 autocracies, and about three in four people lived under autocratic rule. India, the world's largest electorate, is rated an electoral autocracy, and the United States lost its long-held rating as a liberal democracy. Taiwan and South Korea are rated liberal democracies.

Free elections plus strong rights and rule of law

Denmark is regularly rated among the world's strongest democracies, along with its Nordic neighbours.

South Korea moved from military rule to democracy in 1987. In 2024–25 its courts and parliament removed a president who had declared martial law.

Free and fair elections, weaker protections

Brazil returned to democracy in 1985 after 21 years of military rule. In 2025 its supreme court convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro of plotting a coup.

South Africa held its first election open to all races in 1994, ending apartheid, and has kept competitive elections since.

dd-democracy.q: What idea did the American and French revolutions spread?
a: That kings rule by the will of God
That only men of property should rule
That power comes from the people
That the Church should choose governments
dd-democracy.why: The revolutions of 1776 and 1789 declared that power comes from the people, and over the next 150 years the vote widened to all men and women.

dd-democracy.p:
Elections held, but not free or fair

V-Dem rated Hungary an electoral autocracy under Viktor Orbán. In April 2026 voters ousted him, and Péter Magyar's Tisza party won a two-thirds majority.

India held the world's largest election in 2024, with about 640 million votes cast. V-Dem first rated it an electoral autocracy in its 2021 report, and its data now class it as one since 2017, citing pressure on the media and opponents; India's government rejects the label.

The political scientist Samuel Huntington described democracy spreading in 'waves', each followed by a reverse. Many new democracies after World War I fell to dictators, including Mussolini in Italy and Hitler in Germany. After 1945 democracy returned to West Germany, Japan and Italy, and spread to newly independent India. A 'third wave' began with Portugal's Carnation Revolution in 1974 and swept through southern Europe, Latin America, East Asia, Eastern Europe after 1989 and South Africa in 1994. Since about 2010 researchers have recorded a new reverse, as elected leaders in several countries weakened courts, the press and opposition parties.

Today most countries hold elections, but their quality varies widely. By the V-Dem Institute's count, autocracies again outnumbered democracies at the end of 2025, and democracy has declined in many countries since about 2010, including the United States. Yet voters still remove governments peacefully, as in Hungary in 2026, and ideas born in Athens, such as juries and voting, remain everyday parts of public life.

Cleisthenes' reforms make Athens the first known democracy
Magna Carta places England's king under the law
The American and French revolutions proclaim rule by the people
New Zealand is the first country where women vote nationally
A 'third wave' brings democracy to dozens of countries
V-Dem counts more autocracies (92) than democracies (87)

dd-medicine.p: Around 400 BC Greek doctors following Hippocrates began explaining illness by natural causes rather than angry gods, and Galen's writings ruled medicine for over a thousand years. India and China built their own systems, and from the 800s the Islamic world ran large hospitals and wrote textbooks that Europe later studied. Real breakthroughs came in a rush after 1796: Jenner's smallpox vaccine, anaesthesia, antiseptic surgery and the proof, by Pasteur and Koch, that germs cause disease.

dd-medicine.note: Mostly from fewer children dying young: clean water, vaccines and antibiotics.

dd-medicine.p: The 1900s brought insulin, antibiotics, mass vaccination and transplants. Smallpox was wiped out in 1980, and global life expectancy rose from about 32 years in 1900 to about 73 today.

dd-medicine.q: What was the great medical change that came in a rush after 1796?
a: Doctors first explained illness by natural causes
Vaccines, anaesthesia, antiseptic surgery and germ theory
The first hospitals opened in Baghdad
dd-medicine.why: Jenner's smallpox vaccine, anaesthesia, antiseptic surgery and Pasteur and Koch's proof that germs cause disease transformed medicine within a century.

dd-medicine.p: For most of history doctors could describe diseases but rarely cure them, because they did not know what caused them. Microscopes, chemistry, statistics and controlled experiments in the 1800s changed that, showing that microbes spread many deadly diseases. Growing cities, industrial wealth and governments that funded clean water, research and public health turned discoveries into protection for millions.

Around 400 BC Hippocrates of Kos, in Greece, taught that illness had natural causes, and Galen, a Greek doctor in Rome, shaped medicine for over 1,000 years. India's Ayurveda and China's Inner Classic set out their own systems. From the 800s physicians of the Islamic world, in cities such as Baghdad in Iraq and Cairo in Egypt, ran great hospitals and wrote textbooks studied in Europe for centuries.

dd-medicine.q: How did medicine and clean water roughly double how long people live?
a: Mostly by saving babies and children
dd-medicine.why: Low life expectancy in the past was dragged down by child deaths; vaccines, clean water, antibiotics and better food saved children above all.

dd-medicine.p:
Hippocrates c. 400 BC, Galen c. AD 160–200

The Hippocratic doctors explained illness as an imbalance of four body fluids, the humours. The Hippocratic Oath, in changed forms, is still taken by some new doctors.

Galen's many books, based on animal dissection and long practice in Rome, became the unquestioned authority in Europe and the Islamic world until the 1500s.

Hospitals, textbooks and translations, 800s–1300s

Abbasid Baghdad translated Greek medical books into Arabic in the 800s. Its hospitals, called bimaristans, trained doctors and treated the sick for free.

Al-Razi came from Rayy, near Tehran, and led hospitals there and in Baghdad. He tested treatments by comparing groups of patients.

Classic texts of Charaka and Sushruta

The Sushruta Samhita, compiled over centuries, describes surgery including rebuilding noses. Ayurveda, based on balancing three doshas, is still widely practised in India.

For about 2,000 years doctors from Greece to Persia and Europe believed health depended on balancing four body fluids, or humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Fevers meant too much blood, so a standard cure was to let some out, by cutting a vein or applying leeches. Bloodletting lasted astonishingly long: in December 1799 doctors drained a large amount of blood from George Washington as he lay dying of a throat infection. The theory was not foolish for its time, since it pushed doctors to watch diet, sleep and environment. But it had no idea of germs, and it fell only when experiments in the 1800s proved what really caused disease.

In 1796 Edward Jenner in Britain tested the first vaccine, against smallpox. Anaesthesia, first shown in public in the United States in 1846, made long operations bearable. In the 1860s–80s Louis Pasteur in France and Robert Koch in Germany proved that germs cause disease. Insulin, first used to treat diabetes in Canada in 1922, and penicillin, found in London in 1928 and mass-produced in the 1940s, saved millions.

Vaccination, public health, antisepsis, penicillin

Britain gave the world vaccination, Florence Nightingale's modern nursing and Lister's antiseptic surgery. Alexander Fleming noticed penicillin killing bacteria in London in 1928, and an Oxford team turned it into a medicine in 1940–41.

dd-medicine.q: Why could doctors rarely cure diseases for most of history?
a: They had no hospitals to work in
They did not know what caused diseases
They refused to study Greek writings
dd-medicine.why: Doctors could describe illnesses, but theories such as the four humours had no idea of germs, so treatments like bloodletting did little good.

dd-medicine.p:
Germ theory, pasteurisation, vaccines

Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and disease, invented pasteurisation and made a rabies vaccine in 1885. René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816.

Bacteriology, X-rays, the first modern drugs

Robert Koch identified the germs of tuberculosis in 1882 and cholera in 1883. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895, and Paul Ehrlich's Salvarsan of 1910 was the first modern drug designed to kill a germ.

dd-medicine.q: What challenge to health remains today?
a: Life expectancy is now equal everywhere
Huge gaps between countries, and germs that resist antibiotics
dd-medicine.why: A baby in Japan can expect to live about 30 years longer than one in Nigeria, and resistant germs, pandemics and ageing pose new problems.

dd-medicine.p: Temples of healing existed in ancient Greece, and Christian charities in Byzantium cared for the sick. But the great teaching hospital grew up in the Islamic world. The bimaristans of Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo had wards for different illnesses, pharmacies, libraries and students, and treated patients whatever their wealth or faith. According to a later story, the physician al-Razi chose the site for a Baghdad hospital by hanging meat around the city and picking the spot where it rotted slowest. In Europe, hospitals long remained places of charity where the poor went to die, and they became safe only after antiseptics and germ theory arrived.

Worldwide, a baby born in 2023 could expect to live about 73 years, more than twice as long as in 1900, according to UN and other estimates. Lives are longest in places such as Japan, South Korea and Spain, and shortest in countries hit by poverty and conflict, such as Nigeria and Chad. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, and wild polio survives only in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Life expectancy above 83.5 years (UN, 2023)

Hong Kong, at about 85.5 years, had one of the world's highest life expectancies in the UN's 2023 estimates, behind only the tiny states of Monaco and San Marino.

Japan, at about 84.7 years, leads all large countries. Low rates of obesity and heart disease and universal health care are among the reasons usually given.

Life expectancy below 60 years (UN, 2023)

The UN estimates life expectancy in Nigeria at about 54. More women die in pregnancy and childbirth there than in any other country.

Chad has some of the world's highest rates of child and maternal death, and its life expectancy is about 55 years, by UN estimates.

dd-medicine.q: What turned medical discoveries into protection for millions?
a: Governments funding clean water, research and public health
dd-medicine.why: Growing cities, industrial wealth and governments that paid for clean water, research and public health spread the benefits of new science.

dd-medicine.p:
The last two countries where it is endemic

Afghanistan reported more wild polio cases than Pakistan in 2026, by WHO counts, after years in which Pakistan had more.

Pakistan and Afghanistan share one zone of polio spread. Insecurity and distrust of vaccination have slowed eradication.

When we read that life expectancy in 1800 was about 30, it does not mean most people died at 30. The average was dragged down by deaths of babies and children: in many places about four in ten children died before the age of five. Adults who survived childhood often lived into their fifties, sixties or beyond. The great modern change has been saving children, through vaccines, clean water, antibiotics and better food. Today about 4% of children worldwide die before five, according to the UN, though in parts of Africa the figure is still over 10%.

Medicine, together with clean water, better food and sanitation, roughly doubled how long people live, mostly by saving babies and children. That helped the world's population grow from about 1.6 billion in 1900 to over 8 billion. Yet huge gaps remain: a baby in Japan can expect to live about 30 years longer than one in Nigeria. New challenges include chronic diseases, ageing populations, pandemics and germs that resist antibiotics.

Robert Koch identifies the germ that causes tuberculosis
Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin in London
The WHO declares smallpox eradicated

dd-plagues.p: In 541 the first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague reached the Byzantine Empire, and it returned in waves for two centuries. In 1347 a second, deadlier wave, the Black Death, arrived on ships from the Black Sea and swept across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa by 1353, killing perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people. From 1518, smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans devastated the peoples of the Americas.

steps: Besiegers spread it to a Genoese port on the Black Sea.
Rats and fleas reach Sicily in 1347.
A third to half of Europeans die.

items: In western Europe, feudal ties weakened.

dd-plagues.p: The 1918 flu killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide. HIV, recognised in 1981, has killed about 44 million. COVID-19, first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, shut down much of the world in 2020.

dd-plagues.q: What was the Black Death of 1347–1353?
a: A flu pandemic that began in Spain
A smallpox outbreak in the Americas
Bubonic plague that killed perhaps a third to half of Europe
A famine caused by failed harvests
dd-plagues.why: Plague arrived on ships from the Black Sea in 1347 and swept across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa by 1353.

dd-plagues.p: Pandemics follow people. Trade routes, armies, pilgrims and ships carry germs, and crowded cities let them spread. The Black Death travelled along the trade networks that joined Asia and Europe. Indigenous Americans had no immunity to diseases that had circulated in Eurasia for thousands of years. Today air travel can carry a new virus around the world in weeks, but science, vaccines and public health make it far easier to fight.

Plague reached the Black Sea port of Caffa, in Crimea in today's Ukraine, in 1346. Genoese ships carried it to Constantinople, Italy and France in 1347, and it swept on to England and Spain in 1348, Norway in 1349 and Russia by 1352. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people, and many millions across the Middle East and North Africa.

dd-plagues.q: Why did smallpox devastate the peoples of the Americas?
a: They had no immunity to diseases long circulating in Eurasia
Their cities had no water supplies
The Spanish spread it deliberately in every city
It was a new disease that also killed most Europeans
dd-plagues.why: Indigenous Americans had never met diseases that had circulated in Eurasia for thousands of years, so smallpox, measles and others spread with terrible force.

dd-plagues.p:
Florence may have lost over half its people in 1348. The writer Boccaccio set his Decameron among young people fleeing the city.

Pope Clement VI, at Avignon, consecrated the river Rhône so that the dead could be thrown in when the graveyards were full.

King Alfonso XI of Castile died of plague in 1350 while besieging Gibraltar, the only reigning European king known to have died of it.

England lost perhaps 40–50% of its people in 1348–49, according to many modern estimates.

dd-plagues.q: What lasting tools did pandemics help create?
a: The end of all long-distance trade
Quarantine, public health bodies and vaccines
dd-plagues.why: From quarantine in Ragusa and Venice to the WHO in 1948 and vaccines, pandemics built public health; COVID-19 vaccines came in under a year.

dd-plagues.p:
Bergen was hit in 1349. With so many dead, Norway's crown weakened and farms were left empty for generations.

As plague came near, mobs blamed Jews for poisoning wells and destroyed hundreds of Jewish communities in 1348–51.

Plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, identified by Alexandre Yersin in Hong Kong in 1894. It lives in rodents and is carried by their fleas; when infected rats die, the fleas bite people. The bubonic form causes painful swellings, buboes, and killed perhaps half of those infected, while the pneumonic form spread by coughing and was almost always fatal. DNA from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan traces the Black Death's strain to Central Asia around 1338–39. According to the chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi, the Mongol army besieging Caffa catapulted corpses into the city, but ships, rats and trade goods probably did far more to carry it west.

Medieval doctors did not know about germs, but cities learned that keeping travellers apart slowed the plague. In 1377 Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, ordered arrivals from infected places to wait 30 days, a trentino, on nearby islands before entering the city. In 1423 Venice opened the world's first permanent plague hospital, a lazaretto, on an island in its lagoon, and the waiting period grew to 40 days, in Italian quaranta giorni, which gave us the word quarantine. Why 40 is unclear: it may echo the 40 days of Lent. The famous beaked plague-doctor mask, by contrast, dates from the 1600s, not the Black Death.

Justinian's plague broke out in Egypt in 541 and returned in waves for 200 years. Smallpox, carried by Europeans, devastated the peoples of Mexico and the Americas from 1520. The 1918 flu killed an estimated 50 million worldwide. HIV, traced to Kinshasa in today's DR Congo, has killed about 44 million. COVID-19, first identified in China in 2019, killed over 7 million by official counts.

First reported at Pelusium in Egypt

Plague reached the port of Pelusium in 541 and then Alexandria, from where grain ships carried it around the Mediterranean.

dd-plagues.q: How did the Black Death travel from Asia to Europe?
a: Along trade networks, carried by ships, rats and goods
By birds migrating south for the winter
dd-plagues.why: Pandemics follow people: the plague came west along trade routes, and ships, rats and trade goods did most to carry it.

dd-plagues.p:
Spread through central Mexico during the Spanish conquest

Smallpox, measles and other diseases, with war and forced labour, cut central Mexico's population by perhaps 90% within a century, by many estimates.

Traced to Kinshasa; recognised in 1981

HIV crossed from chimpanzees to humans in south-east Cameroon and spread from Kinshasa along railways and rivers decades before it was recognised.

dd-plagues.q: What did the Black Death change for Europe's surviving workers?
a: Wages rose and serfdom weakened in the west
Workers lost the right to move
Most farms switched to enslaved labour
dd-plagues.why: With so many dead, workers were scarce; survivors demanded higher pay, England tried to freeze wages, and serfdom slowly faded in the west.

dd-plagues.p: Smallpox reached the Caribbean by 1518 and Mexico in 1520, with the Spanish expedition of Pánfilo de Narváez. It tore through Tenochtitlan, killing the Aztec emperor Cuitláhuac and many defenders before Hernán Cortés's siege of 1521. It spread south ahead of the Spanish, probably killing the Inca emperor Huayna Capac around 1527 and setting off the civil war that Francisco Pizarro exploited. Smallpox, measles, flu and typhus, together with war, famine and forced labour, cut the population of the Americas by perhaps 50–90% within a century, although estimates of how many people lived there before 1492 vary widely.

The Black Death reshaped Europe's economy. With up to half the workers dead, survivors demanded higher pay; England's Statute of Labourers of 1351 tried to freeze wages, and anger over such laws fed the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. In the west, serfdom slowly faded. The 1918 flu, called 'Spanish' only because neutral Spain's press reported it freely, pushed many countries to create health ministries. HIV transformed sexual health and medicine: from 1996, combination drug treatment turned it from a death sentence into a manageable condition. COVID-19 brought the fastest vaccine development in history, using new mRNA technology, and a lasting shift to remote work.

The Black Death left so few workers that wages rose and serfdom weakened in western Europe, while frightened mobs attacked Jewish communities. Smallpox helped Spain conquer the Aztec and Inca empires. Pandemics also built public health: quarantine, health boards, germ theory, the World Health Organization in 1948 and vaccines, which wiped out smallpox by 1980. COVID-19 vaccines were developed and approved in under a year.

The Black Death sweeps Europe, the Middle East and North Africa
Smallpox strikes the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan
The flu pandemic kills an estimated 50 million people
Doctors in the US first report the disease later called AIDS
COVID-19 is declared a pandemic; much of the world locks down

dd-spices.p: In the 1400s pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg reached Europe after passing through many hands, from Asian growers to Arab traders, Egyptian customs posts and Venetian merchants. Portugal set out to reach the source by sea: Dias rounded Africa in 1488 and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Columbus, sailing west for Spain to find Asia, reached the Americas in 1492.

steps: Pepper, cloves and nutmeg came only from Asia; worth more than gold by weight.
Arab and Venetian traders controlled the route.
Portugal sails round Africa; Spain sends Columbus west.
Portugal, then the Dutch, seize the Spice Islands.

dd-spices.q: Why did Europeans want a sea route to Asia?
a: To bypass middlemen in the spice trade

dd-spices.p: Portugal and then the Netherlands fought their way to control of the spice islands of Indonesia. Meanwhile Columbus's voyages began the Columbian Exchange, a two-way flow of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world.

dd-spices.q: What did Portugal set out to do in the late 1400s?
a: Conquer Venice and take its trade
Reach the source of spices by sea, around Africa
Find a western route to the Americas
Grow pepper and cloves in Europe
dd-spices.why: Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, opening a sea route to the spice lands.

dd-spices.p: Spices were luxuries, valued for flavour, medicine, perfume and prestige, and the profits were enormous because they grew in so few places. Atlantic states such as Portugal and Spain wanted to cut out the Venetian and Muslim middlemen, spread Christianity and win glory. Better ships, navigation and guns let them cross oceans and seize ports, while profits from spices, silver and sugar paid for more voyages.

In 1450 the most prized spices grew in only a few places. Cloves came from a handful of islands in the north Moluccas, and nutmeg only from the tiny Banda Islands, both in today's Indonesia. Pepper grew on the Malabar coast of India, and the finest cinnamon in Sri Lanka. Asian and Arab merchants shipped them west to Egypt, where Venetians from Italy bought them for Europe at large mark-ups.

a: A treaty dividing the world between Spain and Portugal
A Dutch trade in nutmeg for Manhattan
A market in Venice for American goods
A two-way flow of crops, animals, people and diseases
dd-spices.why: Columbus's voyages joined the Americas and the rest of the world, swapping maize, potatoes and chillies for horses, cattle, wheat and sugar, and spreading deadly diseases.

dd-spices.p:
Cloves, nutmeg and mace

Cloves grew only on a few islands such as Ternate and Tidore, and nutmeg only on the Banda Islands. Javanese and Malay traders carried them west.

Malabar coast and Sri Lanka

Sri Lanka grew the finest cinnamon, the inner bark of a local tree, and was a stopping point on routes between Asia and Arabia.

Black pepper, native to the Malabar coast in today's Kerala, was the bulk spice of the trade. Gujarati merchants were among the leading traders of the Indian Ocean.

Malacca, Aden and the Gulf: where cargoes changed hands

Malacca's sultans, Muslim from the early 1400s, made the port a meeting place for merchants from China, India, Arabia and the islands.

Aden, at the mouth of the Red Sea, was where Indian Ocean cargoes were taxed and reloaded for Egypt.

A popular story says Europeans needed spices to hide the taste of rotten meat. Historians reject this: anyone who could afford spices could afford fresh meat. Spices were status symbols, flavourings for the rich, perfumes and medicines, thought to balance the body's humours. Their price came from distance and scarcity. In the 1400s nutmeg grew only on the Banda Islands, and each merchant along the way added a mark-up. Pepper was so valued that, according to the Greek historian Zosimus, the Gothic king Alaric demanded 3,000 pounds of it as part of a ransom from Rome in 408. Later, the Dutch East India Company burned surplus nutmeg to keep prices high.

dd-spices.h: The race for the Spice Islands, 1488–1621
dd-spices.p: Spices reached Europe through many middlemen, so Portugal sought a sea route of its own. Bartolomeu Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Sailing for Spain, Columbus went west in 1492 to find Asia and reached the Americas instead. Portugal seized ports from Goa to Malacca, in Malaysia, but after 1600 the Dutch took control of the spice islands of Indonesia, often by force.

Forts and ports from 1498

Prince Henry's captains crept down Africa's coast from the 1420s. Portugal hoped to bypass Muslim and Venetian middlemen, find Christian allies and grow rich on spices.

Portugal took Goa in 1510 and made it the capital of its Asian empire, the Estado da Índia, which it held until 1961.

dd-spices.q: Why were spices so valuable in Europe?
a: They hid the taste of rotten meat
Every merchant was forced to buy them by law
They grew in so few places and passed through many middlemen
They were the only way to preserve grain
dd-spices.why: Spices were luxuries for flavour, medicine and prestige; nutmeg grew only on the Banda Islands, and each merchant along the way added a mark-up.

dd-spices.p:
Westward voyages; Manila from 1571

Spain backed Columbus's westward plan in 1492. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas split the newly found world between Spain and Portugal.

Magellan was killed on Mactan in 1521. Spain later colonised the islands, named after King Philip II, and founded Manila in 1571.

Founded 1602; ruled the spice islands

The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, had its own army and fleet. From Batavia, today's Jakarta, it forced spice monopolies on the islands.

In 1621 the Dutch conquered the Banda Islands. Historians estimate that of about 15,000 Bandanese, only around 1,000 remained; the rest were killed, enslaved or fled.

dd-spices.q: How does the Columbian Exchange still show today?
a: Spices still come only from Indonesia
In what the whole world eats, from Italian tomatoes to Indian chillies
Most of Europe still trades through Venice
Potatoes are grown only in the Andes
dd-spices.why: Before 1492 Italy had no tomatoes, India and Thailand no chillies and Ireland no potatoes; American crops now feed people worldwide.

dd-spices.p: School books once said the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 cut Europe off from spices and forced it to find new routes. In fact spices kept flowing to Venice through Egypt and Syria, and Portugal's voyages down Africa had begun decades earlier, driven by gold, slaves, crusading zeal and profit. Another favourite tale says the Dutch swapped Manhattan for the nutmeg island of Run. At the Peace of Breda in 1667 each side kept what it held: England kept New Amsterdam, renamed New York, and the Dutch kept Run. It was a settlement of claims rather than a direct trade, though it is often told as one.

Columbus's voyages joined two worlds that had been apart for over 10,000 years. Maize from Mexico, potatoes from Peru and Bolivia, tomatoes, chillies and cassava spread across the globe, feeding growing populations from Ireland to China. Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar cane went the other way, and sugar plantations in places like Brazil were worked by enslaved Africans. European diseases such as smallpox killed millions of Indigenous Americans.

Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cacao

Maize was domesticated in southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago. Mexico also gave the world tomatoes, chillies, beans, avocados, vanilla and turkeys.

Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes of southern Peru and northern Bolivia, perhaps 7,000–10,000 years ago, and thousands of varieties are still grown there.

Where American crops changed diets

By the 1800s millions of poor Irish lived mainly on potatoes. When blight destroyed the crop in 1845–52, about a million people died and a million emigrated.

Tomatoes reached Italy by the 1540s but were long treated with suspicion. Tomato sauce became common only in the 1700s–1800s.

dd-spices.q: What let Portugal and Spain cross oceans and seize ports?
dd-spices.why: Better ships, navigation and guns let Atlantic states cross oceans and take ports, while profits from spices, silver and sugar funded more voyages.

dd-spices.p:
Plantations worked by enslaved Africans

Portuguese Brazil became the world's leading sugar producer by the late 1500s, using millions of enslaved Africans over three centuries.

French Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, was the world's richest sugar colony by the 1780s, until the slave revolution of 1791 that created Haiti.

The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term 'Columbian Exchange' in 1972. Its effects are everywhere. Italian cooking had no tomatoes, Indian and Thai cooking no chillies, and Ireland no potatoes before 1492. Chocolate, vanilla, peanuts, pineapples and turkeys came from the Americas, while coffee, sugar, bananas, wheat, rice, horses and cattle went there. American crops such as maize and sweet potatoes, which grow on poor soils, helped populations grow in China and Africa. But dependence could be dangerous: when blight struck Ireland's potatoes in 1845, the Great Famine killed about a million people.

The spice race launched European empires in Asia and the Americas and the first truly global trade. The Columbian Exchange changed what the whole world eats: potatoes, maize and chillies spread across Europe, Africa and Asia. It also brought catastrophe. Old World diseases killed a large share of Indigenous Americans, by many estimates most of them within a century, and sugar plantations drove the Atlantic slave trade, which carried about 12.5 million Africans across the ocean.

Vasco da Gama reaches India by sailing around Africa
Portugal captures Malacca, the gateway to the spice islands
Magellan's expedition sails around the world, returning with cloves
The Dutch East India Company is founded
The Dutch conquer the Banda Islands to control nutmeg

dd-slavery.p: From the early 1500s Portuguese and then Spanish, Dutch, British, French and other traders shipped enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to work in the Americas. Captives were bought at coastal forts from African rulers and merchants, packed into ships and carried on the Middle Passage, where perhaps one in seven died. Most were put to work growing sugar in Brazil and the Caribbean, and later coffee and cotton.

steps: The Middle Passage: enslaved people packed in ships; 1 in 7 died.
Sugar, cotton, tobacco grown by enslaved labour.

dd-slavery.h: Where enslaved Africans were taken (of 12.5 million)

dd-slavery.q: Which country received the most enslaved Africans?
dd-slavery.why: Brazil was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

dd-slavery.p: In all about 12.5 million people were shipped, the trade peaking in the 1700s. Revolts, Haiti's revolution and abolition campaigns brought bans on the trade from 1807, but slavery itself lasted in Brazil until 1888.

dd-slavery.q: What was the Atlantic slave trade?
a: The shipping of about 12.5 million enslaved Africans to the Americas
A trade in sugar between Brazil and Portugal
European settlers moving to Africa to farm
The movement of Indigenous Americans to Europe
dd-slavery.why: From the early 1500s European traders shipped about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic, most to grow sugar in Brazil and the Caribbean.

dd-slavery.p: European colonists in the Americas wanted cheap labour for plantations and mines, and Indigenous populations had collapsed from disease, conquest and forced labour. Sugar, a hugely profitable crop, needed large gangs of workers. African states and merchants sold captives, mostly taken in wars and raids, in exchange for cloth, guns and other goods. Ideas of racial inferiority grew up to justify enslaving Africans and their children for life.

About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto slave ships, by the estimates of the SlaveVoyages database. Almost half came from West Central Africa, today's Angola and the Congo region. Most of the rest came from the coasts of West Africa, from Senegal to Nigeria. Europeans rarely went inland: they bought captives at coastal forts and ports from African rulers and merchants, mostly people taken in wars and raids.

dd-slavery.q: What populations did the trade create in the Americas?
a: Mainly European communities in the Caribbean
Large African-descended populations in Brazil, the Caribbean and the US
dd-slavery.why: The trade moved more people across the Atlantic than any migration before 1820, creating the large African-descended populations of Brazil, the Caribbean and the United States.

dd-slavery.p:
From Senegal to Liberia

Senegambia was an early source of captives, in the 1500s, and later sent many to French and British colonies.

James Island, in the Gambia River, was a British trading fort from the 1660s.

Today's Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria and Cameroon

The Gold Coast had dozens of European forts, including Elmina and Cape Coast Castle. The Asante kingdom became a major supplier in the 1700s.

The kingdom of Dahomey grew powerful by capturing people in wars and selling them at Ouidah. The Bight of Benin was called the 'Slave Coast'.

The largest source, almost half of all captives

Ports on the Loango coast, in today's Republic of the Congo, supplied many captives to French, Dutch and British ships in the 1700s.

Portuguese Angola, with its ports of Luanda and Benguela, was the single largest source of captives, most of them sent to Brazil.

Captives were chained below deck in spaces often too low to sit upright, for voyages lasting weeks or months. Disease, especially dysentery, killed many, and the sick were sometimes thrown overboard. In 1781 the crew of the British ship Zong threw about 130 Africans into the sea, and its owners then claimed insurance for them as lost cargo. A 1788 diagram of the Liverpool ship Brookes, showing 454 people packed like goods into its hold, became the abolitionists' most powerful image; on one earlier voyage it had carried over 600. Captives resisted, too: revolts broke out on an estimated one voyage in ten.

About 10.7 million Africans survived the Middle Passage, the voyage of one to three months across the Atlantic; perhaps 1.8 million died at sea. Brazil received almost half, and the sugar islands of the Caribbean, such as Jamaica, Haiti and Cuba, most of the rest. Fewer than 4% went to mainland North America, but by 1860 the United States had about 4 million enslaved people.

About 4.9 million arrivals, the most of any land

Brazil imported enslaved Africans for over three centuries to work sugar, gold mines and coffee. Today over half of Brazilians identify as Black or of mixed race.

dd-slavery.q: Why did colonists in the Americas turn to enslaved African labour?
a: African workers were paid more than Europeans
They wanted cheap plantation labour, and Indigenous populations had collapsed
Sugar could only be grown by Africans
dd-slavery.why: Profitable sugar needed large gangs of workers, and disease, conquest and forced labour had devastated Indigenous populations.

dd-slavery.p:
Sugar colonies of Britain, France, Spain, the Netherlands and Denmark

Jamaica's sugar estates were so deadly that the enslaved population fell without constant new arrivals. In 1831–32 the Baptist War, a huge revolt, hastened abolition.

French Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, was the world's richest sugar and coffee colony by the 1780s, with about half a million enslaved people.

Mines, towns and plantations from Mexico to Peru

Cartagena was the main slave port of Spanish South America, from which captives were sent on to Peru and the mines of New Granada.

In the early colonial period New Spain took in many Africans, perhaps about 200,000. Most later merged into Mexico's mixed population.

dd-slavery.q: Which legacy of slavery is still debated today?
a: Racism built to defend slavery, and calls for reparations
Whether Brazil should restore the monarchy
dd-slavery.why: Ideas of racial inferiority grew to justify slavery and outlived it, and debates over memory and reparations continue today.

dd-slavery.p: Slavery existed in many societies, including in Africa, long before the Atlantic trade. What was new was its scale and its basis in race. European traders rarely raided inland; they depended on African kingdoms and merchants, such as Dahomey and the Aro, who sold captives taken in wars, raids or as punishment. Some African rulers, like Afonso I of Kongo, protested against the trade, while others grew rich from it. In Europe and the Americas, ordinary investors, shipbuilders, banks and insurers profited, and consumers bought the sugar, tobacco and cotton that enslaved people grew.

dd-slavery.h: When slavery ended in the Americas, 1793–1888
dd-slavery.p: Enslaved people rose in revolt from Haiti to Jamaica, and campaigners in Britain built a mass movement against the trade. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and freed the enslaved in its colonies in 1834–38. Most new Spanish American republics ended slavery by the 1850s, the United States after its civil war in 1865, Cuba in 1886 and Brazil, the last, in 1888.

Haiti, early Spanish American republics, British colonies

France abolished slavery in Saint-Domingue in 1793–94 under pressure from the revolt. Napoleon's attempt to restore it failed, and Haiti became the first state founded by formerly enslaved people, in 1804.

Mexico abolished slavery in 1829. Its ban was one cause of conflict with American settlers in Texas, who held slaves.

French, Danish and Dutch colonies, most South American states, the US

Colombia, which then included Panama, freed its remaining enslaved people in 1852.

Bolivia declared slavery abolished soon after independence, but the laws were not enforced, and slavery ended in practice only in 1851.

dd-slavery.q: How did European traders usually obtain captives?
a: By buying them at coastal forts from African rulers and merchants
dd-slavery.why: Europeans rarely went inland; African states and merchants sold captives, mostly taken in wars and raids, for cloth, guns and other goods.

dd-slavery.p:
The last strongholds of slavery

Spain abolished slavery in Puerto Rico in 1873, with three years of compulsory labour contracts.

Spain began gradual abolition in Cuba in 1880 and ended it in 1886. Many enslaved and free Black Cubans had fought for independence in the war of 1868–78.

Enslaved people fought for freedom throughout, through escapes, sabotage and revolts. Maroon communities of runaways survived for generations in Jamaica, Suriname and Brazil, and the Haitian Revolution of 1791–1804 terrified slaveholders everywhere. In Britain, Quakers, Thomas Clarkson, William Wilberforce and the formerly enslaved writer Olaudah Equiano built one of the first mass campaigns, with petitions and a sugar boycott said to have involved about 300,000 people in 1791. After abolishing its own trade in 1807, Britain's navy patrolled the African coast, and between 1808 and 1860 it seized about 1,600 slave ships and freed some 150,000 captives.

The trade moved more people across the Atlantic than any migration before 1820 and created the large African-descended populations of Brazil, the Caribbean and the United States. Plantation profits fed European ports, banks and industry, though historians debate how much they drove the Industrial Revolution. In Africa it fuelled wars and drained people from whole regions. Racism built to defend slavery outlived it, and debates over memory and reparations continue today.

pts: Spain allows captives to be shipped straight from Africa to the Americas
The trade's peak, with over 6 million people shipped in the century
Enslaved people rise up in Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti
Britain bans its slave trade; the US follows in 1808
The 13th Amendment ends slavery in the United States
Brazil, the last country in the Americas, abolishes slavery

dd-science.p: In 1543 Copernicus argued that the Earth circles the Sun, and Vesalius published the first accurate atlas of the human body. Tycho Brahe's precise measurements let Kepler show that planets move in ellipses, and from 1609 Galileo's telescope revealed moons around Jupiter. In 1633 the Church condemned Galileo, but the new ideas spread through print and new scientific societies in London and Paris.

items: The Earth goes around the Sun.
Telescope; tried by the Church in 1633.
Test ideas with experiments and evidence.

dd-science.q: What is the scientific method’s key idea?
a: Test ideas against evidence through experiments

dd-science.p: In 1687 Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity explained the heavens and the Earth with the same mathematics. Over the next two centuries chemistry, biology, electricity and medicine were remade in the same way, and by 1900 science was a profession taught in universities and laboratories.

dd-science.q: What did Newton's Principia of 1687 achieve?
a: It proved the Earth was flat
It explained the heavens and Earth with the same laws
It discovered the moons of Jupiter
dd-science.why: Newton showed that one law of gravity moves both falling apples and orbiting planets, uniting heaven and Earth under the same mathematics.

dd-science.p: Printing let scholars share results quickly and check each other's work. Rediscovered Greek texts, many preserved and improved by scholars in the Islamic world, sparked debate about old authorities. New instruments, such as the telescope and microscope, showed things no ancient writer had seen. Rival European states and their rulers competed for prestige, trade and better navigation, and paid for observatories and academies. Historians still debate why this happened in Europe rather than in China or the Islamic world.

In 1543 the Polish astronomer Copernicus, in Poland, put the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the universe. Tycho Brahe of Denmark measured the planets, Kepler worked out their orbits, and in Italy Galileo turned a telescope on the sky. Scientific societies sprang up in Britain and France, and in 1687 Isaac Newton showed that one law of gravity moves both apples and planets.

dd-science.q: How did science change death rates by 1900?
a: Germ theory, vaccines and clean water began a fall in deaths
Death rates rose because of new factories
Only the rich benefited from new discoveries
dd-science.why: Pasteur and Koch proved germs cause disease, and vaccines and clean water began the fall in death rates that let the world's population soar.

dd-science.p:
Copernicus, Vesalius, Tycho Brahe

Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon at Frombork in Royal Prussia, then part of Poland, argued that the Earth spins and circles the Sun. Few accepted it for decades.

Andreas Vesalius, born in Brussels, dissected human bodies himself and showed that the ancient authority Galen, who had worked mainly from animals, was often wrong.

Galileo, Kepler, Harvey

Galileo's telescope revealed Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus in 1609–10. In 1633 the Inquisition condemned him for defending Copernicus, and he spent his last years under house arrest.

Prague was the seat of Emperor Rudolf II, who hired Tycho and then Kepler. Kepler's three laws of planetary motion appeared in 1609 and 1619.

Newton, Huygens, Leeuwenhoek, the first academies

After William Harvey showed in 1628 that the heart pumps blood round the body, the Royal Society (1660), Robert Boyle and Newton made England a leader. Newton's Principia (1687) united heaven and Earth under the same laws.

The Dutch Republic, with its printers and relative tolerance, was a haven for science. Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656.

Galileo was a devout Catholic, and for years he had friends in Rome, including the future Pope Urban VIII. In 1616 the Church ruled that the Sun-centred view was contrary to Scripture and told him not to defend it. His 1632 Dialogue did so anyway, and seemed to mock the Pope's views. In 1633 the Inquisition forced him to recant, banned the book and kept him under house arrest until his death in 1642. He was threatened but not tortured. The story that he muttered 'And yet it moves' after recanting is a legend, first recorded over a century later. In 1992 Pope John Paul II acknowledged the Church had erred.

Scientists set out to test theories in the field. French expeditions to Ecuador and Lapland, in 1735–44, proved Newton right that the Earth bulges at the equator. James Cook sailed to Tahiti in 1769 to time Venus crossing the Sun. Alexander von Humboldt explored Spanish America, from Venezuela to Mexico. In 1835 a young Charles Darwin reached the Galápagos Islands on HMS Beagle.

French expeditions to the equator and the Arctic

The French Geodesic Mission worked near Quito in 1736–43. Its measurements, with Lapland's, showed the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, as Newton had predicted.

In 1736–37 Pierre-Louis Maupertuis measured a degree of latitude in the Torne valley, today on the Finnish–Swedish border, near the Arctic Circle.

dd-science.q: How did printing help the Scientific Revolution?
a: It let the Church control new ideas
It replaced the need for experiments
It let scholars share results quickly and check each other's work
It made telescopes cheaper to build
dd-science.why: Printed books spread results fast, so others could test and challenge them, and even Galileo's condemnation could not stop the new ideas spreading.

dd-science.p:
Astronomy, botany and mapping in the Pacific

Cook observed the 1769 transit of Venus at Tahiti. Observations from dozens of places around the world gave a far better estimate of the Earth–Sun distance.

Cook spent six months in 1769–70 charting New Zealand's coasts, the first detailed European map of the islands.

Plants, rocks, climate and peoples of Spanish America

Humboldt and the botanist Aimé Bonpland explored the Orinoco in 1800 and confirmed that it is linked by a natural channel to the Amazon basin.

In Bogotá Humboldt met José Celestino Mutis, who led a long Spanish botanical expedition in New Granada.

dd-science.q: What is the lasting legacy of the Scientific Revolution today?
a: Trust in ancient authorities like Galen
A ban on publishing unchecked ideas
Science taught only by the Church
A method of testing ideas by experiment and publishing them
dd-science.why: Testing ideas against observation and publishing so others can check them still drives modern medicine, computing and space flight.

dd-science.p: Isaac Newton did much of his early work in 1665–66, when plague closed Cambridge University and he went home to Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire. According to his friend William Stukeley, the elderly Newton said that seeing an apple fall in the garden there set him thinking about gravity. Whether or not the story is polished, it was his own; the idea of the apple hitting his head is a later embellishment. His insight was that the force pulling an apple down is the same one holding the Moon in orbit, weakening with the square of the distance. He spent the next twenty years on the mathematics before publishing the Principia in 1687.

By 1900 science had changed daily life. Chemists in France named the elements, physicists in Britain tamed electricity, and Darwin explained evolution. Louis Pasteur in France and Robert Koch in Germany proved that germs cause disease, leading to vaccines and safer surgery. Mendeleev in Russia drew up the periodic table, and laboratories in the United States began to invent for profit.

Vaccination, electricity, evolution

Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the basis of electric generators. James Clerk Maxwell explained light as an electromagnetic wave in the 1860s, and Darwin published his theory of evolution in 1859.

Modern chemistry, germ theory, radioactivity

Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and disease, and made a rabies vaccine in 1885. In 1898 Marie Curie, born in Warsaw, and Pierre Curie discovered polonium and radium in Paris.

dd-science.q: Why could Galileo and Leeuwenhoek see what no ancient writer had seen?
a: They used new instruments like the telescope and microscope
They were paid by the Pope
dd-science.why: Galileo's telescope revealed Jupiter's moons and Leeuwenhoek's microscopes showed single-celled 'little animals', challenging old authorities with direct observation.

dd-science.p:
Research universities, bacteriology, X-rays

German research universities, with laboratories and doctoral training, became the model for the world. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.

A popular myth says that before Columbus or Copernicus, people believed the Earth was flat. In fact educated Europeans had known it was a sphere since ancient Greek times; the Greek scholar Eratosthenes estimated its size around 240 BC. Nor did science start from nothing in 1543. Scholars in the Islamic world, such as Ibn al-Haytham, who studied light and vision around 1020, had built on Greek learning, and Copernicus used mathematical tools first developed by astronomers at Maragha in Persia. What changed was the scale: printed books, regular experiments and open debate turned scattered insights into a lasting, self-correcting enterprise.

Science gave humanity a method: test ideas against careful observation and experiment, and publish so others can check them. Its discoveries powered the Industrial Revolution, gave Europe and North America great military and economic advantages, and, through vaccines, clean water and germ theory, began the fall in death rates that let the world's population soar. The same approach drives modern medicine, computing and space flight.

items: The rules of the very small; behind chips and lasers.

dd-capitalism.p: Capitalism is an economic system in which private owners, not the state, run most businesses and markets set prices. Its modern form began in the 1600s, when Dutch and English trading companies sold shares to investors. In 1776 Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations argued that free markets and competition make nations rich.

items: Prices set by supply and demand
Self-interest can serve the common good.

dd-capitalism.p: Most rich countries combine both.

dd-capitalism.q: Who wrote The Wealth of Nations?

dd-capitalism.p: The Industrial Revolution turned capitalism into a world system of factories, railways, banks and global trade, creating huge wealth and harsh inequality. Crashes such as the Great Depression led governments to regulate markets, and after the Cold War most of the world, including China, embraced markets in some form.

Markets rewarded people who invented, invested and took risks, and joint-stock companies let many investors share the costs and dangers of big ventures. Secure property rights, banks and stock exchanges made it easier to raise money. In the 20th century, the failures of planned economies persuaded many countries that markets delivered growth more reliably.

dd-capitalism.q: What made the Dutch East India Company a milestone in capitalism?
a: It was run by the king
It sold shares that investors could buy and resell
It printed the first paper money
dd-capitalism.why: From 1602 the VOC raised money from many investors by selling shares, traded on Amsterdam's exchange, often called the first modern stock market.

dd-capitalism.p: Modern capitalism grew up in Europe's richest trading nations. In the Netherlands, the Dutch East India Company sold shares from 1602, and its trading posts stretched from South Africa to Indonesia and Japan. Britain followed with its own East India Company and the Bank of England. In 1776 the Scot Adam Smith argued that free markets, not monopolies, were the true source of the wealth of nations.

Home of the VOC and the Amsterdam exchange

In the 1600s the small Dutch Republic was Europe's richest trading nation, with the biggest merchant fleet and the first modern stock exchange.

East India Company, Bank of England

The East India Company, chartered in 1600, grew from a trading firm into a private army and government ruling much of India.

dd-capitalism.q: Which country began market reforms under Deng Xiaoping in 1978?
dd-capitalism.why: Deng's reforms let farmers sell surplus crops and opened China to foreign investment, starting decades of rapid growth.

dd-capitalism.p:
Parts of Java and the Spice Islands, the Cape and coastal Ceylon

The VOC made Batavia, today's Jakarta, its Asian headquarters in 1619 and fought wars to control the trade in nutmeg, cloves and pepper.

The VOC founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station for ships sailing between Europe and Asia.

In 1602 the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, raised money by selling shares that anyone could buy and later resell, and Amsterdam's exchange became the first modern stock market. Investors shared both the profits and the risks of long voyages to Asia. England's East India Company, chartered in 1600, and the Bank of England, founded in 1694, showed how private money could fund trade and even wars. These companies were also tools of empire: the VOC fought wars in Indonesia, and the English company eventually ruled much of India.

Adam Smith, a Scottish professor, argued in 1776 that people pursuing their own interest in free markets are led 'as if by an invisible hand' to benefit society: a baker sells good bread not out of kindness but to earn a living. Smith attacked mercantilism, the policy of hoarding gold and protecting home industries with tariffs and monopolies, and praised the division of labour, using a pin factory as his example. He also warned that business owners often conspire against the public, and said the state must provide defence, justice and public works.

Factories, steam power and railways began in Britain around 1760 and made it the 'workshop of the world'. Belgium was the first to follow on the continent, then France, Germany and the United States, which by 1900 had the world's largest economy. Japan industrialised after 1868 and Russia from the 1890s. Industrial capitalism created vast fortunes, big cities and a new working class, and with it trade unions and socialism.
Coal, cotton, steam engines and a global empire gave Britain a head start; by 1850 it made about half the world's iron and cotton cloth.

dd-capitalism.q: What did Adam Smith argue in The Wealth of Nations?
a: Free markets and competition make nations rich
dd-capitalism.why: Smith argued that self-interest in free markets benefits society 'as if by an invisible hand', and attacked mercantilist tariffs and monopolies.

dd-capitalism.p: Railways, steel, oil and mass immigration made the United States the world's largest economy, and men like Carnegie and Rockefeller among the richest people in history.

After 1868 Meiji Japan built railways, shipyards and textile mills, often starting them as state firms and then selling them to private companies.

Finance minister Sergei Witte drove a rush of railway building and foreign investment in the 1890s, including the Trans-Siberian Railway.

dd-capitalism.q: What started the 2008 global financial crisis?
a: Risky mortgage lending in the United States
A war in the Middle East
dd-capitalism.why: Banks made and traded huge numbers of risky American home loans; when house prices fell, the losses spread through the global financial system.

dd-capitalism.p: Capitalism grew in booms and busts. After the Wall Street Crash of 1929, banks failed and by 1933 about a quarter of American workers were unemployed. The British economist John Maynard Keynes argued that governments should spend to revive demand in a slump, and after World War II most Western countries built mixed economies, with welfare states, regulated banks and some state-owned industries. In the 1970s high inflation and slow growth turned many against this model, and economists such as Milton Friedman argued for freer markets, lower taxes and less regulation.

From the late 1970s, governments across the world turned to markets. Chile began in 1975 and China in 1978. Margaret Thatcher in Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States cut taxes and regulation. Vietnam opened up in 1986 and India in 1991. When communism fell, Eastern Europe and Russia switched to markets in a rush known as 'shock therapy'.

Economists trained in Chicago, the 'Chicago Boys', freed prices and trade under General Pinochet's dictatorship from 1975.

Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops and opened special economic zones to foreign investors.

The Doi Moi ('renovation') reforms of 1986 brought markets to communist Vietnam.

In 1991, facing a currency crisis, finance minister Manmohan Singh scrapped licences and cut tariffs and controls.

dd-capitalism.q: What did Keynes say governments should do in an economic slump?
dd-capitalism.why: After the Great Depression, Keynes argued that government spending could revive demand and jobs, shaping the mixed economies built after World War II.

dd-capitalism.p:
Poland's 1990 'shock therapy', designed by Leszek Balcerowicz, freed prices and trade almost overnight.

Prices were freed in January 1992, and rushed privatisation created a small class of super-rich 'oligarchs'.

From the late 1970s a wave of market reforms swept the world. Chile's military government opened its economy from 1975, China's Deng Xiaoping began reforms in 1978, and Margaret Thatcher in Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States cut taxes and sold off or deregulated industries. Vietnam followed in 1986, and after communism collapsed, Eastern Europe and Russia switched to markets almost overnight, often painfully. India opened up in 1991. Global trade boomed, but the 2008 financial crisis, which began with risky American mortgage lending, revived old doubts about unregulated markets.

Capitalism has helped lift billions of people out of poverty, especially since China and India opened their economies. But it also brings booms and busts, such as the 2008 financial crisis, and wide gaps between rich and poor. Arguments about how far governments should tax, regulate and spend remain at the heart of politics almost everywhere.

dd-pirates.p: From the mid-1600s buccaneers based at Tortuga and Port Royal raided Spanish towns and ships in the Caribbean, often with licences from England or France. In the 1690s pirates sailed the 'Pirate Round' to the Indian Ocean, where Henry Every seized a Mughal treasure ship in 1695.

items: North African raiders took Europeans as slaves.

dd-pirates.s: Privateers were pirates licensed by a government.
dd-pirates.why: Like Francis Drake, who raided Spain for England.

dd-pirates.p: The busiest years came after 1715, when crews based at Nassau in the Bahamas, led by men such as Benjamin Hornigold, Blackbeard and Charles Vane, attacked merchant shipping, and later crews such as Bartholomew Roberts's raided from Newfoundland to West Africa. Then the tide turned: Woodes Rogers took back Nassau in 1718, Blackbeard was killed that November, and by about 1726 the great pirate crews were gone.

dd-pirates.q: What was the 'pirate republic' at Nassau?
a: A Spanish fort guarding silver fleets
A Royal Navy base for hunting pirates
A pirate haven in the Bahamas from about 1715 to 1718
dd-pirates.why: Hundreds of pirates, including Hornigold, Blackbeard and Vane, used Nassau's harbour in the neglected Bahamas until Woodes Rogers arrived as governor in 1718.

dd-pirates.p: Spanish silver and the booming trade in sugar, slaves and Asian goods offered rich prizes on long, poorly guarded routes. Wars between European powers trained thousands of sailors as privateers, licensed raiders, and when peace came in 1713 many were thrown out of work. Merchant sailors faced low pay and brutal discipline, so some joined pirates willingly. Weak colonial government and merchants happy to buy cheap goods gave pirates safe harbours.

dd-pirates.h: Pirate havens in the Caribbean, c. 1715
dd-pirates.p: Spain's silver fleets sailed from Veracruz and Cartagena to Havana, then home through the Florida Straits, past islands held by rival empires. Pirates used havens in the gaps: buccaneers at Tortuga in French Haiti and Port Royal in English Jamaica in the 1600s, then the 'pirate republic' at Nassau in the Bahamas until 1718. Blackbeard sailed from Nassau and died off North Carolina.

dd-pirates.q: Why could pirates find safe harbours in the Americas?
a: Weak colonial government and merchants keen on cheap goods
They were all pardoned each year
dd-pirates.why: Colonies like the Bahamas were neglected, and merchants in places such as New York financed pirates and bought their stolen goods.

dd-pirates.p:
Most of the mainland and the big islands

Havana was where Spain's fleets gathered each year before sailing home with silver from Mexico and Peru.

Spanish Puerto Rico licensed its own privateers, who raided British shipping.

Jamaica, the Bahamas and small islands

England took Jamaica from Spain in 1655 and at first welcomed buccaneers as a defence. Port Royal later turned to hanging pirates.

The Bahamas were a neglected English colony. After 1713 hundreds of pirates used Nassau's harbour, until the first royal governor arrived in 1718.

dd-pirates.q: What does this history suggest about piracy today?
a: It returns wherever states are weak, as off Somalia
It ended for good in the 1720s
It exists only in novels and films
It is now legal under licence
dd-pirates.why: Piracy never vanished; it reappeared off Somalia in the 2000s, while novels and films reshaped the golden age into a romantic legend.

dd-pirates.p:
Saint-Domingue, plus Martinique and Guadeloupe

French buccaneers settled western Hispaniola from Tortuga, and Spain recognised it as French Saint-Domingue in 1697.

Edward Teach, or Thatch, was a pirate for only about two years, from 1716 to 1718, but no pirate is more famous. In late 1717 he captured a French slave ship and renamed it Queen Anne's Revenge, armed with dozens of cannon. In May 1718 he blockaded Charleston for about a week and released his hostages for a chest of medicines. Soon after, his flagship ran aground off North Carolina; its wreck was found in 1996. He accepted a royal pardon but returned to piracy, and on 22 November 1718 he died fighting a Royal Navy party at Ocracoke. According to a 1724 book, he lit slow fuses under his hat to frighten victims.

Many pirate crews signed written articles, rules that every man swore to. Captains were usually elected and could be voted out, and a quartermaster shared out the loot, with the captain typically taking only one and a half or two shares. Some articles promised payouts for lost limbs, banned gambling or fighting on board, and set punishments such as marooning. Crews were young, mostly former merchant sailors and navy men, and included many men of African descent, some free crewmen and some still treated as slaves. Life was crowded, often drunk and dangerous, and most pirate careers ended within a few years at the end of a rope or in a fight.

dd-pirates.h: The Pirate Round to the Indian Ocean, 1690s
dd-pirates.p: In the 1690s some pirates sailed from the Americas round Africa to the Indian Ocean, a voyage called the Pirate Round. They sheltered at Île Sainte-Marie off Madagascar and hunted rich Indian ships in the Red Sea and Arabian Sea. In 1695 Henry Every captured the Mughal ship Ganj-i-Sawai, and the anger in Mughal India put the English East India Company in danger.

The richest state in the Indian Ocean

Bengal was one of the Mughal Empire's richest provinces, famous for its cotton cloth.

The Mughal Empire ruled most of India. When its ships were plundered by English pirates, Emperor Aurangzeb's officials briefly shut down English trade and confined English merchants.

dd-pirates.q: Why did so many sailors turn to piracy after 1713?
a: Peace threw thousands of trained privateers out of work
Spain paid them to attack England
The Royal Navy doubled its wages
Pirates were legally licensed by Parliament
dd-pirates.why: Wars had trained thousands as licensed privateers; when peace came in 1713 many lost their work, and harsh merchant life pushed others to join willingly.

dd-pirates.p:
Madagascar's coast was outside European rule

Madagascar had no European colony and lay near the shipping lanes. Pirates settled on its east coast in the 1690s–1720s, some marrying into local families.

Walking the plank is mostly fiction: there is almost no evidence for it in the golden age, and the few recorded cases come from later. Buried treasure was rare, because pirates usually spent or shared loot quickly; the best-known real case is William Kidd's cache on Gardiners Island near New York, dug up by the authorities in 1699. Treasure maps marked with an X, peg legs and parrots owe more to Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island (1883) than to history. The Jolly Roger was real, though flags varied, and a black flag usually offered mercy if a ship surrendered.

dd-pirates.q: How was the golden age of piracy brought to an end?
a: Pirates retired rich on buried treasure
A great hurricane destroyed their ships
Pardons, naval patrols and colonial courts with mass hangings
dd-pirates.why: The 1717 pardon, Rogers taking Nassau, navy hunts and local trials under a 1700 law broke the havens; by about 1726 the great crews were gone.

dd-pirates.p: In 1717 King George I offered a pardon to pirates who surrendered, and in July 1718 Woodes Rogers, a former privateer, arrived at Nassau as governor with warships. Many pirates accepted the pardon; those who carried on were hunted down. Under a 1700 law, colonial courts could try pirates without sending them to London, and mass hangings followed. The navy killed Bartholomew Roberts, the most successful pirate of the age, off West Africa in 1722, and 52 of his crew were hanged at Cape Coast Castle. By the late 1720s the great Atlantic pirate crews had gone.

Britain's Royal Navy, colonial courts and a 1717 royal pardon broke the pirate havens, and hundreds of pirates were hanged, which helped make the Atlantic safe for the trade of growing empires. Piracy never vanished, and it returns wherever states are weak, as off Somalia in the 2000s. The golden age also left a powerful legend, reshaped by novels and films, of free outlaws under the skull and crossbones.
