The royal family's flight is stopped at Varennes
War with Austria and Prussia; France becomes a republic
Louis XVI is executed and the Terror begins
Robespierre falls and the Terror ends; slavery is abolished
Napoleon Bonaparte seizes power in the coup of Brumaire

dd-latam.p: In 1791 enslaved people in French Saint-Domingue rose up, and in 1804 they founded Haiti. When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808 and deposed its king, Spain's colonies set up their own governing councils, and many soon declared independence. Years of brutal war followed. Simón Bolívar fought from Venezuela across the Andes to Bogotá and Quito, while José de San Martín led an army from Argentina over the Andes into Chile and then by sea to Peru.

items: Dreamed of a united Gran Colombia.
A priest whose 1810 cry began revolt.
A Portuguese prince who declared independence in 1822.

steps: Conquered Spain in 1808; the king was captured.
American and French revolutions inspired them.
By 1826 Spain had lost all mainland colonies.

dd-latam.p: Victory at Ayacucho in 1824 ended Spanish power in South America. Mexico won independence in 1821, and Brazil broke from Portugal in 1822 under a Portuguese prince. Only Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish, until 1898.

dd-latam.q: What happened to Spain's American empire between about 1808 and 1825?
a: Most of its colonies won independence in years of war
Spain sold its colonies to the United States
It united into one large independent republic
dd-latam.why: About twenty new countries emerged; by 1824 Ayacucho ended Spanish power in South America, and only Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish until 1898.

dd-latam.p: American-born creoles resented rule by officials sent from Spain, trade limits and new taxes from the Bourbon reforms. The ideas of the Enlightenment and the American and French revolutions offered a model, while Haiti's revolution both inspired and frightened them. The real trigger was Napoleon's conquest of Spain, which left the colonies without a legitimate king. Elites also feared revolts from below, so many sought independence on their own terms.

In 1800 Spain claimed everything from California to Cape Horn, ruling through great viceroyalties, and Portugal ruled Brazil. American-born whites, the creoles, owned land and mines but were kept from top posts, which went to officials from Spain. Below them were Indigenous peoples, people of mixed descent and enslaved Africans. Next door, in French Haiti, enslaved people had risen in 1791 and were fighting for freedom.

dd-latam.q: What happened to Bolívar's dream of a united South America?
a: It came true and lasted until 1898
Spain accepted it as a self-governing dominion
It failed: Gran Colombia split apart by 1831
dd-latam.why: Gran Colombia broke into Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador in 1830 to 1831, and Bolívar died in 1830 as his union fell apart.

dd-latam.p:
Viceroyalty ruled from Mexico City, with Central America and the Caribbean

New Spain was Spain's richest colony, a major source of the world's silver.

Cuba was booming as a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans. It stayed Spanish until 1898.

Viceroyalty ruled from Bogotá, with the captaincy of Venezuela

Venezuela's cocoa-growing creole elite produced the leader of the north's independence wars, Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas in 1783.

Viceroyalty ruled from Lima; Chile a captaincy general within it, its south held by the Mapuche

Lima was the old heart of Spanish South America, and Peru's elite stayed loyal to Spain longer than any other.

dd-latam.h: Haiti, the first to break free
dd-latam.p: Saint-Domingue produced more sugar and coffee than any other colony in the world, worked by about half a million enslaved Africans. In August 1791 they rose up. A formerly enslaved man, Toussaint Louverture, became the revolution's leader and France abolished slavery in 1794. When Napoleon sent a large army in 1802 to restore French control, Toussaint was captured and died in a French prison, but his successor Jean-Jacques Dessalines, helped by yellow fever, defeated the French. Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804. It later armed Bolívar on condition that he free enslaved people. France forced Haiti to pay a huge indemnity from 1825, a burden that weighed on it for generations.

Haiti won independence in 1804. When Napoleon seized Spain in 1808, its colonies began to govern themselves. Simón Bolívar freed Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador, while José de San Martín crossed the Andes to free Chile and entered Lima. Their armies finished Spanish rule in Peru in 1824. Mexico broke free in 1821, and Brazil became an empire under a Portuguese prince in 1822.

The first independent country in Latin America

Haiti's revolution was the only successful uprising of enslaved people to found a state. France made it pay a huge indemnity from 1825 in return for recognition.

dd-latam.q: What was the real trigger for the independence movements in Spanish America?
a: The discovery of silver at Potosí
Napoleon's conquest of Spain, leaving the colonies without a legitimate king
A ban on the Catholic Church in the colonies
Bolívar's election as king of Spain
dd-latam.why: When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808 and deposed its king, the colonies set up their own governing councils, and many soon declared independence.

dd-latam.p:
Independent in 1821

Hidalgo's 1810 revolt was crushed, but in 1821 a royalist officer, Agustín de Iturbide, changed sides and Mexico won independence.

Freed by Bolívar and Sucre, 1819–1825

Venezuela declared independence in 1811, but its First Republic fell within a year. Victory at Carabobo in 1821 finally secured it.

Bolívar made Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama one state, Gran Colombia, in 1819–1822.

dd-latam.q: Which outcome of independence still shapes Latin America today?
a: Spanish and Portuguese remain the region's shared languages
Indigenous majorities have ruled most countries since 1825
The region is still governed from Madrid
dd-latam.why: The new states kept the languages of their former rulers, while power stayed mostly with creole elites rather than Indigenous or Black majorities.

dd-latam.p: Simón Bolívar, a rich creole from Caracas, lost two early attempts to free Venezuela. In 1819 he led a small army through flooded plains and over a freezing Andes pass to surprise the Spanish at Boyacá. Over the next five years he and his general Antonio José de Sucre freed what are now five countries, and Bolivia took his name. José de San Martín, a career officer born in Argentina, trained the Army of the Andes and led it across mountain passes in 1817, freeing Chile and then Lima. After meeting Bolívar in Guayaquil in 1822 he stepped aside and died in France in 1850. Bolívar died in 1830, his dream of a united South America in ruins.

Bolívar's Gran Colombia split into Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador in 1830–31, and the Central American federation broke into five states. Mexico lost about half its land to the United States by 1848. Paraguay was crushed by Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay in 1864–70. Spain kept Cuba and Puerto Rico until the US defeated it in 1898.

One state from 1819 to 1830–31

Venezuela left Gran Colombia in 1830 under José Antonio Páez, one of the many military strongmen, or caudillos, who ruled the new nations.

Colombia kept Panama until 1903, when Panama broke away with US backing.

dd-latam.q: Why did creole elites resent Spanish rule?
a: Spain had freed all enslaved people against their wishes
They were forbidden to own land or mines
Top posts went to Spaniards, and trade limits and taxes hurt them
Spain forced them to speak Portuguese
dd-latam.why: American-born creoles owned land and mines but were kept from top posts, and they disliked trade limits and new taxes from the Bourbon reforms.

dd-latam.p:
Texas broke away in 1836; the rest was lost in 1848

Mexico lost Texas in 1836 and, after the 1846–48 war, everything from California to New Mexico: about half its land, counting Texas.

The US gained California, Nevada, Utah and most of Arizona and New Mexico in 1848, after annexing Texas in 1845.

Independence was led mostly by creole elites, and for many people it changed less than its speeches promised. Enslaved people often won freedom by fighting, and Chile abolished slavery in 1823 and Mexico in 1829, but it lasted into the 1850s in Venezuela, Peru and Argentina, until 1886 in Spanish Cuba and until 1888 in Brazil. Indigenous communities lost some colonial protections, and their lands were often taken by new landowners. Generals who had won the wars, the caudillos, ruled many countries for decades. Still, the new republics abolished noble titles and, on paper at least, made all free men equal citizens.

About twenty new countries emerged, but Bolívar's dream of unity failed: Gran Colombia and the Central American federation broke apart. Military strongmen, border wars and foreign debt marked much of the century, and Mexico lost about half its land to the US. Slavery ended slowly, last in Brazil in 1888, and creole elites, not Indigenous or Black majorities, held power. Spanish and Portuguese remain the shared languages of the region today.

Spain loses Cuba and Puerto Rico to the US

dd-ireland.p: The 1801 Act of Union made all of Ireland part of the United Kingdom. From 1845 potato blight brought the Great Famine: about a million people died and millions emigrated. Campaigns for home rule failed until 1914, and in 1916 republicans staged the Easter Rising in Dublin.

steps: Six northern counties stay in the UK; the rest becomes the Irish Free State.
Catholics faced unfair voting, housing and jobs in Northern Ireland.
IRA and loyalist paramilitaries; British army; 3,500 killed.

r: Want to stay in the UK

dd-ireland.p: After a war of independence, the island was partitioned: 26 counties became the Irish Free State, later the Republic of Ireland, while six north-eastern counties stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland. There, from the late 1960s, three decades of conflict known as the Troubles killed about 3,500 people, until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998.

dd-ireland.q: How was Ireland divided after its war of independence?
a: Ireland was split between Britain and France
Six north-eastern counties stayed in the UK; 26 became a Free State
The whole island became an independent republic
Dublin stayed British while the rest became free
dd-ireland.why: Partition created Northern Ireland inside the UK and the self-governing Irish Free State, which became a republic in 1949.

dd-ireland.p: Centuries of English and then British rule had left most land in the hands of a mainly Protestant elite, while the Catholic majority were mostly poor tenants. The Famine deepened bitterness towards British government. In the north-east, however, Protestants descended largely from 17th-century settlers formed a majority and wanted to remain British. These two identities, nationalist and unionist, could not both be satisfied, and partition, then disputes over equality and power in Northern Ireland, followed.

dd-ireland.h: The Great Famine and the emigrants, 1845–1855
dd-ireland.p: Under the 1801 Act of Union, all of Ireland was ruled from London as part of the United Kingdom. Millions of poor Irish people lived almost entirely on potatoes, and from 1845 a blight rotted the crop year after year. About 1 million people died of hunger and disease, and by 1855 about 2 million had left, most for the United States, Canada and Britain.

dd-ireland.q: What did the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 change in Northern Ireland?
a: It made Northern Ireland part of the Republic
It ended all contact between North and South
It gave unionists sole control of the government
It set up power sharing and let a majority decide its status
dd-ireland.why: Northern Ireland stays in the UK while a majority there wishes, and its government must include both unionists and nationalists.

dd-ireland.p:
The whole island was part of the United Kingdom from 1801

About 8.5 million people lived on the island before the Famine. Death and emigration cut that by a fifth to a quarter, and the island still has fewer people today.

Ruled Ireland, and took in hundreds of thousands of emigrants

London's relief was limited by a belief that markets should not be disturbed. Public works and, in 1847, soup kitchens feeding about 3 million people a day came late and were soon cut back.

The US took the most famine emigrants. Irish Catholics met hostility from nativists but became a powerful force in the cities of the north-east.

About 100,000 people sailed for British North America in 1847 alone, on crowded ships that came to be called 'coffin ships'. Many thousands died at sea or on arrival.

The blight, a mould from the Americas, destroyed about three-quarters of the potato harvest in 1846, and 1847 became 'Black '47'. The government in London set up public works, then soup kitchens, but officials such as Charles Trevelyan believed the market should not be disturbed and that the Irish poor had to help themselves. Grain and cattle were still shipped out of Ireland in the worst years, though food imports in 1847 were larger. Evicted families crowded into workhouses where fever spread. Most historians blame callous policy and ideology rather than a plan to kill, but the Famine left a lasting grievance. In 1847 the Choctaw Nation in America, itself recently expelled from its lands, sent $170 in aid.

Most Irish Catholics wanted home rule or independence, but most Protestants in the north-east, unionists, wanted to stay in the United Kingdom. After the Easter Rising of 1916 and a war of independence from 1919 to 1921, the island was divided. Six north-eastern counties became Northern Ireland, inside the UK, and 26 counties became the self-governing Irish Free State, today's Ireland, in December 1922.

26 counties; a republic from 1949

The Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 split nationalists, and pro- and anti-Treaty forces fought a civil war in 1922–23. The Free State left the Commonwealth and became a republic in 1949.

dd-ireland.q: Why did the Great Famine leave such lasting bitterness towards British government?
a: Britain had planted the potato blight deliberately
Ireland had no contact with Britain at the time
London's limited relief, shaped by belief in the free market, came late
The Famine was confined to England
dd-ireland.why: Officials believed markets should not be disturbed; relief came late and was cut back, and most historians blame callous policy rather than a plan to kill.

dd-ireland.p:
Including Northern Ireland's six counties

Britain created Northern Ireland under the Government of Ireland Act of 1920. Its six counties had a Protestant, unionist majority of about two-thirds, and a large Catholic minority.

Nationalists, mostly Catholic, saw Ireland as one nation with a right to rule itself. Unionists, mostly Protestant and concentrated in Ulster, saw themselves as British and feared a Dublin parliament dominated by Catholics. When Home Rule seemed certain in 1912, about 470,000 unionists signed the Ulster Covenant or its women's Declaration, and both sides formed armed volunteer forces. Partition left a Catholic minority of about a third in Northern Ireland, where unionist governments held power from 1921 to 1972; Catholics complained of discrimination in jobs, housing and voting boundaries. The Irish Free State, in turn, became overwhelmingly Catholic. Symbols still divide: many nationalists say Derry, many unionists Londonderry.

dd-ireland.q: Why did Brexit make the Irish border a delicate question again?
a: It forced Ireland to leave the European Union too
The border now separates the EU from a UK outside it
It undid partition and reunited the island
It ended power sharing in Northern Ireland
dd-ireland.why: Ireland and the UK joined the European Community together in 1973; once the UK left, the Irish border became a frontier between the EU and a non-member.

dd-ireland.p: In Northern Ireland, unionists, mostly Protestant, ran the government for 50 years, and many Catholics, mostly nationalists, protested discrimination. In 1968–69 civil rights marches led to riots, and British troops arrived. For three decades republican and loyalist paramilitaries and the security forces were caught in a conflict that killed about 3,500 people. The United Kingdom, Ireland and the local parties, with help from the United States, reached the Good Friday Agreement in 1998.
Ireland's 1937 constitution claimed the whole island. In 1998 voters there approved the peace deal by 94% and dropped that claim; in Northern Ireland 71% voted yes.

dd-ireland.q: Why could Ireland not simply become one self-governing country in 1921?
a: Unionists in the north-east, mostly Protestant, wanted to stay British
Nationalists wanted to remain in the United Kingdom
The United States opposed Irish independence
Most Catholics lived in Ulster and wanted British rule
dd-ireland.why: Nationalist and unionist identities could not both be satisfied, so the north-east, with a unionist majority, stayed in the UK.

dd-ireland.p:
Including Northern Ireland

Britain sent troops in August 1969 and ruled Northern Ireland directly from London from 1972. About 3,500 people died in 1969–2001, over half of them civilians; the IRA's bombs also struck English cities.

Secret contacts in the early 1990s led to IRA and loyalist ceasefires in 1994. The Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998 rested on compromise. Northern Ireland stays in the UK as long as a majority there wishes, and Ireland dropped its constitutional claim to the whole island. A power-sharing government must include both unionists and nationalists, and new bodies link North and South. Paramilitary prisoners were released early, and the IRA declared an end to its armed campaign in 2005. Voters approved the deal by 71% in Northern Ireland and 94% in the Republic. John Hume and David Trimble shared the 1998 Nobel Peace Prize. The power-sharing government has often been suspended, but large-scale violence has not returned.

Ireland became a sovereign republic, joined the European Community with the UK in 1973 and grew into one of Europe's richest economies. Under the Good Friday Agreement, Northern Ireland is governed by power sharing between unionists and nationalists, and its status can change only if a majority there votes for it. Since February 2024 Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill has served as the first nationalist First Minister. Brexit made the Irish border a delicate question again.

pts: Act of Union makes Ireland part of the United Kingdom
The Great Famine: about a million die, millions emigrate
Easter Rising in Dublin
Anglo-Irish Treaty; partition and the Irish Free State
Riots in Derry and Belfast; British troops are deployed
Good Friday Agreement approved by voters on both sides of the border

dd-mexico.p: Mexico's war of independence began with Miguel Hidalgo's revolt in 1810 and ended in 1821. Decades of coups followed, Texas broke away, and after the US–Mexican War of 1846–48 Mexico lost about half its territory. Benito Juárez defeated a French-installed emperor in the 1860s, and Porfirio Díaz then ruled for over 30 years.

items: Deep ties with the US economy.

dd-mexico.q: How much territory did Mexico lose to the US in 1848?

dd-mexico.p: The revolution of 1910–1920 toppled him and killed hundreds of thousands. Its heirs formed a party, later called the PRI, that ruled for 71 years, nationalised oil in 1938 and redistributed land. NAFTA bound Mexico to the US economy from 1994, the PRI lost power in 2000, and from 2006 a war against drug cartels brought soaring violence.

Independent Mexico inherited deep inequality from Spanish rule and a huge, thinly settled north that it could not defend against an expanding United States. Díaz's rapid growth enriched foreign investors and large landowners while most villagers lost their land, which fuelled the revolution. Afterwards the ruling party kept peace by absorbing unions, farmers and rivals and by managing elections. Its economic crises in the 1980s and 1990s pushed Mexico towards free trade and, in time, real democracy.

dd-mexico.q: What did the Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920 achieve?
a: It won Mexico's independence from Spain
It toppled Porfirio Díaz, and its heirs ruled Mexico for 71 years
It returned Texas and California to Mexico
dd-mexico.why: The revolution ended Díaz's long rule at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives, and the party its victors formed, later the PRI, governed until 2000.

dd-mexico.p: In 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo launched a revolt against Spanish rule, and in 1821 Mexico won independence, stretching from Oregon's border to Central America. Within a generation it lost about half its land. Texas broke away in 1836 and joined the United States in 1845. The US then invaded, took Mexico City in 1847, and in 1848 forced Mexico to cede California and the Southwest.
Mexico won independence in 1821 under Agustín de Iturbide, who was proclaimed emperor in 1822. It became a republic in 1824, but coups and civil wars followed for decades.

Texas 1836–45, the Mexican Cession 1848, the Gadsden Purchase 1853

The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the US California, Nevada, Utah and most of Arizona and New Mexico, and confirmed Texas as American. The US paid $15 million.

dd-mexico.q: How did the PRI keep power for 71 years?
a: By letting presidents rule for life
By absorbing unions, farmers and rivals and by managing elections
dd-mexico.why: The party traded jobs, land and favours for votes, rigged results when needed and repressed dissent, a system called 'the perfect dictatorship'.

dd-mexico.p:
Joined the Mexican Empire in 1822, left in 1823

Spain's Central American lands joined Iturbide's empire in 1822 and left in 1823, except Chiapas, which chose to stay with Mexico in 1824.

Costa Rica was the southernmost land briefly tied to the Mexican Empire. Central America formed its own federation in 1823.

From 1929 the revolution's party, renamed the PRI in 1946, won every presidential election for 71 years. Presidents served a single six-year term and then picked their successor, a ritual called the 'dedazo', the tap of the finger. The party gave jobs, land and favours to unions and peasant leagues in return for votes, and rigged results when needed. It also repressed dissent: on 2 October 1968, days before the Mexico City Olympics, troops fired on student protesters at Tlatelolco, killing dozens and possibly hundreds. In 1990 the Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa called the system 'the perfect dictatorship'. It ended peacefully when Vicente Fox of the opposition PAN won the presidency in 2000.

The 1917 constitution promised land to the villages and made the nation the owner of everything under the soil. President Lázaro Cárdenas (1934–40) carried it out: he handed out about 18 million hectares to peasant communities, and on 18 March 1938 he expropriated the foreign oil companies, creating the state firm Pemex. Mexicans queued to donate money, jewellery and even chickens to help pay compensation. The revolution also had a cultural side: the government paid painters such as Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros to cover public buildings with giant murals of Mexico's Indigenous past and its struggles, art still seen by millions.

In 1910 Francisco Madero rose against Porfirio Díaz, who had ruled Mexico for over 30 years. Díaz fell in 1911, but Madero was murdered in 1913, and rival armies, including Pancho Villa's in the north and Emiliano Zapata's peasants in the south, fought for a decade. The United States intervened twice, and Germany tried to lure Mexico into World War I. Hundreds of thousands died.

Torn by revolution and civil war

Estimates of the revolution's dead range from several hundred thousand to over a million, and many more fled north. The victors' party later ruled Mexico for 71 years.

dd-mexico.q: Why did Mexico lose about half its territory in the 1830s and 1840s?
a: It sold the land to pay for independence
Its huge, thinly settled north was indefensible against the expanding US
Britain took it in exchange for oil rights
dd-mexico.why: Texas broke away in 1836, and after the US–Mexican War of 1846 to 1848 Mexico ceded California and the Southwest.

dd-mexico.p:
Occupied Veracruz in 1914 and chased Villa in 1916–17

About 10,000 US troops under General John Pershing hunted Villa in Chihuahua in 1916–17 without catching him. Many Mexicans moved to the US to escape the fighting.

Offered Mexico an alliance against the US in 1917

In the 1917 Zimmermann Telegram, Germany offered to help Mexico regain Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined the war. Mexico declined, but the leak helped bring the US into the war.

dd-mexico.q: What is Mexico's relationship with the United States like today?
a: Mexico trades mainly with China and little with the US
Deeply tied economically, but strained by trade, migration and cartels
The US has annexed northern Mexico
Mexico has closed its border to US trade
dd-mexico.why: Since NAFTA Mexico has become the largest US trading partner, while tariffs, migration and drugs and guns crossing the border strain relations.

dd-mexico.p: Mexican smuggling gangs grew rich in the 1990s, when cocaine routes from Colombia shifted from the Caribbean to Mexico. In December 2006 President Felipe Calderón sent the army against the cartels. Killing their leaders split them into warring factions, and violence soared: official INEGI figures record well over 400,000 homicides since 2007, and more than 130,000 people are listed as missing. Most guns used by the cartels are smuggled from the US, the main market for their drugs, now including fentanyl. The jailed Sinaloa boss Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán is serving life in the US, and in February 2026 troops killed 'El Mencho', head of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

Mexico, home to about 133 million people, sends roughly four-fifths of its exports to the United States, its partner with Canada in the USMCA trade pact, which replaced NAFTA in 2020. At its July 2026 review the US declined to extend the pact unchanged, amid US tariffs on Mexican cars and steel. President Claudia Sheinbaum has stepped up the fight against drug cartels while rejecting any US military action on Mexican soil.

Morena, the party founded by Andrés Manuel López Obrador, has governed since 2018. Official INEGI figures record well over 400,000 homicides since 2007, and more than 130,000 people listed as missing.

Free trade since NAFTA in 1994; USMCA since 2020

Mexico was the largest US trading partner in 2025. In 2025 the US labelled several Mexican cartels terrorist groups. Over 35 million people of Mexican origin live in the US.

Canada joined NAFTA with Mexico and the US in 1994. In 2026 both Canada and Mexico sought a long extension of the USMCA, while the US pressed for changes.

dd-mexico.q: What fuelled the revolution against Porfirio Díaz?
a: Growth enriched foreign investors and landowners while villagers lost their land
Díaz had refused all foreign investment
Díaz had nationalised the oil industry
dd-mexico.why: Díaz's rapid growth benefited a few, and the 1917 constitution later promised land to the villages and national ownership of minerals and oil.

dd-mexico.p:
Many migrants crossed Mexico from here towards the US

Guatemala shares Mexico's southern border. For years migrants from Central America, and later from much further away, crossed Mexico to reach the US.

Honduras was a major source of migrants in the 2010s, driven by poverty and gang violence. Crossings through Mexico fell sharply in 2025 under tighter US and Mexican controls.

Since NAFTA, car plants and electronics factories have made northern Mexico part of one North American production line, and by 2023 Mexico had overtaken China as the largest source of US imports. That closeness brings pressure. In 2025 and 2026 the US imposed tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminium, linked trade talks to migration and fentanyl, and declined to extend the USMCA unchanged at its 2026 review. President Sheinbaum, who took office in October 2024, sent troops to the border, sent dozens of cartel figures to the US and raised tariffs on Chinese goods, while insisting that any US military action on Mexican soil would violate its sovereignty.

Mexico is now deeply tied to the US: it is the largest US trading partner, tens of millions of Americans have Mexican roots, and migrants send home about $60 billion a year. Cartel violence, fed by US demand for drugs and by guns from the US, remains its gravest problem. Since 2018 Morena, the movement of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, has dominated politics, and in 2024 Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first woman president.

dd-germany.p: In 1871, after wars with Denmark, Austria and France, Prussia's Otto von Bismarck united the German states into an empire, which grew into Europe's industrial powerhouse. Germany lost World War I, and the Weimar Republic that followed was battered by hyperinflation and the Great Depression. In 1933 Adolf Hitler took power, built a dictatorship, launched World War II and murdered about 6 million Jews in the Holocaust.

dd-germany.s: Germans have a word for coming to terms with the past: Vergangenheitsbewältigung.
dd-germany.why: Remembering Nazi crimes is central to German identity.

dd-germany.p: Defeated in 1945, Germany lost its eastern lands and was occupied, and in 1949 it split into a democratic West and a communist East. The Berlin Wall divided the two from 1961 until crowds breached it in 1989, and Germany reunited peacefully in 1990.

Germany came late to national unity, and it was made by Prussian arms rather than by a popular revolution. Its rapid rise unsettled its neighbours, and its leaders' gamble in 1914 led to a defeat many Germans refused to accept. The Versailles treaty, economic collapse and fear of communism helped the Nazis win mass support. After 1945 the Cold War decided Germany's fate: the Soviet Union and the Western Allies each built a German state in their own image.

dd-germany.q: How was Germany first united in 1871?
a: Through Prussian-led wars against Denmark, Austria and France
By a popular revolution that overthrew all the German kings
By a vote of all German-speaking peoples, including Austria
By a treaty imposed by Britain
dd-germany.why: Bismarck's 'blood and iron' made Germany through three short wars, and the King of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in 1871.

dd-germany.p: Prussia's chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, united Germany through three short wars: against Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–71. On 18 January 1871 the King of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles. The new German Empire left Austria out, took Alsace-Lorraine from France and stretched east across much of today's Poland.

25 states led by Prussia, founded 1871

The empire joined Prussia with kingdoms such as Bavaria, Saxony and Württemberg. Prussia held about two-thirds of its land, and its king was always emperor.

Today's Poland was then split between Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary. Germany held the largest share, including Silesia, Pomerania, Poznań and much of the Baltic coast.

Left out of the new Germany after losing to Prussia in 1866

Austria had led the German Confederation until Prussia beat it in 1866. Bismarck then built a smaller Germany without it, and the two became allies in 1879.

Bohemia and Moravia, home to many German speakers, belonged to Austria. The decisive battle of 1866 was fought here, at Königgrätz.

dd-germany.q: What happened to Germany's eastern lands after 1945?
a: They became an independent Prussian state
They were shared between Britain and France
They went to Poland and the USSR; millions of Germans were expelled
dd-germany.why: Everything east of the Oder and Neisse rivers went to Poland and the Soviet Union, and some 12 million Germans fled or were expelled westwards.

dd-germany.p:
Lost Alsace and part of Lorraine in 1871

France lost the war of 1870–71, paid a large indemnity and gave up Alsace and part of Lorraine. Winning them back became a French national aim.

In 1862 Otto von Bismarck told Prussia's parliament that the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes but by 'iron and blood'. He then fought three short wars in seven years and let France's declaration of war in 1870 unite the southern German states behind Prussia. As chancellor until 1890 he built a web of alliances to keep France isolated, and introduced the world's first national health insurance, accident insurance and old-age pensions, partly to win workers away from the socialists. His successor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, let the alliances lapse and built a navy to rival Britain's, helping create the tensions that led to 1914.

The Weimar Republic, founded in 1919, gave women the vote and fostered a burst of art, science and film, but it was blamed for the hated peace treaty. In 1923 hyperinflation made money almost worthless: a loaf of bread cost billions of marks by November. A few calmer years ended with the Great Depression, which left about 6 million Germans jobless by 1932. The Nazis became the largest party in July 1932 with 37% of the vote, and conservative politicians, believing they could control him, had Hitler appointed chancellor in January 1933. Within months he had banned other parties, crushed the unions and opened the first concentration camps.

Defeat in World War I cost Germany its colonies and about an eighth of its land in Europe, including Alsace-Lorraine and a corridor to the sea for the new Poland. Hitler's war to undo this ended in 1945 with a far greater loss: everything east of the Oder and Neisse rivers went to Poland and the Soviet Union. Some 12 million Germans fled or were expelled westwards.
Germany lost about a quarter of its 1937 territory in 1945. West Germany accepted the Oder–Neisse border in 1970, and united Germany confirmed it by treaty in 1990.

dd-germany.q: Which conditions helped the Nazis win mass support?
a: A booming economy and a popular peace treaty
The Versailles treaty, economic collapse and fear of communism
A Soviet invasion of Germany in 1930
dd-germany.why: Hyperinflation in 1923 and the Great Depression, which left about 6 million jobless, discredited the Weimar Republic and made the Nazis the largest party in 1932.

dd-germany.p:
Under the 1919 Treaty of Versailles and later votes

France regained Alsace-Lorraine in 1918. Nazi Germany annexed it in 1940, and it returned to France in 1945.

Belgium received the small districts of Eupen and Malmedy in 1920. Their German-speaking community still has its own parliament.

Lands east of the Oder–Neisse line, 1945

Poland gained Poznań and a corridor to the Baltic in 1919, then Silesia, Pomerania and southern East Prussia in 1945, while losing its own east to the Soviet Union. Its whole map moved west.

The Soviet Union took northern East Prussia around Königsberg in 1945. As Kaliningrad, it is now a Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania.

dd-germany.q: What is united Germany's place in Europe today?
a: It is outside the EU but tied to it by treaty
It is the EU's largest economy, now spending heavily on defence
It still has two separate governments
It depends on Russian gas more than ever
dd-germany.why: Since 1990 Germany has been the EU's largest economy and most populous member, and after 2022 it cut its reliance on Russian gas and raised defence spending.

dd-germany.p: East Germany called its border fortifications an 'anti-fascist protection rampart', but their real purpose was to stop people leaving: about 2.7 million had fled west between 1949 and 1961. Behind the Wall, the East offered jobs, cheap rents and childcare, but long waits for goods: ordering a Trabant car could mean waiting over ten years. The Stasi secret police employed about 91,000 staff by 1989 and relied on a large network of informers, often neighbours, colleagues or even spouses. After reunification, citizens could read their own Stasi files, and millions of people have asked to see them.

dd-germany.h: Divided Germany in the Cold War, 1949–1990
dd-germany.p: In 1949 the zones held by the Western Allies became West Germany, a democracy that joined NATO, and the Soviet zone became East Germany, a communist state in the Warsaw Pact. In 1961 East Germany walled off West Berlin. In 1989 Hungary opened its border, East Germans fled west or protested, and the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November. Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.

West Germany (FRG) and East Germany (GDR), 1949–1990

West Germany grew rich in the 'economic miracle' of the 1950s; East Germany became the Eastern bloc's most industrial state but lagged far behind. On 3 October 1990 the East's states joined the Federal Republic.

Western alliance, founded 1949; West Germany joined in 1955

The US kept large forces in West Germany and flew in supplies during the Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948–49. Tens of thousands of US troops are still based in Germany, though in May 2026 the US announced it would cut their number.

Britain held an occupation zone in north-west Germany and a sector of Berlin, and with France, the US and the Soviet Union signed the 1990 treaty ending Allied rights.

dd-germany.q: Why was Germany split into two states in 1949?
a: Germans voted to divide their country
France insisted on a separate Rhineland state
The Cold War: each side built a Germany in its own image
The Nazi party survived in the east
dd-germany.why: The Western Allies' zones became democratic West Germany, in NATO, and the Soviet zone became communist East Germany, in the Warsaw Pact.

dd-germany.p:
Soviet-led alliance, 1955–1991; East Germany was a founder

The Soviet Union kept hundreds of thousands of troops in East Germany. In 1990 Mikhail Gorbachev accepted a united Germany in NATO, and the last Russian troops left in 1994.

Poland's Solidarity movement won partly free elections in June 1989, months before the Wall fell, showing that change in the bloc was possible.

After 1945 Germany slowly confronted the Nazi era. West Germany agreed in 1952 to pay reparations to Israel and to Holocaust survivors, and its own courts tried Auschwitz guards in the 1960s. In 1970 Chancellor Willy Brandt knelt in silence at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, an image that came to symbolise German remorse. Today schoolchildren visit former camps, Berlin has a large Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe beside the Brandenburg Gate, and over 100,000 small brass 'Stumbling Stones' set in pavements across Europe name individual victims outside the homes where they lived.

West Germany built a stable democracy and, with France, the core of what became the European Union. Since 1990 united Germany has been the EU's largest economy and most populous member, with about 83 million people. Its long reliance on Russian gas and on exports to China was shaken after 2022, and under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in office since May 2025, it is spending heavily on defence. Gaps in wealth and voting between east and west remain.

Hitler becomes chancellor and builds a Nazi dictatorship
Defeat in World War II; Germany is occupied and loses its east
East Germany builds the Berlin Wall
The Wall falls on 9 November; Germany reunites on 3 October 1990

dd-iran.p: In 1906 a constitutional revolution gave Iran a parliament, but Russia and Britain soon split it into zones of influence, and oil struck in 1908 made it a prize. Reza Shah seized power in the 1920s and modernised by force. In 1951 Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the British-run oil industry, and in 1953 a coup backed by the CIA and Britain's MI6 removed him.

steps: The US and UK overthrow elected PM Mossadegh.
Modernising but repressive, backed by the US.
Ayatollah Khomeini creates an Islamic Republic.

dd-iran.p: His son Mohammad Reza Shah ruled ever more harshly until a mass uprising in 1978–79 brought Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini to power and created an Islamic republic. Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war. Decades of sanctions and nuclear disputes followed, and in 2026 US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

Iran's oil and its position between Russia, the Gulf and India drew outside powers in, and many Iranians came to see foreign meddling, above all the 1953 coup, as the root of their troubles. The Shah's rapid Westernisation, repression by his SAVAK secret police and a widening gap between rich and poor united clerics, leftists, liberals and bazaar merchants against him. After 1979 the new state defined itself against the US and Israel, which in turn saw its nuclear programme, missiles and armed allies as a threat.

dd-iran.q: What did the revolution of 1978 to 1979 do to Iran?
a: It restored the shah after a coup
It made Iran a communist state allied to Moscow
It ended the monarchy and made Iran an Islamic republic
It divided Iran into Russian and British zones
dd-iran.why: A mass uprising drove out Mohammad Reza Shah and brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power, creating a state ruled under a senior Islamic jurist.

dd-iran.p: In 1906 Iranians forced the Qajar shah to accept a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis. A year later Russia and Britain, ruler of India, split Persia into zones of influence without asking it. Oil struck in 1908 made the south vital to Britain. In 1925 an army officer, Reza Khan, made himself shah, and in 1935 he asked the world to call the country Iran.

Independent, but split into zones of influence in 1907

Persia stayed independent, but under the 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention Russia claimed the north, Britain the south-east, and a neutral zone lay between. Both powers occupied parts of it in World War I.

Took Persia's Caucasus lands in 1813–1828

Russia had taken Persia's lands in the Caucasus by 1828. In 1911 its troops helped crush Persia's constitutional government.

Northern Azerbaijan was Persian until Russia won it in 1813–1828. Many Azerbaijanis still live in Iran, which has more of them than Azerbaijan does.

dd-iran.q: How did the Islamic Republic define itself after 1979?
a: As a close ally of the United States
As a neutral state with no foreign interests
Against the US and Israel, building armed allies abroad
dd-iran.why: Its enmity with the US and Israel, and its allies such as Hezbollah and the Houthis, shaped decades of sanctions and nuclear disputes.

dd-iran.p:
Britain's empire in South Asia

Britain wanted Persia's south-east as a buffer for India. From 1914 the Royal Navy ran on oil, much of it from Persia.

In 1951 Iran's parliament nationalised the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, which had paid Iran far less than it paid the British government in taxes. Its champion, the elderly Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, became a national hero. Britain answered with a boycott of Iranian oil, and after failing to dislodge him it won over the US, which feared a communist takeover. In August 1953 a CIA and MI6 plan, carried out with Iranian officers, paid crowds and royalists, toppled Mosaddegh, who was jailed and then kept under house arrest until his death. The Shah returned stronger, and US firms took a large share of Iran's oil. The CIA formally acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.

Khomeini's system rests on velayat-e faqih, guardianship by a senior Islamic jurist. The Supreme Leader commands the armed forces, appoints the head of the judiciary and state media, and has the final say on big decisions. Iranians do elect a president and parliament, but the Guardian Council, twelve clerics and lawyers, vets every candidate and can strike down laws it judges un-Islamic. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, created in 1979 to protect the revolution, grew into a military and business empire. An elected Assembly of Experts chooses the leader: Khomeini ruled until 1989, Ali Khamenei until 2026, and in March 2026 the Assembly chose his son Mojtaba.

In 1979 a revolution drove out Mohammad Reza Shah, and Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini made Iran an Islamic republic. Students seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days. In 1980 Iraq invaded, hoping to seize oil-rich land from a weakened neighbour. With loans from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, it fought Iran to a standstill until a 1988 ceasefire. Perhaps 500,000 people died.

Islamic Republic from April 1979

Iran lost most of the war's dead. It used volunteers, including teenage Basij fighters, in mass attacks, and accepted a UN ceasefire in 1988, which Khomeini likened to drinking poison.

dd-iran.q: Why did many Iranians come to resent foreign powers?
a: Foreign meddling, above all the 1953 coup that removed Mosaddegh
Foreign powers had refused to buy Iranian oil since 1908
Britain had annexed Iran as a colony
The US had invaded Iran in 1980
dd-iran.why: After Mosaddegh nationalised the British-run oil industry, a CIA and MI6-backed coup toppled him in 1953, and the shah returned stronger.

dd-iran.p:
Under Saddam Hussein, invaded Iran in 1980

Saddam Hussein expected a quick victory over a country in chaos. Iraq used chemical weapons against Iranian troops and its own Kurds.

Lent Iraq tens of billions of dollars

Saudi Arabia feared Iran's revolution would spread among Gulf Shias and lent Iraq billions of dollars.

Kuwait lent Iraq billions too. Iraq's demand to have the debts cancelled helped lead to its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.

dd-iran.q: What happened in 2026 that has left Iran's future deeply uncertain?
a: US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Khamenei, and war continued
Iran signed a lasting peace treaty with Israel
The shah's son was restored to the throne
Iran joined the 2015 nuclear deal again
dd-iran.why: Strikes killed Khamenei in February 2026, his son Mojtaba succeeded him, and the war disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

dd-iran.p: Iranian women are highly educated, and for years made up about half or more of university students, but since the early 1980s the law has required them to cover their hair in public. In September 2022 Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died after being detained by the morality police over her headscarf. Protests spread across the country under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom', with women burning their scarves in the streets. Security forces killed over 500 people, according to the group Iran Human Rights, and several protesters were executed. A new wave of protests over a collapsing currency began in December 2025. Iran's government said over 3,000 died in the January 2026 crackdown; rights groups counted more.

In June 2025 Israel and the United States bombed Iran's nuclear sites in a twelve-day war. On 28 February 2026 they struck again, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; his son Mojtaba succeeded him. Iran fired missiles at Israel, US bases and Gulf oil sites, and choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. A truce agreed in April broke down in July. In October 2026 the US paused strikes for talks, but attacks on ships went on.
Iran's government and the rights group HRANA each counted over 3,000 Iranian dead in the 2026 war. Iran calls the strikes illegal aggression.

Attacked Iran in June 2025 and from February 2026

The US cited Iran's nuclear programme, missiles and killing of protesters. It blockaded Iran's ports, and over 20 US service members had been killed by autumn 2026.

Israel saw Iran's nuclear programme and armed allies as a threat to its existence. Iran fired hundreds of missiles at it in 2026.

dd-iran.q: Why did such different groups unite against the shah in the 1970s?
a: He had given up Iran's oil to the Soviet Union
Rapid Westernisation, secret-police repression and a widening wealth gap
He had declared war on Iraq
He had made Iran an Islamic state
dd-iran.why: Clerics, leftists, liberals and bazaar merchants were united against the shah's rule, enforced by the SAVAK secret police.

dd-iran.p:
Struck by Iranian missiles and drones; most host US bases

Saudi Arabia was hit by Iranian strikes and, according to Reuters, struck back quietly. In October 2026 Houthi missiles hit Riyadh's main airport, killing at least 13 people.

The UAE, home to US forces and a hub for Gulf trade, was struck repeatedly by Iranian missiles and drones.

Under the 2015 nuclear deal Iran limited its uranium enrichment in return for sanctions relief, but President Trump pulled the US out in 2018, and Iran then enriched uranium to 60%, close to weapons grade, while saying it did not seek a bomb. After Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023, Israel badly weakened Hezbollah and Iran's other allies, and Iran and Israel struck each other directly for the first time in 2024. In June 2025 Israel and the US bombed Iran's nuclear sites. Their 2026 war, which killed Khamenei, disrupted the world's oil supply. By October 2026 a spring truce had collapsed, and talks through Pakistan and Qatar had not ended the fighting.

The Islamic Republic built a network of allied armed groups, such as Lebanon's Hezbollah and Yemen's Houthis, and a nuclear programme it says is peaceful. Sanctions hurt its economy, and protest movements, from 2009 to 2022 and again in January 2026, were put down by force. The 2025 and 2026 wars with Israel and the US killed thousands, disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and left Iran's future deeply uncertain.

Islamic Revolution; students seize the US embassy

US and Israeli strikes kill Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei

dd-koreas.p: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it harshly until its defeat in 1945. American and Soviet troops then split the peninsula at the 38th parallel, meant as a temporary line. In 1948 two states appeared: a US-backed South under Syngman Rhee and a Soviet-backed North under Kim Il Sung. In June 1950 the North invaded.

dd-koreas.s: The Korean War ended with a peace treaty.
dd-koreas.why: Only an armistice in 1953: technically still at war.

dd-koreas.p: A US-led UN force drove it back almost to China, China's armies pushed the UN south again, and the front settled near the old line. An armistice in July 1953 created the Demilitarised Zone, but no peace treaty. The South later grew rich and democratic, while the North became a nuclear-armed family dictatorship.

Korea was divided because the Cold War began just as Japan's empire collapsed. Neither superpower would accept a united Korea run by the other's side, and both Korean leaders wanted to reunite the country on their own terms. The war froze the split, and each state then built its identity in opposition to the other.

dd-koreas.q: How did the Korean War of 1950 to 1953 end?
a: With a peace treaty reuniting Korea
With an armistice near the old line, but no peace treaty
With North Korea conquering the whole peninsula
With Korea returned to Japanese rule
dd-koreas.why: After the front swung south and north, it settled near the 38th parallel; the 1953 armistice created the Demilitarised Zone, but no peace treaty was ever signed.

dd-koreas.p: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it for 35 years. It built railways, mines and factories, but for Japan's benefit, and it banned protest and later tried to replace Korean language and names with Japanese ones. Korea, then one country covering today's North Korea and South Korea, was freed when Japan surrendered in August 1945.
Japan won control of Korea by defeating China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, made it a protectorate, and annexed it in August 1910.

Taiwan from 1895, Korea from 1910

Seoul, renamed Keijō, was the colonial capital. Hundreds of thousands of Koreans were sent to work in Japan, many by force, and many women were forced into military brothels.

Japan built heavy industry and hydroelectric dams in the north, which left the North more industrialised than the South in 1945.

dd-koreas.q: How did the two Koreas develop after the war?
a: Both became poor military dictatorships to this day
The North grew rich while the South stayed poor
Both became democracies allied to China
The South became rich and democratic; the North a nuclear-armed dictatorship
dd-koreas.why: Export-led growth and the 1987 protests made the South rich and democratic, while the Kim family built nuclear weapons in an isolated North.

dd-koreas.p:
Japanese puppet state in northeast China, 1932–1945

Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and ran it as Manchukuo. Korean communist guerrillas, including the young Kim Il Sung, fought the Japanese there.

On 25 June 1950 North Korean tanks crossed the 38th parallel, took Seoul in three days and drove the South's army and the first US troops into a corner around Pusan. In September General Douglas MacArthur landed at Inchon, cut the North's supply lines and pushed north towards the Chinese border. In late 1950 hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops struck back, and in the frozen mountains around the Chosin Reservoir US Marines had to fight their way out. From mid-1951 the war became a bloody stalemate near the 38th parallel while truce talks dragged on for two years. Common estimates put the dead at about 3 million, more than half of them civilians.

In 1960 South Korea was one of the world's poorest countries, with an income of under $200 a person, and most economists believe the more industrialised North was richer into the 1970s. Under the military ruler Park Chung-hee, who seized power in 1961, the state steered cheap loans to family-run conglomerates such as Samsung and Hyundai and pushed exports: first wigs and textiles, then ships, steel, cars and microchips. Growth was rapid but came with repression until mass protests won democracy in 1987. By 2025, according to the Bank of Korea, the South's income per person was about $37,000, roughly 28 times the North's, and its total economy about 56 times larger.

In August 1945 the US and the Soviet Union split Korea at the 38th parallel, and in 1948 two rival states were founded. In June 1950 North Korea invaded South Korea and pushed its army back to Pusan. A UN force led by the United States counterattacked from Inchon, then China intervened. The 1953 armistice froze the front near where it began, and no peace treaty was ever signed.

Backed by the Soviet Union and China

The Democratic People's Republic of Korea was founded in September 1948 under Kim Il Sung, who invaded the South in June 1950 with Stalin's approval.

a: Koreans voted for two separate states
China and Japan agreed to share the peninsula
The Cold War began as Japan's empire fell; the superpowers split it
The Korean War had split the country
dd-koreas.why: US and Soviet troops split Korea at the 38th parallel, meant as a temporary line, and neither would accept a united Korea run by the other's side.

dd-koreas.p:
Backed by UN forces from 16 countries, led by the US

The Republic of Korea was founded in August 1948 under Syngman Rhee. Seoul changed hands four times during the war.

Kim Il Sung ruled from 1948 until his death in 1994, building a personality cult and the ideology of Juche, or self-reliance. His son Kim Jong Il inherited a country whose economy collapsed when Soviet aid ended. In the famine of the mid-1990s, estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to over two million. Since 2011 the grandson, Kim Jong Un, has ruled. A 2014 UN inquiry found crimes against humanity, including political prison camps estimated to hold 80,000–120,000 people. Kim had his uncle executed in 2013, and his half-brother was murdered with a nerve agent in Malaysia in 2017. His daughter, Kim Ju Ae, is widely seen as a possible successor.

dd-koreas.q: What did North Korea signal about reunification in 2024?
a: It agreed to reunify under the South's government
It called the South a hostile state and dropped reunification
It signed a peace treaty with the South
It withdrew from its alliance with China
dd-koreas.why: Kim Jong Un formally gave up reunification and signed a defence treaty with Russia, deepening the peninsula's split.

dd-koreas.h: The two Koreas and their allies, 2026
dd-koreas.p: More than 70 years after the war, the two Koreas could hardly be more different. South Korea is a democracy and a rich exporter, with a treaty alliance with the United States. North Korea is a one-party dynasty under Kim Jong Un, with nuclear weapons and treaties with China and, since 2024, Russia. In 2024 Kim declared the South a hostile state and dropped the goal of reunification.
North Korea has about 26 million people and has been ruled by the Kim family since 1948. It has carried out six nuclear tests, the last in 2017.

Treaties with China (1961) and Russia (2024)

China has been North Korea's treaty ally since 1961 and handles the large majority of its trade.

Russia and North Korea signed a mutual defence treaty in June 2024. North Korea then sent thousands of troops and large amounts of ammunition to help Russia against Ukraine.

dd-koreas.q: What turned the Korean War into a long stalemate after late 1950?
a: China's armies entered and pushed UN forces south again
The Soviet Union invaded South Korea
The US withdrew all its troops
Japan joined the war on the North's side
dd-koreas.why: As UN forces neared its border, China intervened with hundreds of thousands of troops, and from mid-1951 the front stuck near the 38th parallel.

dd-koreas.p: South Korea has about 51 million people and has been a democracy since 1987. Its income per person is roughly 28 times the North's, by Bank of Korea estimates.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 2003 and tested its first nuclear device in 2006. Five more tests followed, the largest in 2017, which it called a hydrogen bomb. It has also tested missiles that experts believe can reach the whole United States. Years of talks, sanctions and three meetings between Kim Jong Un and President Trump in 2018–19 failed to stop the programme, and in 2023 North Korea wrote its nuclear status into its constitution. SIPRI estimated it had about 60 warheads in January 2026. Its closer ties with Russia since 2024 have brought it money, oil and, many analysts fear, military technology.

The Korean War killed millions and left the peninsula one of the most heavily armed places on Earth, with US troops still in the South. Millions of families were separated. South Korea became a top-15 world economy and a cultural force, from Samsung to K-pop. North Korea, poor and isolated, has built nuclear weapons, and in 2024 it formally gave up the goal of reunification.

Japan surrenders; Korea is split at the 38th parallel
The Korean War, ended by an armistice but no peace treaty
Mass protests win South Korea direct presidential elections
North Korea carries out its first nuclear test
North Korea calls the South a hostile state and signs a defence treaty with Russia

dd-turkey.p: After the Ottoman Empire's defeat in World War I, Mustafa Kemal led a war of independence against Greek, Armenian and Allied forces and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923. As president he abolished the caliphate, replaced Islamic law with European codes and Arabic script with the Latin alphabet, and gave women the vote. Multi-party elections came in 1950, but the army, seeing itself as guardian of his legacy, seized power or forced out governments in 1960, 1971, 1980 and 1997.

items: Swiss civil code, the fez banned.

dd-turkey.why: Atatürk moved it from Istanbul in 1923.

dd-turkey.p: Turkey joined NATO in 1952 and invaded Cyprus in 1974. From 2002 Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AK Party dominated politics, and after a failed coup in 2016 he gained sweeping presidential powers.

Kemal and his circle blamed the empire's decline on religious tradition and believed only a secular, Western-style nation-state could survive among the great powers. Their reforms were imposed from above, and many pious Anatolians and Kurds felt left out. That divide, between a secular elite backed by the army and a conservative, religious majority, shaped Turkish politics for decades and helped Erdoğan rise.

dd-turkey.q: What did Mustafa Kemal create from the defeated Ottoman Empire?
a: A secular Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923
A new Islamic caliphate based in Ankara
dd-turkey.why: After a war of independence, Kemal founded the republic, abolished the caliphate and replaced Islamic law and Arabic script with European codes and the Latin alphabet.

dd-turkey.p: After the Ottoman defeat in 1918, the Allies occupied Istanbul and planned to carve up Anatolia. Mustafa Kemal, an Ottoman general, rallied resistance from Ankara. His forces fought Armenia in the east and drove the Greek army out of the west by 1922. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne recognised Turkey's borders, and the Arab lands stayed under French rule in Syria and Lebanon and British rule in Iraq, Jordan and Palestine.

Declared 29 October 1923

The Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, replaced the harsher 1920 Treaty of Sèvres. The republic was declared in October, with Mustafa Kemal as president.

Invaded western Anatolia, 1919–1922

Greece landed at İzmir in 1919 and pushed deep into Anatolia before its defeat in 1922. A 1923 exchange sent about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians to Greece and about 400,000 Muslims to Turkey.

dd-turkey.q: Which divide in Turkish society helped Erdoğan rise to power?
a: Between Istanbul and Ankara over the capital
Between NATO supporters and pro-Soviet communists
Between a secular, army-backed elite and a conservative, religious majority
dd-turkey.why: Many pious Anatolians felt left out by Kemal's reforms; Erdoğan's AK Party won in 2002 and later gained sweeping presidential powers after the 2016 coup attempt.

dd-turkey.p:
Fought the Turkish nationalists in 1920

Turkish nationalist forces defeated the Armenian republic in 1920, and Kars stayed Turkish. Armenia then became Soviet. In 1915–16 most Ottoman Armenians were killed or died in deportations, which the great majority of historians call genocide; Turkey rejects the term.

Between 1924 and 1935 Mustafa Kemal remade daily life. The caliphate was abolished in 1924 and religious courts and Sufi lodges closed. The fez was banned in 1925, and Swiss, Italian and German law codes replaced Islamic law. In 1928 the Latin alphabet replaced Arabic script within months, and Kemal toured the country with a chalkboard teaching the new letters. Women won the vote in national elections in 1934, before women in France or Italy. A 1934 law required everyone to take a surname, and parliament gave Kemal the name Atatürk, 'Father of the Turks'. He ruled as a one-party leader until his death in 1938, and insulting his memory is still a crime.

Kurds make up perhaps 15–20 percent of Turkey's people, by most estimates. The early republic defined everyone as Turkish, crushed Kurdish revolts in 1925 and 1937–38, and for decades restricted the Kurdish language. In 1984 the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), led by Abdullah Öcalan and listed as a terrorist group by Turkey, the US and the EU, began an armed insurgency. About 40,000 people were killed, and thousands of Kurdish villages were emptied in the 1990s. Öcalan was captured in Kenya in 1999. After a 2013–15 peace process collapsed, Öcalan called in February 2025 for the PKK to disarm, and in May it announced it would dissolve.

Turkey joined NATO in 1952, alongside its old rival Greece, after Stalin demanded bases on the Turkish Straits. It bordered the Soviet Union in the Caucasus, today's Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan, and US missiles on Turkish soil were traded away in the 1962 Cuban crisis. At home the army, guardian of Atatürk's secular legacy, ousted governments in 1960, 1971 and 1980. In 1974 Turkey invaded Cyprus, which remains divided.

NATO member from 1952

Turkey sent troops to the Korean War, which helped win it NATO membership. It became a multi-party democracy in 1950, but the army intervened about once a decade.

dd-turkey.q: Why did Kemal and his circle impose secular, Western-style reforms?
a: The Allies made them a condition of the Treaty of Lausanne
They blamed the empire's decline on religious tradition
They wanted to join the European Union
dd-turkey.why: They believed only a secular, Western-style nation-state could survive among the great powers, so reforms were imposed from above.

dd-turkey.p:
Greece joined NATO with Turkey in 1952, but the two allies quarrelled bitterly over Cyprus and the Aegean Sea, and came close to war in 1987 and 1996.

US Jupiter nuclear missiles were based in Italy and Turkey. Their quiet removal in 1963 was part of the deal that ended the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Soviet Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan's Nakhchivan exclave formed the USSR's border with Turkey, one of only two places where NATO directly bordered the Soviet Union.

The closed Turkish–Armenian border was a Cold War front line. Turkey closed it again in 1993 over the Karabakh war, and it stayed shut for decades.

dd-turkey.q: How does Turkey's position in the world look today?
a: A NATO member and regional power balancing West, Russia and Middle East
Neutral, with no troops outside its borders
A Russian ally that has left NATO
dd-turkey.why: Turkey has NATO's second-largest army and troops in Syria, Iraq and Libya, yet buys Russian air defences and gas and has mediated between Russia and Ukraine.

dd-turkey.p: A former Istanbul mayor from a pious, working-class background, Erdoğan led the AK Party to victory in 2002 and became prime minister in 2003. Early on he tamed the army, began EU membership talks and presided over fast growth. Over time his rule grew more personal: protests over Istanbul's Gezi Park in 2013 were put down hard, and after the 2016 coup attempt, which he blames on the Gülen movement, over 150,000 people were detained or dismissed. A 2017 referendum created a powerful presidency. High inflation, which peaked above 80 percent in 2022, hurt living standards, and the opposition won major cities in 2019 and 2024. Erdoğan's term runs until 2028.

Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has led Turkey since 2003, first as prime minister, then as a powerful president. Turkey keeps troops in northern Syria and Iraq, in Libya, Qatar and Somalia, and helped Azerbaijan win its wars over Karabakh. It hosts millions of Syrians, sells drones widely and has mediated between Russia and Ukraine. In 2025 the Kurdish militant PKK announced it would disband, after a war of over 40 years.
Erdoğan won the 2023 election. In March 2025 his main rival, Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, was jailed on corruption charges he calls political; his trial was still going on in October 2026.

Turkey opened a base in Qatar in 2015 and stood by it during the 2017–21 Saudi-led blockade.

Turkey's largest overseas military training base opened in Mogadishu in 2017.

dd-turkey.q: Why did Turkey's army overthrow or force out governments several times after 1950?
a: It wanted Turkey to leave NATO
It saw itself as guardian of Atatürk's secular legacy
It was ordered to by the Soviet Union
It sought to restore the sultan
dd-turkey.why: The army, backing a secular elite, intervened in 1960, 1971, 1980 and 1997 against governments it distrusted.

dd-turkey.p:
'One nation, two states'

Turkish drones and support helped Azerbaijan defeat Armenian forces in 2020, and it retook all of Karabakh in 2023.

Turkey straddles two continents, with Istanbul spanning the Bosphorus, and its foreign policy reflects that. It is a NATO member with the alliance's second-largest army and has been an EU candidate since 1999, though membership talks have been frozen since 2018. It also buys Russian air defences and gas, hosts millions of Syrian refugees, and builds influence across the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia. Turkish drones have shaped wars from Libya to Karabakh and Ukraine. Erdoğan has positioned Turkey as a broker, hosting Russian–Ukrainian talks, while condemning Israel over Gaza and staying out of the 2026 war on Iran.

Turkey became a large industrial economy of over 85 million people and a regional power, with troops in Syria, Iraq, Libya and beyond. Under Erdoğan religion returned to public life, while critics, journalists and opposition leaders, including Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, were jailed, which his government says is a matter for independent courts. In 2025 the PKK announced it would disband, and in August 2026 parliament passed a law setting out terms for its fighters to disarm and return.
