sections.t: For Israelis, 1948 is the War of Independence: a state for a people just emerging from the Holocaust, defended against five Arab armies, at the cost of about 6,000 lives, around 1% of its Jewish population. For Palestinians it is the Nakba, the 'catastrophe': about 700,000 people, over half the Arab population, fled or were driven out, and Israel did not let them return. Historians, including Israeli 'new historians' using army archives from the 1980s, have shown that both flight from fear and deliberate expulsions occurred. In the decades after 1948, most of the roughly 800,000 Jews of the Arab world also left or were forced out, many to Israel. Today UNRWA registers about 6 million Palestinian refugees and their descendants.

At Oslo in 1993 Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization recognised each other and agreed on interim self-rule, leaving borders, Jerusalem, refugees and settlements for later. Those talks never succeeded. Each side blames the other. Many Israelis point to Palestinian rejection of offers in 2000 and 2008 and to suicide bombings in the 1990s and 2000s, which killed hundreds of Israelis. Many Palestinians point to the continued growth of settlements, checkpoints and military rule, which they say made a viable state impossible. Rabin's assassination in 1995, the bloody second intifada of 2000–05 and the split between Fatah in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza after 2007 deepened mutual distrust.

On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led fighters broke into southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and taking 251 hostages: the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel answered with a bombing campaign and invasion aimed at destroying Hamas. By October 2026 more than 74,000 people had been killed in Gaza, by the count of its Hamas-run health ministry, and most of its 2 million people had been displaced, many repeatedly. In 2025 UN-backed experts declared famine in parts of Gaza, a finding Israel disputed. South Africa accused Israel of genocide at the International Court of Justice, and in 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Netanyahu, his former defence minister and a Hamas military commander. Israel rejects the accusations as baseless.

A US-brokered ceasefire began on 10 October 2025. All living hostages were freed within days in exchange for about 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, and the remains of the last hostage, Ran Gvili, were recovered in January 2026. But the plan's second stage stalled: Hamas had not disarmed despite talks on a phased handover of weapons, an international stabilisation force was only beginning to form, and Israel kept control of over half of Gaza. Gaza's health ministry counted over 1,500 more deaths after the truce by October 2026. In the West Bank, settlement building and settler violence rose sharply, according to the UN. Polls showed many Israelis and Palestinians doubting that a two-state solution could still work.

dd-holocaust.what: After taking power in 1933, the Nazis stripped Germany's Jews of their rights, property and citizenship, and in the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938 burned hundreds of synagogues. When Germany conquered Poland in 1939, it forced Jews into sealed ghettos. From June 1941 German units and local collaborators shot Jews across the occupied Soviet lands. From 1942 trains carried Jews from all over Europe to death camps in occupied Poland, such as Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau, where most were gassed on arrival. By 1945 about six million Jews had been murdered, two in every three in Europe. Roma, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war and others were also persecuted and killed.
dd-holocaust.why: Hatred of Jews had deep roots in European history, and in the 19th century it took a new, racial form. Nazi ideology made it central: Hitler saw Jews as a racial enemy to blame for Germany's defeat and for communism. Persecution grew step by step, and war, conquest and the invasion of the Soviet Union turned it into mass murder. Historians debate how far it followed a plan, but it needed the work of many thousands of officials, soldiers and collaborators, and the indifference of many more.
dd-holocaust.after: Survivors faced a destroyed world; many could not go home, and hundreds of thousands moved to Israel, the United States and elsewhere. Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg, and the word 'genocide' was coined to name the crime, banned by a UN convention in 1948. The Holocaust shaped human rights law and Germany's postwar identity, and it is remembered every 27 January, the day Auschwitz was liberated.

sections.t: The Nazis aimed to murder every Jew within their reach, and about six million were killed, including about 1.5 million children. They also persecuted others they saw as racially or politically undesirable. According to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, they and their allies killed at least 250,000, and possibly up to 500,000, Roma and Sinti; 250,000–300,000 disabled people; about 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war, mostly through starvation; and about 1.8 million non-Jewish Polish civilians. Croatia's Ustaša regime murdered over 310,000 Serbs. Tens of thousands of German political opponents and people labelled 'asocial' or 'criminal' died, as did about 1,700 Jehovah's Witnesses, hundreds or possibly thousands of gay men, and Black Germans.

The murder grew out of earlier crimes. From 1939 the Nazi 'euthanasia' programme killed disabled patients in gas chambers, and its staff later ran the death camps. About 2 million Jews were shot near their homes, often at pits dug at the edge of town. Gassing was then industrialised: at Treblinka, Sobibor and Bełżec, staffed by a few dozen SS men and around 100 auxiliary guards each, almost everyone was killed within hours of arrival. Railways, police, civil servants and companies all played a part. The Nazis tried to hide the crime, using code words such as 'resettlement' and later digging up and burning bodies, but they left enormous written evidence.

Jews resisted in many ways. In the Warsaw ghetto, historian Emanuel Ringelblum's secret team buried an archive in milk cans so the world would know, and in April 1943 young fighters held off German troops for nearly a month. Prisoners revolted at Treblinka, Sobibor and Auschwitz, and thousands of Jews fought as partisans in the forests of Belarus and Lithuania. Some non-Jews risked death to help. Danes ferried Jews to Sweden, the Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara issued over 2,000 transit visas, and Oskar Schindler protected about 1,200 workers. Yad Vashem has honoured more than 28,000 such rescuers as 'Righteous Among the Nations', while noting that most people did nothing.

Soviet troops reached Majdanek in July 1944 and Auschwitz on 27 January 1945. British and American soldiers who entered Bergen-Belsen, Buchenwald and Dachau in April 1945 found thousands of starving prisoners and unburied dead, and filmed them as evidence. The Nuremberg trials of 1945–46 judged leading Nazis, and Israel tried Adolf Eichmann, an organiser of the deportations, in 1961. Many perpetrators were never punished. Israel's Yad Vashem, founded in 1953, collects the names of the murdered, and the UN made 27 January International Holocaust Remembrance Day in 2005. Many European countries now ban Holocaust denial, and many Roma mark 2 August, when in 1944 the SS murdered almost 2,900 Roma and Sinti left in the 'Gypsy family camp' at Auschwitz-Birkenau.

dd-pacific.what: Japan, which had seized Manchuria in 1931, went to full-scale war with China in July 1937, took the capital Nanjing and massacred many of its people. In December 1941 it attacked the US fleet at Pearl Harbor and, within six months, conquered the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Burma and the Dutch East Indies. At Midway in June 1942 the US Navy sank four Japanese carriers. From Guadalcanal onwards, American forces fought island by island towards Japan, while bombers burned its cities. After the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet attack on Manchuria, Japan surrendered in August 1945.
dd-pacific.why: Japan's military-dominated government sought an empire in Asia for raw materials, markets and security, and the war in China became a costly stalemate. When Japan moved into French Indochina in 1941, the US, Britain and the Netherlands froze its assets and cut off its oil, most of which came from the US. Rather than give up China, Japan's leaders gambled on seizing Southeast Asia's oil and crippling the US Navy, hoping America would accept a negotiated peace.
dd-pacific.after: The war killed perhaps 20 million or more people across Asia and the Pacific, most of them Chinese; estimates vary widely. Japan lost its empire, was occupied by the US and rebuilt as a pacifist democracy and US ally. Korea was divided, China's civil war resumed, and the defeat of European colonial rulers by Japan speeded independence across Southeast Asia. The atomic bombs opened the nuclear age.

sections.t: Japan's leaders believed their country needed an empire to survive as a great power, and the army increasingly controlled policy. After seizing Manchuria in 1931 and invading China in 1937, Japan found itself bogged down in a war it could not finish. When it occupied southern French Indochina in July 1941, the US, Britain and the Netherlands answered with an oil embargo, and Japan had reserves of oil for perhaps 18 months to two years. The US demanded withdrawal from China. Japan's leaders chose war, planning to seize the oil of the Dutch East Indies and knock out the US fleet, though some, including Admiral Yamamoto, warned that Japan could not win a long war.

Six months after Pearl Harbor, Yamamoto tried to lure the remaining US carriers into a trap near Midway Atoll. But American codebreakers had read enough of Japan's naval code to learn the plan, and Admiral Nimitz placed three carriers in ambush. On 4 June, after waves of US attacks failed, dive bombers caught the Japanese carriers while they were refuelling and rearming their planes in the hangars below, and set three ablaze in minutes; a fourth was hit later that day and sank the next morning. The US lost the carrier Yorktown. Japan lost four fleet carriers and many skilled aircrew, and never again took the offensive in the central Pacific.

In 1945 US leaders faced a planned invasion of Japan, with casualty estimates that varied widely and remain debated. President Truman and his advisers argued that the bombs saved lives by ending the war quickly. Since the 1960s some historians have argued that Japan was close to surrender, that alternatives such as letting it keep its emperor or waiting for the Soviet attack might have worked, and that impressing the Soviet Union was a motive. Others reply that Japan's leaders were still divided after both bombs, and the emperor himself had to break the deadlock. Many scholars now see the bombs and the Soviet declaration of war together as forcing the surrender.

dd-vietnam.what: In 1945 Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam independent, and his communist-led Viet Minh fought France until its defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The Geneva Accords split the country at the 17th parallel, and the promised elections never came. In the South, communist guerrillas, the Viet Cong, rose against the US-backed government, supplied from the North along the Ho Chi Minh Trail. From 1965 the United States sent combat troops and bombed the North, peaking at over 540,000 soldiers. The 1968 Tet Offensive turned American opinion against the war. US forces left after the 1973 Paris Peace Accords, and in April 1975 Saigon fell to the North.
dd-vietnam.why: For Vietnamese communists this was a war for independence and unification, first against France and then against the US-backed South. For the United States it was a front in the Cold War: leaders believed that if South Vietnam fell, communism would spread across Southeast Asia like falling dominoes. Each president feared being blamed for 'losing' Vietnam, so commitment grew step by step.
dd-vietnam.after: Vietnam was reunited under communist rule in 1976, and Laos and Cambodia also became communist in 1975, where the Khmer Rouge then killed a vast share of Cambodia's people. Hundreds of thousands of 'boat people' fled Vietnam. In the US the defeat bred distrust of government and caution about foreign wars. Vietnam opened its economy from 1986, restored relations with the US in 1995, and is now a fast-growing trading partner.

sections.t: In 1954 President Eisenhower compared Southeast Asia to a row of dominoes: if one country fell to communism, the rest would follow. That 'domino theory' guided four presidents. The US funded France's war, then backed the South Vietnamese leader Ngo Dinh Diem and sent military advisers, about 16,000 by 1963. In August 1964 North Vietnamese boats attacked the destroyer USS Maddox in the Gulf of Tonkin. A second attack reported two days later almost certainly never happened, as a later US National Security Agency study concluded. Even so, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution almost unanimously, letting President Johnson wage war without a declaration. Marines landed at Da Nang in March 1965.

On 30–31 January 1968, during the Tet lunar new year truce, communist forces attacked more than 100 towns and cities across South Vietnam at once. Commandos even got inside the US embassy compound in Saigon. In Hue the fighting lasted nearly a month, and communist forces killed thousands of civilians there. Militarily the offensive failed: the Viet Cong lost tens of thousands of fighters and did not spark the uprising they hoped for. Politically it was a turning point. American leaders had said the war was being won, and viewers now saw it on television. On 31 March President Johnson announced he would not seek re-election and began moves towards peace talks.

Vietnam was the first 'television war', and it split America. Young men were drafted, and many saw the system as unfair, because student deferments shielded the better off. Protests grew from campus teach-ins in 1965 to marches of hundreds of thousands. News of the My Lai massacre broke in 1969; only one officer, Lieutenant William Calley, was convicted. In May 1970 National Guard troops shot dead four students at Kent State University in Ohio. The 1971 Pentagon Papers showed that officials had long doubted the war could be won. The draft ended in 1973, and Congress passed the War Powers Resolution to limit presidents' power to make war.

dd-berlin.what: In 1945 the victors split Germany and its capital, Berlin, into four zones. In June 1948 the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin, and for eleven months American and British planes kept its two million people alive. In 1949 Germany became two states, and over the next twelve years well over 2.5 million East Germans fled west, most through Berlin's open sector border. On 13 August 1961 East Germany sealed it, and the Berlin Wall split the city for 28 years. In 1989, as communism weakened across Eastern Europe, East Germans fled through Hungary and protested in the streets. On 9 November the Wall opened, and on 3 October 1990 Germany reunited.
dd-berlin.why: Berlin was split because the wartime allies could not agree on Germany's future, and it sat deep inside the Soviet zone. The blockade was Stalin's attempt to push the West out. The Wall was built because East Germany was losing its young and skilled workers to the richer West. It fell because Mikhail Gorbachev would no longer use Soviet troops to prop up communist rulers, and East Germans, by fleeing and protesting, forced the issue.
dd-berlin.after: Reunification merged the East into West Germany's democracy and economy, at great cost; eastern wages and jobs took decades to catch up. Berlin became the capital again, and parliament moved into the rebuilt Reichstag in 1999. The Stasi's secret police files were opened to the people they had watched. Since February 2018 the Wall has been gone for longer than it stood, and only short stretches remain as memorials.

sections.t: The first barrier, on 13 August 1961, was barbed wire, soon replaced by concrete. By the 1980s the border around West Berlin, about 155 km long, had two walls with a 'death strip' between them, lit at night and watched from about 300 towers, with dogs, trip wires and anti-vehicle trenches. East German guards had orders to stop escapes, if necessary by shooting. In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie for about a day. In 1962 eighteen-year-old Peter Fechter was shot and bled to death in the strip in full view of West Berliners. According to the Berlin Wall Memorial, at least 140 people were killed at the Wall or died in connection with it.

Over 5,000 people escaped across the Wall, by many accounts. Two days after the border closed, the young guard Conrad Schumann jumped over the barbed wire, a moment caught in a famous photograph. In the first months people leapt from windows of houses on Bernauer Strasse, whose fronts stood on the border line, until they were bricked up. Students dug tunnels from the West: in October 1964, 57 people crawled to freedom through 'Tunnel 57'. Others hid in car boots, used forged passports or crashed through checkpoints. In February 1989 Chris Gueffroy became the last person shot dead trying to cross; weeks later, Winfried Freudenberg died when his gas balloon crashed in West Berlin.

On 9 November 1989 the East German politburo member Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a live press conference. Asked when they took effect, he looked at his notes and said 'immediately, without delay', though they were meant for the next day. Thousands of East Berliners went to the crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse, the officer in charge, Harald Jäger, faced a growing crowd and no clear orders, and at about 11.30 pm he opened the gate. Others followed. That night Berliners climbed onto the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, and soon people were chipping at it with hammers. Nobody had decided to end the Wall; a mistake and the crowds did it.

dd-partition.what: By 1946 Britain wanted to leave India quickly, but the Congress party, which sought one united India, and the Muslim League, which demanded Pakistan, could not agree. Communal riots spread from Calcutta in August 1946. The last viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, brought the handover forward to August 1947, and British India was split: Pakistan became independent on 14 August, India on 15 August. The new borders through Punjab and Bengal were announced two days later. Hindus and Sikhs fled east and Muslims west, and both sides carried out massacres. In October fighting began over Kashmir, and in January 1948 Gandhi was assassinated by a Hindu nationalist.
dd-partition.why: Under British rule, Hindu and Muslim politics drifted apart; separate electorates for Muslims from 1909 hardened the divide, and historians debate how far Britain encouraged it. The Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah argued that Muslims were a separate nation who would be dominated in a Hindu-majority India, and from 1940 demanded Pakistan. Congress leaders rejected this. Weakened by the Second World War, Britain chose a fast exit over a negotiated settlement.
dd-partition.after: Partition left India and Pakistan bitter rivals. They have fought wars in 1947–48, 1965, 1971 and 1999, and clashed again in May 2025; both tested nuclear weapons in 1998. In 1971 East Pakistan broke away as Bangladesh. Kashmir remains divided and claimed by both. Families split by the border still cannot easily visit, and the memory of 1947 shapes Hindu–Muslim relations in the region today.

sections.h: A line drawn in five weeks
sections.t: Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India, arrived in July 1947 to chair the commissions that would divide Punjab and Bengal. He had about five weeks, out-of-date maps and census figures, and orders to follow Muslim and non-Muslim majorities while weighing 'other factors' such as rivers, railways and canals. Many villages, farms and holy places ended up on the wrong side for their people. To avoid blame falling on the British at the handover, the award was published only on 17 August, two days after independence. Radcliffe refused his fee and, it is said, burned his papers.

The partition was one of the largest migrations in history: somewhere between 10 and 20 million people moved, on foot in columns stretching for miles, by bullock cart and by crowded train. Hindu, Sikh and Muslim mobs and militias attacked one another; trains sometimes arrived carrying only the dead. Estimates of deaths range from about 200,000 to 2 million, and a figure of about 1 million is often cited. Women suffered especially: an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 were abducted, and many were raped, and some families killed their own women to 'save their honour'. Many survivors never spoke of what they saw, and oral history projects began recording them only decades later.

Princely states could choose India or Pakistan. Kashmir's Hindu Maharaja, Hari Singh, ruling a Muslim majority, hesitated. In October 1947 Pashtun tribal fighters from Pakistan invaded, and he signed accession to India in return for troops. The war ended with a UN ceasefire in 1949 along a line that, renamed the Line of Control in 1972, still divides the region. A promised plebiscite never took place. An insurgency in the Indian-held valley since 1989 has killed tens of thousands, and drove most Kashmiri Hindus, the Pandits, from their homes in 1990. In 2019 India ended the region's autonomy; in 2026 its elected government, in office since 2024, was still demanding that statehood be restored.

The two countries remember the same year differently. In India, 15 August is a day of freedom, and partition is often remembered as a tragedy and a wound to the nation; since 2021 India has also marked 14 August as 'Partition Horrors Remembrance Day'. In Pakistan, 14 August celebrates the birth of a homeland for South Asia's Muslims, achieved at great cost. For Bangladeshis, 1971 matters more. Novels such as Khushwant Singh's 'Train to Pakistan' and Saadat Hasan Manto's stories, written by people who lived through it, remain some of the most powerful records of the violence.

dd-rwanda.what: In 1959 a Hutu uprising overthrew Rwanda's Tutsi monarchy, and over the next years thousands of Tutsi were killed and hundreds of thousands fled abroad. In 1990 their children's army, the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), invaded from Uganda. A 1993 peace deal collapsed when President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane was shot down on 6 April 1994. Hutu extremists then killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in 100 days, while the UN withdrew most of its peacekeepers. The RPF won the war in July, and some 2 million Hutu fled abroad, most of them into Zaire. Rwanda's pursuit of the militias among them set off two Congo wars, from 1996 to 2003; the second drew in nine African countries.
dd-rwanda.why: Under Belgian rule the categories of Hutu and Tutsi hardened into fixed 'races' on identity cards, and Belgium governed through a Tutsi elite. After 1959 Hutu-led governments treated Tutsi as second-class citizens. The RPF invasion, economic crisis and a power-sharing deal that threatened Habyarimana's circle let extremists organise militias, import machetes and spread hate through radio. In Congo, a collapsing state, armed refugees and rich minerals turned Rwanda's war into a regional one.
dd-rwanda.after: Under Paul Kagame, in charge since 1994 and president since 2000, Rwanda rebuilt fast and became one of Africa's most orderly economies, though critics and rights groups say dissent is harshly repressed. Eastern Congo has never known lasting peace: the M23 rebels, backed by Rwanda according to UN experts, took Goma and Bukavu in 2025, and despite US- and Qatari-brokered deals the war went on in October 2026.

sections.t: Hutu and Tutsi speak the same language, Kinyarwanda, share the same religion and lived side by side for centuries. Before colonial rule the labels were partly about status and cattle: Tutsi were often herders and the royal court was Tutsi, and people could sometimes move between groups. German and then Belgian colonisers, influenced by racial theories, treated Tutsi as a superior race from the north. In 1933 Belgium issued identity cards stating each person's group. In 1994 those cards decided who lived and died at roadblocks. Today Rwanda has dropped the labels from its cards and officially promotes a single Rwandan identity.

The killing was organised. Officials, soldiers and the Interahamwe militia, linked to the ruling party, used lists of names, and local leaders called on villagers to take part in 'work'. Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines had spent months calling Tutsi 'cockroaches'; during the killings it broadcast names and hiding places. Neighbours killed neighbours, mostly with machetes and clubs. Churches, schools and stadiums, where Tutsi had sheltered in earlier waves of violence, became sites of mass murder. Some Hutu risked their lives to hide Tutsi. At the Hôtel des Mille Collines in Kigali, manager Paul Rusesabagina sheltered over 1,200 people, a story told in the film 'Hotel Rwanda', though some survivors dispute his account.

UN commander Roméo Dallaire warned in January 1994 that militias were stockpiling weapons and drawing up lists, but was told not to raid the caches. After ten Belgian peacekeepers were killed on 7 April, the Security Council cut his force to 270. Western countries flew out their own citizens and left. US officials avoided the word 'genocide', which could have created a duty to act. France launched Opération Turquoise in June, saving some lives but also, critics say, letting the organisers escape to Zaire. President Clinton apologised in 1998, and in 2021 France's President Macron acknowledged France's 'responsibilities' while denying complicity.

Over 100,000 suspects filled Rwanda's prisons after 1994, far too many for its courts. From 2002 to 2012 the country revived gacaca, village courts where elected local judges heard nearly 2 million cases, letting survivors learn how relatives died and perpetrators confess for lighter sentences. The UN tribunal in Arusha convicted 62 people, and in 1998 delivered the first genocide conviction by an international court. Rwanda abolished the death penalty in 2007. Each April the country mourns during Kwibuka, 'remember'. Women hold over 60 percent of the seats in its lower house of parliament, a world record, while rights groups say opposition politicians and journalists are jailed or silenced.

dd-ukraine.what: Ukraine became independent when the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, and in 1994 gave up its nuclear weapons in return for promises to respect its borders. In 2014 protests in Kyiv toppled a pro-Russian president; Russia then seized Crimea, and Russian-backed separatists took part of the Donbas. On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion. Ukraine held Kyiv, and that autumn retook much of the north-east and the city of Kherson. The war then became a grinding struggle of trenches, artillery and drones. In October 2026 Russia held about a fifth of Ukraine, and US-led talks had brought only brief truces, no lasting ceasefire.
dd-ukraine.why: Russia's leaders saw Ukraine as part of Russia's historic sphere and called NATO's expansion towards it a threat; Vladimir Putin argued in 2021 that Russians and Ukrainians were 'one people'. Most Ukrainians wanted their own path, closer to Europe, especially after 2014. Ukraine and its Western backers call the war an unprovoked war of conquest; Russia calls it a defence against NATO and of Russian speakers, claims that most historians and international bodies reject.
dd-ukraine.after: It is Europe's deadliest war since 1945, with hundreds of thousands of soldiers killed and millions of Ukrainians made refugees. It sharply cut Europe's reliance on Russian gas, brought Finland and Sweden into NATO and set off the biggest rise in European defence spending since the Cold War. Russia turned towards China, Iran and North Korea. Drone warfare, pioneered here at scale, is changing how armies everywhere fight.

sections.t: The two sides tell very different stories. Russia's government says NATO broke a promise, made as Germany reunified in 1990, not to expand east, and that a Western-leaning Ukraine threatened Russia's security and its Russian speakers. It framed the 2022 invasion as a 'special military operation' to 'demilitarise and denazify' Ukraine. Western officials say no such promise was ever agreed, and that countries are free to choose their alliances. Ukraine's government and most scholars point to Putin's own words denying that Ukraine is a real nation, and to Russia's annexation of four regions it did not even fully hold, as evidence of a war for territory.

After the fast-moving battles of 2022, the front hardened into hundreds of kilometres of trenches and minefields, like a First World War front watched from the sky. Cheap drones changed everything. Small first-person-view (FPV) drones, flown by operators wearing goggles, hunt soldiers and vehicles miles behind the lines, so that troops move in tiny groups and tanks hide under metal 'cope cages'. Both sides now build millions of drones a year. Russia fires waves of Shahed-type drones and missiles at cities and power stations, while Ukraine's long-range drones strike oil refineries deep inside Russia. In June 2025 Ukraine hit bombers at airbases across Russia using drones smuggled in on lorries.

For Ukrainians the war is part of daily life. Air-raid alerts sound on phones across the country, and people in Kyiv have spent nights in metro stations. Russian strikes on power stations brought rolling blackouts every winter since 2022, and cafés ran on generators. Most men aged 23 to 60 may not leave the country, so families have been split, with about 5.8 million Ukrainians living abroad as refugees and millions more displaced inside the country. Ukraine says nearly 20,000 children have been taken to Russia; in 2023 the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin over these deportations, which Russia calls evacuations.

dd-terror.what: On 11 September 2001 al-Qaeda hijackers killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania. President George W. Bush declared a 'war on terror'. In October US-led forces invaded Afghanistan and toppled the Taliban, who had sheltered Osama bin Laden. In 2003 the US and Britain invaded Iraq, citing weapons of mass destruction that did not exist, and years of insurgency and sectarian war followed. Bin Laden was killed in Pakistan in 2011. From the chaos in Iraq and Syria rose the Islamic State, which held a 'caliphate' from 2014 to 2019. In August 2021 US troops left Afghanistan and the Taliban returned to power.
dd-terror.why: Al-Qaeda, founded by veterans of the 1980s war against the Soviets in Afghanistan, blamed the United States for its troops in Saudi Arabia, its support for Israel and for Arab rulers it called corrupt, and hoped attacks would draw America into a ruinous war. After 9/11, US leaders resolved to strike terrorists and the states that sheltered them before they could attack again, an approach that critics said led to overreach in Iraq.
dd-terror.after: The Costs of War project at Brown University estimates over 900,000 people were killed directly in the post-9/11 wars, and millions more died of indirect causes. The US spent about $8 trillion. Air travel brought new security checks, and governments gained wide surveillance powers. The Iraq war strengthened Iran, and ISIS's rise fed Syria's civil war and a refugee crisis that changed European politics. The Taliban still ruled Afghanistan in 2026.

sections.t: On a clear Tuesday morning 19 men, 15 of them Saudi citizens, hijacked four airliners with box cutters and knives. At 8:46 a.m. the first struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center; the second hit the South Tower 17 minutes later, as millions watched live on television. A third plane hit the Pentagon. On the fourth, passengers who had learned of the other attacks by phone stormed the cockpit, and it crashed in a Pennsylvania field, short of its probable target in Washington. Both towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 victims died, including 343 New York firefighters. The 9/11 Commission later found that US agencies had missed warning signs.

The war on terror raised hard questions about law and rights. From January 2002 the US held suspected militants at Guantanamo Bay in Cuba, outside normal courts; about 780 men passed through it, many never charged, and about 15 remained in 2026. The CIA held prisoners in secret 'black sites' and used 'enhanced interrogation', including waterboarding, which a 2014 Senate report found brutal and ineffective; President Obama said the US had 'tortured some folks', while former CIA officials defended the programme. Photos of abuse at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq in 2004 shocked the world. Supporters argued such measures helped prevent further attacks on the scale of 9/11, which did not happen.

After the Iraq invasion, al-Qaeda in Iraq, led by Abu Musab al-Zarqawi, bombed Shia shrines and markets to provoke civil war. It was weakened by 2010, but survivors regrouped in Syria's civil war and, as the Islamic State, seized Mosul in 2014. ISIS ran its 'caliphate' like a state, with taxes, courts and schools, while carrying out mass executions, enslaving Yazidi women and spreading propaganda online that drew some 40,000 foreigners to join it. It inspired or directed attacks from Paris to Sri Lanka. A coalition of over 80 countries helped Iraqi and Kurdish-led forces destroy it by 2019.

In February 2020 the Trump administration signed a deal with the Taliban to withdraw US troops. President Biden completed the pullout in August 2021, as the Afghan army collapsed and the Taliban swept into Kabul; crowds clung to departing aircraft at the airport. Al-Qaeda's leader Ayman al-Zawahiri was killed by a US drone in Kabul in 2022. Neither al-Qaeda nor ISIS has struck the West on the scale of 9/11 since, but their affiliates have grown in Africa's Sahel and Somalia. The 9/11 accused at Guantanamo had still not been tried 25 years after the attacks; a military judge has set their trial for 2028.

dd-syria.what: In December 2010 a young Tunisian street vendor set himself on fire, and protests against ageing dictators spread across the Arab world. Tunisia's president fled in January 2011, Egypt's Hosni Mubarak resigned in February, and Libya's Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown and killed by October with NATO air support. In Syria, Bashar al-Assad met peaceful protests with bullets, and the country slid into civil war. Russia, Iran and Hezbollah fought for him; Turkey, the Gulf states and the West backed rebels, and the Islamic State seized the east. Assad survived for 13 years, until a lightning rebel offensive took Damascus on 8 December 2024 and he fled to Moscow.
dd-syria.why: Across the region, young and fast-growing populations faced unemployment, corruption, rising food prices and police brutality under rulers who had held power for decades. Satellite television and social media let protests spread quickly. In Syria the Assad family's rule rested on the army and security services, many of whose leaders came from its Alawite minority, so the regime fought rather than fell, and the war became a sectarian and international proxy struggle.
dd-syria.after: Only Tunisia became a lasting democracy, and in 2021 its president took sweeping powers. Egypt's army returned in 2013, while Libya and Yemen fell into wars. Syria's war killed hundreds of thousands and drove millions abroad, helping fuel Europe's 2015 migrant crisis. Since Assad's fall, Ahmed al-Sharaa's government has won sanctions relief and taken over the Kurdish-run north-east, but sectarian killings, Israeli troops in the south and ruined cities left its future uncertain in 2026.

sections.t: In March 2011 security forces in the southern town of Daraa arrested and reportedly tortured a group of boys for spraying anti-government slogans on walls. Protests over their treatment spread, and soldiers fired on crowds. Some soldiers deserted rather than shoot, forming the Free Syrian Army. In 2011 an amnesty freed hundreds of jailed Islamist militants, which critics saw as deliberate. The government portrayed the uprising as terrorism, and over time hardline jihadist groups came to dominate the armed opposition. The government used barrel bombs, sieges that starved whole districts, and, according to UN and international investigators, chemical weapons, including sarin at Ghouta in 2013. A former military photographer codenamed 'Caesar' smuggled out tens of thousands of photographs of detainees who died in custody.

Syria became a battlefield for outside powers. Iran saw Assad as a vital ally and the land link to Hezbollah in Lebanon, and sent commanders and militias. Russia's air campaign from September 2015 turned the war, helping Assad retake Aleppo in 2016 and most of the country by 2018. The US first armed some rebels, then focused on destroying the Islamic State, working with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces. Turkey, which sees those Kurdish forces as part of the PKK, sent its own army across the border from 2016. Israel struck Iranian targets hundreds of times. By 2020 the front lines froze, and Syria's economy collapsed under war, sanctions and a drug trade in captagon pills.

Under the nom de guerre Abu Mohammad al-Jolani, Ahmed al-Sharaa fought with al-Qaeda in Iraq, spent years in US detention, and in 2012 founded the Nusra Front, al-Qaeda's Syrian branch. In 2016 he broke with al-Qaeda, and his Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) went on to run Idlib as a strict but more pragmatic administration. In late 2024, with Russia distracted by Ukraine and Hezbollah weakened by war with Israel, HTS-led forces took Aleppo, Hama and Homs in days, and Assad's army melted away. As president, Sharaa swapped fatigues for suits and promised a state for all Syrians. Critics, including many Alawites, Druze and Kurds, doubt that promise, especially after the killings of 2025.

After Assad's fall, crowds opened prisons such as Sednaya, and families searched for some of the more than 100,000 people missing, by rights groups' counts. In 2025 the US and the EU lifted most sanctions, the UN dropped its sanctions on Sharaa, and Gulf states and Turkey offered aid and investment. In 2025 the World Bank put reconstruction costs at about $216 billion. By mid-2026 the UN refugee agency counted over 1.7 million refugees home from abroad, though millions remained abroad. In January 2026 a decree recognised Kurdish as a national language, and the government took much of the oil-rich north-east from the Kurdish-led SDF, which dissolved into the army in August. US-mediated talks with Israel over its forces in the south had produced no deal by October 2026.

dd-humans.what: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa: fossils from Morocco are about 300,000 years old. For most of our history we shared the planet with other humans, Neanderthals in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans further east. Roughly 60,000–50,000 years ago small bands left Africa and spread fast, reaching Australia by at least 50,000 years ago and Europe by 45,000. By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone. During the last Ice Age people crossed from Siberia into the Americas, reaching Chile by about 14,500 years ago. Then, from about 9500 BC, people in the Middle East, China, New Guinea and the Americas each began to farm.
dd-humans.why: Our species spread thanks to language, planning, long-distance trade and flexible tools, which let small groups adapt to deserts, rainforests and Arctic cold. Swings in climate opened and closed routes: low Ice Age seas joined Siberia to Alaska and Australia to New Guinea. Farming began as the climate warmed and steadied after about 10,000 BC, when wild cereals were plentiful and growing populations had fewer new lands to move into.
dd-humans.after: Farming fed far more people per square kilometre than hunting and gathering, so farmers multiplied and spread, pushing aside or absorbing foragers on most continents. Villages grew into towns and, by about 3500 BC, into the first cities, with kings, priests and writing. Every person alive today descends from those early Africans, and most people outside Africa still carry a little Neanderthal DNA.

sections.t: Neanderthals were not the brutish cavemen of old cartoons. They had brains as large as ours, made fine stone tools, controlled fire, hunted mammoths and bison, wore ochre and eagle talons, and cared for their sick. When modern humans arrived they met, and sometimes had children together: most people of non-African descent carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, and Papuans also carry about 4% from Denisovans. Some of these genes still matter, affecting immunity, skin and, in Tibetans, a Denisovan gene that helps with life at high altitude. Why Neanderthals vanished about 40,000 years ago is debated: competition, small and inbred populations, climate swings and absorption into our own species probably all played a part.

Long before writing, people made art. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone engraved a block of red ochre with criss-cross lines about 75,000 years ago. The oldest dated rock art is a hand stencil on Muna, an island off Sulawesi in Indonesia, at least 67,800 years old; its fingertips appear to have been reshaped to look like claws. In Europe, painters filled Chauvet Cave in France with lions, rhinos and horses about 36,000 years ago, and Lascaux about 17,000 years ago. Carved ivory figures, bone flutes and shell beads show people who sang, decorated themselves and traded over hundreds of kilometres. What the images meant to their makers remains a mystery.

Farming did not make life easier at first. Skeletons show that early farmers were often shorter than the hunter-gatherers before them, with worn joints from grinding grain, more tooth decay and signs of malnutrition, because they relied on a few crops. Living close together and beside their animals, they caught new diseases; measles and smallpox, for example, are thought to have evolved from animal infections over the following millennia. But a field fed many more mouths than the wild, so farming populations boomed. Surplus grain could be stored, taxed and fought over, and that opened the way to property, inequality, warfare and, eventually, kings and states.

Much of this story was rewritten in the last 20 years by ancient DNA. In 2010 the Swedish geneticist Svante Pääbo and his team published a draft Neanderthal genome, proving that our ancestors had interbred with them. The same year, DNA from a single finger bone in Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed the Denisovans, a human group nobody had known existed. Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for this work. Proteins, which survive longer than DNA, have since identified Denisovan fossils in China and off Taiwan. New dating methods keep pushing dates back, so every figure in this chapter may change.

dd-languages.what: Around 4000–3000 BC herders on the steppes north of the Black Sea probably spoke the ancestor of the Indo-European languages, which their descendants carried across Europe and into Iran and India. Other families spread too: Bantu languages with farmers across central and southern Africa, Austronesian languages by canoe from Taiwan to Madagascar and Hawaii. Later, empires and religions made a few languages dominant: Latin, then Arabic after 632, then from 1492 Spanish, Portuguese, English and French. Today about 7,000 languages survive, but just a few dozen are spoken by most people, and many small ones are disappearing.
dd-languages.why: Languages spread when their speakers grow in number or power. Farming and herding let populations expand into new land; conquerors, traders and missionaries brought their languages with them; and people switched to the language of jobs, schools, religion and government. Nation-states from the 1800s promoted one standard language, and modern media and cities speed the shift to big languages.
dd-languages.after: The world's language map still traces old migrations and empires: Spanish and Portuguese in Latin America, English and French across Africa, Arabic from Morocco to Iraq. English became the global language of science, business and the internet. Linguists estimate that roughly two in five languages are endangered, mostly Indigenous languages with few young speakers, though revivals such as Hebrew and Māori show decline can be reversed.

sections.h: How we know languages are related
sections.t: In 1786 William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, noticed that Sanskrit was strikingly similar to Greek and Latin and suggested they had 'sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists'. Linguists then found regular sound patterns linking words across languages: English father, Latin pater and Sanskrit pitṛ; English mother, Latin mater and Sanskrit mātṛ. Using such patterns they reconstructed parts of the lost parent language, Proto-Indo-European, including words for wheels and horses. Most scholars, backed since 2015 by ancient DNA, place its speakers on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, though some argue for earlier roots south of the Caucasus or in Anatolia.

A language rarely spreads because it is easier or better; it spreads because its speakers have power, wealth or numbers. Latin replaced Celtic tongues in Gaul and Spain under Roman rule and became French, Spanish, Portuguese and Italian. Arabic became the everyday language of North Africa and the Middle East over centuries after the Islamic conquests, while Persia kept Persian. Trade created common languages, or lingua francas, such as Swahili on the East African coast and Malay in Southeast Asian ports. In the 1800s and 1900s national schools, armies and radio pushed regional languages, from Breton in France to Indigenous languages in the Americas, toward the national standard.

In 1600 English was spoken by perhaps 5 million people, almost all in Britain. British colonisation, then the economic and cultural power of the United States after 1945, made it the most widely spoken language on Earth, with about 1.5 billion speakers, most of whom learned it as a second language. It is the main language of science, aviation and the internet. Mandarin still has the most native speakers, about a billion, and Spanish, Hindi and Arabic each have hundreds of millions. Many linguists expect English to remain the main global language, though machine translation may reduce the need to learn it.

When parents stop passing a language to their children, it can vanish within a few generations. Most endangered languages are Indigenous ones pushed aside by colonisation, boarding schools and the pull of bigger languages: in Australia only about 12 of over 250 original languages are still learned by children. Yet revivals happen. Hebrew, used for nearly 2,000 years mainly in prayer and study, became the everyday language of millions of Israelis within a century. Māori 'language nests' from 1982 and Welsh-medium schools have brought new young speakers, and communities now record elders and teach languages online.

dd-writing.what: Around 3300–3000 BC scribes in the cities of Mesopotamia began pressing signs into clay to keep track of grain, animals and workers. Egypt developed hieroglyphs at about the same time, China wrote on oracle bones by about 1250 BC, and Mesoamerican peoples created their own scripts centuries later. Sometime around 1900–1500 BC Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt invented a much simpler idea, the alphabet, with one sign per sound. Phoenician traders spread it, the Greeks added vowels and the Romans passed it to Europe. China invented paper and printing, and Gutenberg's press of the 1450s made books cheap in Europe. Today most adults in the world can read.
dd-writing.why: Writing began as bookkeeping. As cities, temples and kings collected taxes and traded goods, they needed records that outlasted memory. Pictures for things slowly became signs for sounds, which let scribes write names, laws and stories. The alphabet spread because a few dozen letters were far easier to learn than hundreds of signs, and traders, empires and religions carried it with them.
dd-writing.after: Writing made history possible: laws, contracts, holy books, science and literature could be kept and shared across centuries. For thousands of years reading belonged to a small elite of scribes and priests, but printing and then mass schooling changed that. Today about 88% of adults can read, according to UNESCO, though some 740 million still cannot. The scripts on the map still trace old empires and faiths.

sections.t: The first writing was not poetry but paperwork. Most early tablets from Uruk list rations, sheep, beer and workers, with numbers and signs for things. Some scholars think clay tokens used for counting goods led to the idea. Only over centuries did scribes learn to write full sentences, and literature such as the Epic of Gilgamesh came much later. Learning cuneiform took years in a 'tablet house', where boys, and a few girls, copied signs and model texts. Many tablets survive only because clay hardens in fire: when enemies burned palace libraries, such as Ashurbanipal's at Nineveh, they baked thousands of texts for us to read.

Many scripts were forgotten and had to be decoded. The Rosetta Stone, found by French soldiers in Egypt in 1799, repeated one decree in Greek and Egyptian, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion used it to show that hieroglyphs mixed signs for sounds and ideas. Cuneiform was cracked in the mid-1800s with the help of a three-language royal inscription at Behistun in Iran. In 1952 Michael Ventris showed that Linear B from Crete recorded an early form of Greek, and from the 1950s Yuri Knorozov and others unlocked Maya glyphs. The Indus script and Easter Island's rongorongo remain unread.

China invented paper by the 100s BC and woodblock printing by the 700s; the oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, dates from 868. Bi Sheng made movable clay type in the 1040s, and Korea printed a book with metal type, the Jikji, in 1377. In Europe, Gutenberg's press of about 1455 had far fewer letters to manage, and by 1500 presses in over 200 towns had turned out millions of books, helping spread the Reformation and science. In 1820 only about one adult in eight in the world could read; mass schooling, and now phones, changed that.

dd-money.what: Money began as a way of keeping accounts: by about 3000 BC Mesopotamian temples recorded debts in barley and silver weighed in shekels. Around 630 BC the kingdom of Lydia stamped the first coins, and coins soon spread across Greece, Persia, India and China. China's Song dynasty issued the first government paper money in the 1020s. Italian, then Dutch and English, bankers built modern banking, shares and national debts, while American silver became the first global currency. In the 1800s most major currencies were tied to gold, but in 1971 the last link was cut. Today almost all money is digital, and its value rests on trust in the governments and central banks that issue it.
dd-money.why: Money solves practical problems. It lets people compare the value of very different things, store wealth and settle debts with strangers. Rulers had their own reasons: coins and paper money made it easier to pay soldiers and collect taxes, and the right to issue money was a source of profit and power. Each new form, from coins to banknotes to cards and phones, spread because it made trade cheaper, faster or safer.
dd-money.after: Money shaped the modern world. Banks, stock markets and cheap government borrowing helped the Dutch and British build trading empires and fund industrial growth. Central banks now steer whole economies by setting interest rates, and their mistakes can bring inflation or depression. The US dollar's role as the world's main currency gives the United States unusual financial power, and new digital forms, from phone payments to cryptocurrencies, are changing how billions of people pay.

sections.t: Textbooks long taught that before money people bartered, swapping a cow for some shoes, until money was invented to make trade easier. Anthropologists have found little evidence of any society that ran mainly on barter. In small communities people more often gave and owed, keeping track of favours and debts, and barter mostly happened between strangers. Money also took many surprising forms. Cowrie shells served as money from China to West Africa. On the Pacific island of Yap, giant stone discs called rai, some taller than a person, were quarried on Palau and changed owners without being moved: everyone simply knew who owned which stone.

A banknote is worth something only because people trust that others will accept it. Marco Polo, visiting Kublai Khan's China in the late 1200s, was amazed that people traded gold and pearls for printed paper. When governments print too much, that trust collapses. In Germany in November 1923 a US dollar cost about 4.2 trillion marks, and people were paid twice a day to spend wages before prices rose. In Hungary in 1946 prices doubled roughly every 15 hours, the worst inflation on record, and in 2009 Zimbabwe issued a 100 trillion dollar note. Most central banks today aim for steady inflation of about 2% a year.

sections.h: The rise and fall of gold
sections.t: Britain tied the pound to gold in the early 1800s, and by the 1870s Germany, France, the United States and others had followed. Under this gold standard, notes could be swapped for a fixed weight of gold, which kept prices stable but limited how much money could be created. It broke down during the First World War and the Great Depression, when countries that left gold early recovered faster. In 1944, at Bretton Woods, the Allies tied their currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce. As dollars piled up abroad, President Nixon ended that link on 15 August 1971, and paper money has floated on trust ever since.

dd-democracy.what: Around 508 BC Athens let its male citizens vote directly on laws, and Rome ran a republic with elected officials until its emperors took over. After centuries of kings, assemblies such as Iceland's Althing and England's Parliament slowly limited royal power. The American and French revolutions of 1776 and 1789 declared that power comes from the people, and over the next 150 years the vote spread from men of property to all men and then to women. Democracy collapsed across much of Europe in the 1920s and 1930s, then spread in waves after 1945 and again after 1974, reaching most of the world by 2000.
dd-democracy.why: Rulers who needed taxes and soldiers had to bargain with the people who paid and fought, and assemblies grew out of that bargain. Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke argued that government needs the consent of the governed. Printing, trade, cities and mass schooling created citizens who demanded a say, and workers, women and colonised peoples campaigned for decades to win it. Wars, economic crises and coups explain the retreats.
dd-democracy.after: Today most countries hold elections, but their quality varies widely. By the V-Dem Institute's count, autocracies again outnumbered democracies at the end of 2025, and democracy has declined in many countries since about 2010, including the United States. Yet voters still remove governments peacefully, as in Hungary in 2026, and ideas born in Athens, such as juries and voting, remain everyday parts of public life.

sections.t: Athenian democracy was direct: there were no elected representatives in the modern sense. Adult male citizens, perhaps 30,000 to 60,000 men, could attend the Assembly on the Pnyx hill, about 40 times a year, and vote by show of hands on laws, taxes and war. A Council of 500, chosen by lot each year, prepared its business, and most officials were also picked by lottery, since Athenians thought elections favoured the rich. Juries of hundreds of citizens decided court cases. Once a year citizens could vote to exile a powerful politician for ten years by scratching his name on pottery shards, called ostracism. Women, slaves and foreign residents, the majority of people, could not vote.

Magna Carta is often hailed as the birth of English liberty, but in 1215 it was a peace deal between King John and rebel barons, mostly about their own rights and taxes. It failed: within weeks the Pope annulled it at John's request, and civil war resumed. Reissued in revised form in 1216, 1217 and 1225, it became a symbol. Its most famous clause promised that no free man would be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land. Centuries later, English lawyers and American revolutionaries cited it against royal power. Only three of its clauses are still law in England and Wales.

In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to let women vote, after a petition led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures. Finland went further in 1906, letting women stand for parliament, and elected 19 of them the next year. In Britain the suffragettes of Emmeline Pankhurst smashed windows and went on hunger strike; women over 30 won the vote in 1918. American women won it through the 19th Amendment in 1920, French women in 1944, and Swiss women in national elections only in 1971. Saudi Arabian women first voted, in local elections, in 2015.

The political scientist Samuel Huntington described democracy spreading in 'waves', each followed by a reverse. Many new democracies after World War I fell to dictators, including Mussolini in Italy and Hitler in Germany. After 1945 democracy returned to West Germany, Japan and Italy, and spread to newly independent India. A 'third wave' began with Portugal's Carnation Revolution in 1974 and swept through southern Europe, Latin America, East Asia, Eastern Europe after 1989 and South Africa in 1994. Since about 2010 researchers have recorded a new reverse, as elected leaders in several countries weakened courts, the press and opposition parties.

dd-medicine.what: Around 400 BC Greek doctors following Hippocrates began explaining illness by natural causes rather than angry gods, and Galen's writings ruled medicine for over a thousand years. India and China built their own systems, and from the 800s the Islamic world ran large hospitals and wrote textbooks that Europe later studied. Real breakthroughs came in a rush after 1796: Jenner's smallpox vaccine, anaesthesia, antiseptic surgery and the proof, by Pasteur and Koch, that germs cause disease. The 1900s brought insulin, antibiotics, mass vaccination and transplants. Smallpox was wiped out in 1980, and global life expectancy rose from about 32 years in 1900 to about 73 today.
dd-medicine.why: For most of history doctors could describe diseases but rarely cure them, because they did not know what caused them. Microscopes, chemistry, statistics and controlled experiments in the 1800s changed that, showing that microbes spread many deadly diseases. Growing cities, industrial wealth and governments that funded clean water, research and public health turned discoveries into protection for millions.
dd-medicine.after: Medicine, together with clean water, better food and sanitation, roughly doubled how long people live, mostly by saving babies and children. That helped the world's population grow from about 1.6 billion in 1900 to over 8 billion. Yet huge gaps remain: a baby in Japan can expect to live about 30 years longer than one in Nigeria. New challenges include chronic diseases, ageing populations, pandemics and germs that resist antibiotics.

sections.t: For about 2,000 years doctors from Greece to Persia and Europe believed health depended on balancing four body fluids, or humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Fevers meant too much blood, so a standard cure was to let some out, by cutting a vein or applying leeches. Bloodletting lasted astonishingly long: in December 1799 doctors drained a large amount of blood from George Washington as he lay dying of a throat infection. The theory was not foolish for its time, since it pushed doctors to watch diet, sleep and environment. But it had no idea of germs, and it fell only when experiments in the 1800s proved what really caused disease.

Temples of healing existed in ancient Greece, and Christian charities in Byzantium cared for the sick. But the great teaching hospital grew up in the Islamic world. The bimaristans of Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo had wards for different illnesses, pharmacies, libraries and students, and treated patients whatever their wealth or faith. According to a later story, the physician al-Razi chose the site for a Baghdad hospital by hanging meat around the city and picking the spot where it rotted slowest. In Europe, hospitals long remained places of charity where the poor went to die, and they became safe only after antiseptics and germ theory arrived.

When we read that life expectancy in 1800 was about 30, it does not mean most people died at 30. The average was dragged down by deaths of babies and children: in many places about four in ten children died before the age of five. Adults who survived childhood often lived into their fifties, sixties or beyond. The great modern change has been saving children, through vaccines, clean water, antibiotics and better food. Today about 4% of children worldwide die before five, according to the UN, though in parts of Africa the figure is still over 10%.

dd-plagues.what: In 541 the first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague reached the Byzantine Empire, and it returned in waves for two centuries. In 1347 a second, deadlier wave, the Black Death, arrived on ships from the Black Sea and swept across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa by 1353, killing perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people. From 1518, smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans devastated the peoples of the Americas. The 1918 flu killed an estimated 50 million people worldwide. HIV, recognised in 1981, has killed about 44 million. COVID-19, first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, shut down much of the world in 2020.
dd-plagues.why: Pandemics follow people. Trade routes, armies, pilgrims and ships carry germs, and crowded cities let them spread. The Black Death travelled along the trade networks that joined Asia and Europe. Indigenous Americans had no immunity to diseases that had circulated in Eurasia for thousands of years. Today air travel can carry a new virus around the world in weeks, but science, vaccines and public health make it far easier to fight.
dd-plagues.after: The Black Death left so few workers that wages rose and serfdom weakened in western Europe, while frightened mobs attacked Jewish communities. Smallpox helped Spain conquer the Aztec and Inca empires. Pandemics also built public health: quarantine, health boards, germ theory, the World Health Organization in 1948 and vaccines, which wiped out smallpox by 1980. COVID-19 vaccines were developed and approved in under a year.

sections.t: Plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, identified by Alexandre Yersin in Hong Kong in 1894. It lives in rodents and is carried by their fleas; when infected rats die, the fleas bite people. The bubonic form causes painful swellings, buboes, and killed perhaps half of those infected, while the pneumonic form spread by coughing and was almost always fatal. DNA from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan traces the Black Death's strain to Central Asia around 1338–39. According to the chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi, the Mongol army besieging Caffa catapulted corpses into the city, but ships, rats and trade goods probably did far more to carry it west.

Medieval doctors did not know about germs, but cities learned that keeping travellers apart slowed the plague. In 1377 Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, ordered arrivals from infected places to wait 30 days, a trentino, on nearby islands before entering the city. In 1423 Venice opened the world's first permanent plague hospital, a lazaretto, on an island in its lagoon, and the waiting period grew to 40 days, in Italian quaranta giorni, which gave us the word quarantine. Why 40 is unclear: it may echo the 40 days of Lent. The famous beaked plague-doctor mask, by contrast, dates from the 1600s, not the Black Death.

Smallpox reached the Caribbean by 1518 and Mexico in 1520, with the Spanish expedition of Pánfilo de Narváez. It tore through Tenochtitlan, killing the Aztec emperor Cuitláhuac and many defenders before Hernán Cortés's siege of 1521. It spread south ahead of the Spanish, probably killing the Inca emperor Huayna Capac around 1527 and setting off the civil war that Francisco Pizarro exploited. Smallpox, measles, flu and typhus, together with war, famine and forced labour, cut the population of the Americas by perhaps 50–90% within a century, although estimates of how many people lived there before 1492 vary widely.

The Black Death reshaped Europe's economy. With up to half the workers dead, survivors demanded higher pay; England's Statute of Labourers of 1351 tried to freeze wages, and anger over such laws fed the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. In the west, serfdom slowly faded. The 1918 flu, called 'Spanish' only because neutral Spain's press reported it freely, pushed many countries to create health ministries. HIV transformed sexual health and medicine: from 1996, combination drug treatment turned it from a death sentence into a manageable condition. COVID-19 brought the fastest vaccine development in history, using new mRNA technology, and a lasting shift to remote work.

dd-spices.what: In the 1400s pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg reached Europe after passing through many hands, from Asian growers to Arab traders, Egyptian customs posts and Venetian merchants. Portugal set out to reach the source by sea: Dias rounded Africa in 1488 and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Columbus, sailing west for Spain to find Asia, reached the Americas in 1492. Portugal and then the Netherlands fought their way to control of the spice islands of Indonesia. Meanwhile Columbus's voyages began the Columbian Exchange, a two-way flow of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world.
dd-spices.why: Spices were luxuries, valued for flavour, medicine, perfume and prestige, and the profits were enormous because they grew in so few places. Atlantic states such as Portugal and Spain wanted to cut out the Venetian and Muslim middlemen, spread Christianity and win glory. Better ships, navigation and guns let them cross oceans and seize ports, while profits from spices, silver and sugar paid for more voyages.
dd-spices.after: The spice race launched European empires in Asia and the Americas and the first truly global trade. The Columbian Exchange changed what the whole world eats: potatoes, maize and chillies spread across Europe, Africa and Asia. It also brought catastrophe. Old World diseases killed a large share of Indigenous Americans, by many estimates most of them within a century, and sugar plantations drove the Atlantic slave trade, which carried about 12.5 million Africans across the ocean.

sections.t: A popular story says Europeans needed spices to hide the taste of rotten meat. Historians reject this: anyone who could afford spices could afford fresh meat. Spices were status symbols, flavourings for the rich, perfumes and medicines, thought to balance the body's humours. Their price came from distance and scarcity. In the 1400s nutmeg grew only on the Banda Islands, and each merchant along the way added a mark-up. Pepper was so valued that, according to the Greek historian Zosimus, the Gothic king Alaric demanded 3,000 pounds of it as part of a ransom from Rome in 408. Later, the Dutch East India Company burned surplus nutmeg to keep prices high.

School books once said the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 cut Europe off from spices and forced it to find new routes. In fact spices kept flowing to Venice through Egypt and Syria, and Portugal's voyages down Africa had begun decades earlier, driven by gold, slaves, crusading zeal and profit. Another favourite tale says the Dutch swapped Manhattan for the nutmeg island of Run. At the Peace of Breda in 1667 each side kept what it held: England kept New Amsterdam, renamed New York, and the Dutch kept Run. It was a settlement of claims rather than a direct trade, though it is often told as one.

The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term 'Columbian Exchange' in 1972. Its effects are everywhere. Italian cooking had no tomatoes, Indian and Thai cooking no chillies, and Ireland no potatoes before 1492. Chocolate, vanilla, peanuts, pineapples and turkeys came from the Americas, while coffee, sugar, bananas, wheat, rice, horses and cattle went there. American crops such as maize and sweet potatoes, which grow on poor soils, helped populations grow in China and Africa. But dependence could be dangerous: when blight struck Ireland's potatoes in 1845, the Great Famine killed about a million people.

dd-slavery.what: From the early 1500s Portuguese and then Spanish, Dutch, British, French and other traders shipped enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to work in the Americas. Captives were bought at coastal forts from African rulers and merchants, packed into ships and carried on the Middle Passage, where perhaps one in seven died. Most were put to work growing sugar in Brazil and the Caribbean, and later coffee and cotton. In all about 12.5 million people were shipped, the trade peaking in the 1700s. Revolts, Haiti's revolution and abolition campaigns brought bans on the trade from 1807, but slavery itself lasted in Brazil until 1888.
dd-slavery.why: European colonists in the Americas wanted cheap labour for plantations and mines, and Indigenous populations had collapsed from disease, conquest and forced labour. Sugar, a hugely profitable crop, needed large gangs of workers. African states and merchants sold captives, mostly taken in wars and raids, in exchange for cloth, guns and other goods. Ideas of racial inferiority grew up to justify enslaving Africans and their children for life.
dd-slavery.after: The trade moved more people across the Atlantic than any migration before 1820 and created the large African-descended populations of Brazil, the Caribbean and the United States. Plantation profits fed European ports, banks and industry, though historians debate how much they drove the Industrial Revolution. In Africa it fuelled wars and drained people from whole regions. Racism built to defend slavery outlived it, and debates over memory and reparations continue today.

sections.t: Captives were chained below deck in spaces often too low to sit upright, for voyages lasting weeks or months. Disease, especially dysentery, killed many, and the sick were sometimes thrown overboard. In 1781 the crew of the British ship Zong threw about 130 Africans into the sea, and its owners then claimed insurance for them as lost cargo. A 1788 diagram of the Liverpool ship Brookes, showing 454 people packed like goods into its hold, became the abolitionists' most powerful image; on one earlier voyage it had carried over 600. Captives resisted, too: revolts broke out on an estimated one voyage in ten.

Slavery existed in many societies, including in Africa, long before the Atlantic trade. What was new was its scale and its basis in race. European traders rarely raided inland; they depended on African kingdoms and merchants, such as Dahomey and the Aro, who sold captives taken in wars, raids or as punishment. Some African rulers, like Afonso I of Kongo, protested against the trade, while others grew rich from it. In Europe and the Americas, ordinary investors, shipbuilders, banks and insurers profited, and consumers bought the sugar, tobacco and cotton that enslaved people grew.

Enslaved people fought for freedom throughout, through escapes, sabotage and revolts. Maroon communities of runaways survived for generations in Jamaica, Suriname and Brazil, and the Haitian Revolution of 1791–1804 terrified slaveholders everywhere. In Britain, Quakers, Thomas Clarkson, William Wilberforce and the formerly enslaved writer Olaudah Equiano built one of the first mass campaigns, with petitions and a sugar boycott said to have involved about 300,000 people in 1791. After abolishing its own trade in 1807, Britain's navy patrolled the African coast, and between 1808 and 1860 it seized about 1,600 slave ships and freed some 150,000 captives.

dd-science.what: In 1543 Copernicus argued that the Earth circles the Sun, and Vesalius published the first accurate atlas of the human body. Tycho Brahe's precise measurements let Kepler show that planets move in ellipses, and from 1609 Galileo's telescope revealed moons around Jupiter. In 1633 the Church condemned Galileo, but the new ideas spread through print and new scientific societies in London and Paris. In 1687 Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity explained the heavens and the Earth with the same mathematics. Over the next two centuries chemistry, biology, electricity and medicine were remade in the same way, and by 1900 science was a profession taught in universities and laboratories.
dd-science.why: Printing let scholars share results quickly and check each other's work. Rediscovered Greek texts, many preserved and improved by scholars in the Islamic world, sparked debate about old authorities. New instruments, such as the telescope and microscope, showed things no ancient writer had seen. Rival European states and their rulers competed for prestige, trade and better navigation, and paid for observatories and academies. Historians still debate why this happened in Europe rather than in China or the Islamic world.
dd-science.after: Science gave humanity a method: test ideas against careful observation and experiment, and publish so others can check them. Its discoveries powered the Industrial Revolution, gave Europe and North America great military and economic advantages, and, through vaccines, clean water and germ theory, began the fall in death rates that let the world's population soar. The same approach drives modern medicine, computing and space flight.

sections.t: Galileo was a devout Catholic, and for years he had friends in Rome, including the future Pope Urban VIII. In 1616 the Church ruled that the Sun-centred view was contrary to Scripture and told him not to defend it. His 1632 Dialogue did so anyway, and seemed to mock the Pope's views. In 1633 the Inquisition forced him to recant, banned the book and kept him under house arrest until his death in 1642. He was threatened but not tortured. The story that he muttered 'And yet it moves' after recanting is a legend, first recorded over a century later. In 1992 Pope John Paul II acknowledged the Church had erred.

Isaac Newton did much of his early work in 1665–66, when plague closed Cambridge University and he went home to Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire. According to his friend William Stukeley, the elderly Newton said that seeing an apple fall in the garden there set him thinking about gravity. Whether or not the story is polished, it was his own; the idea of the apple hitting his head is a later embellishment. His insight was that the force pulling an apple down is the same one holding the Moon in orbit, weakening with the square of the distance. He spent the next twenty years on the mathematics before publishing the Principia in 1687.

A popular myth says that before Columbus or Copernicus, people believed the Earth was flat. In fact educated Europeans had known it was a sphere since ancient Greek times; the Greek scholar Eratosthenes estimated its size around 240 BC. Nor did science start from nothing in 1543. Scholars in the Islamic world, such as Ibn al-Haytham, who studied light and vision around 1020, had built on Greek learning, and Copernicus used mathematical tools first developed by astronomers at Maragha in Persia. What changed was the scale: printed books, regular experiments and open debate turned scattered insights into a lasting, self-correcting enterprise.

dd-capitalism.what: Capitalism is an economic system in which private owners, not the state, run most businesses and markets set prices. Its modern form began in the 1600s, when Dutch and English trading companies sold shares to investors. In 1776 Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations argued that free markets and competition make nations rich. The Industrial Revolution turned capitalism into a world system of factories, railways, banks and global trade, creating huge wealth and harsh inequality. Crashes such as the Great Depression led governments to regulate markets, and after the Cold War most of the world, including China, embraced markets in some form.
dd-capitalism.why: Markets rewarded people who invented, invested and took risks, and joint-stock companies let many investors share the costs and dangers of big ventures. Secure property rights, banks and stock exchanges made it easier to raise money. In the 20th century, the failures of planned economies persuaded many countries that markets delivered growth more reliably.
dd-capitalism.after: Capitalism has helped lift billions of people out of poverty, especially since China and India opened their economies. But it also brings booms and busts, such as the 2008 financial crisis, and wide gaps between rich and poor. Arguments about how far governments should tax, regulate and spend remain at the heart of politics almost everywhere.

sections.t: In 1602 the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, raised money by selling shares that anyone could buy and later resell, and Amsterdam's exchange became the first modern stock market. Investors shared both the profits and the risks of long voyages to Asia. England's East India Company, chartered in 1600, and the Bank of England, founded in 1694, showed how private money could fund trade and even wars. These companies were also tools of empire: the VOC fought wars in Indonesia, and the English company eventually ruled much of India.

Adam Smith, a Scottish professor, argued in 1776 that people pursuing their own interest in free markets are led 'as if by an invisible hand' to benefit society: a baker sells good bread not out of kindness but to earn a living. Smith attacked mercantilism, the policy of hoarding gold and protecting home industries with tariffs and monopolies, and praised the division of labour, using a pin factory as his example. He also warned that business owners often conspire against the public, and said the state must provide defence, justice and public works.

Capitalism grew in booms and busts. After the Wall Street Crash of 1929, banks failed and by 1933 about a quarter of American workers were unemployed. The British economist John Maynard Keynes argued that governments should spend to revive demand in a slump, and after World War II most Western countries built mixed economies, with welfare states, regulated banks and some state-owned industries. In the 1970s high inflation and slow growth turned many against this model, and economists such as Milton Friedman argued for freer markets, lower taxes and less regulation.

From the late 1970s a wave of market reforms swept the world.
