Chile's military government opened its economy from 1975, China's Deng Xiaoping began reforms in 1978, and Margaret Thatcher in Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States cut taxes and sold off or deregulated industries. Vietnam followed in 1986, and after communism collapsed, Eastern Europe and Russia switched to markets almost overnight, often painfully. India opened up in 1991. Global trade boomed, but the 2008 financial crisis, which began with risky American mortgage lending, revived old doubts about unregulated markets.

dd-pirates.what: From the mid-1600s buccaneers based at Tortuga and Port Royal raided Spanish towns and ships in the Caribbean, often with licences from England or France. In the 1690s pirates sailed the 'Pirate Round' to the Indian Ocean, where Henry Every seized a Mughal treasure ship in 1695. The busiest years came after 1715, when crews based at Nassau in the Bahamas, led by men such as Benjamin Hornigold, Blackbeard and Charles Vane, attacked merchant shipping, and later crews such as Bartholomew Roberts's raided from Newfoundland to West Africa. Then the tide turned: Woodes Rogers took back Nassau in 1718, Blackbeard was killed that November, and by about 1726 the great pirate crews were gone.
dd-pirates.why: Spanish silver and the booming trade in sugar, slaves and Asian goods offered rich prizes on long, poorly guarded routes. Wars between European powers trained thousands of sailors as privateers, licensed raiders, and when peace came in 1713 many were thrown out of work. Merchant sailors faced low pay and brutal discipline, so some joined pirates willingly. Weak colonial government and merchants happy to buy cheap goods gave pirates safe harbours.
dd-pirates.after: Britain's Royal Navy, colonial courts and a 1717 royal pardon broke the pirate havens, and hundreds of pirates were hanged, which helped make the Atlantic safe for the trade of growing empires. Piracy never vanished, and it returns wherever states are weak, as off Somalia in the 2000s. The golden age also left a powerful legend, reshaped by novels and films, of free outlaws under the skull and crossbones.

sections.t: Edward Teach, or Thatch, was a pirate for only about two years, from 1716 to 1718, but no pirate is more famous. In late 1717 he captured a French slave ship and renamed it Queen Anne's Revenge, armed with dozens of cannon. In May 1718 he blockaded Charleston for about a week and released his hostages for a chest of medicines. Soon after, his flagship ran aground off North Carolina; its wreck was found in 1996. He accepted a royal pardon but returned to piracy, and on 22 November 1718 he died fighting a Royal Navy party at Ocracoke. According to a 1724 book, he lit slow fuses under his hat to frighten victims.

Many pirate crews signed written articles, rules that every man swore to. Captains were usually elected and could be voted out, and a quartermaster shared out the loot, with the captain typically taking only one and a half or two shares. Some articles promised payouts for lost limbs, banned gambling or fighting on board, and set punishments such as marooning. Crews were young, mostly former merchant sailors and navy men, and included many men of African descent, some free crewmen and some still treated as slaves. Life was crowded, often drunk and dangerous, and most pirate careers ended within a few years at the end of a rope or in a fight.

Walking the plank is mostly fiction: there is almost no evidence for it in the golden age, and the few recorded cases come from later. Buried treasure was rare, because pirates usually spent or shared loot quickly; the best-known real case is William Kidd's cache on Gardiners Island near New York, dug up by the authorities in 1699. Treasure maps marked with an X, peg legs and parrots owe more to Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island (1883) than to history. The Jolly Roger was real, though flags varied, and a black flag usually offered mercy if a ship surrendered.

In 1717 King George I offered a pardon to pirates who surrendered, and in July 1718 Woodes Rogers, a former privateer, arrived at Nassau as governor with warships. Many pirates accepted the pardon; those who carried on were hunted down. Under a 1700 law, colonial courts could try pirates without sending them to London, and mass hangings followed. The navy killed Bartholomew Roberts, the most successful pirate of the age, off West Africa in 1722, and 52 of his crew were hanged at Cape Coast Castle. By the late 1720s the great Atlantic pirate crews had gone.

dd-enlightenment.what: The Enlightenment was an 18th-century movement of writers and scientists who believed that reason and evidence, rather than tradition, Church or king, should guide human affairs. Building on Newton's laws of motion of 1687, thinkers such as John Locke, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Adam Smith and Immanuel Kant questioned how societies should be run. They argued for natural rights to life, liberty and property, freedom of speech and religion, government by consent and the separation of powers. Books, pamphlets, salons and the great French Encyclopédie spread these ideas across Europe and the Americas, where they inspired the American Revolution of 1776, the French Revolution of 1789 and the Haitian Revolution, which ended in 1804.
dd-enlightenment.why: The Scientific Revolution showed that nature followed laws people could discover, which encouraged thinkers to apply reason to society too. Europe's wars of religion had left many weary of intolerance. Growing literacy, cheap printing, coffee houses and a rising middle class created an eager public for new ideas, while censorship was often easy to dodge by printing abroad, especially in the Dutch Republic.
dd-enlightenment.after: Enlightenment ideas underpin modern democracies, constitutions, free speech and human rights, and the belief that science can improve lives. Yet many of its thinkers accepted slavery and the exclusion of women. Later campaigners, from abolitionists to Mary Wollstonecraft, attacked these contradictions using the Enlightenment's own arguments about equal rights.

sections.t: Before the Enlightenment, most Europeans accepted that kings ruled by the will of God and that the Church decided what was true. Enlightenment thinkers asked people to test ideas by reason and evidence instead. Kant summed it up in 1784 with the motto 'Dare to know'. Voltaire mocked religious intolerance and was jailed in the Bastille and later exiled from Paris for his writing. Many thinkers were still believers, but they wanted religion to be a private choice, not something enforced by the state. Scientists, from Newton to the chemist Antoine Lavoisier, were heroes of the age.

John Locke argued that people are born with natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that a government which breaks its trust may be overthrown. Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) proposed splitting power between a legislature, an executive and courts so that no one could become a tyrant. Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762) opened with 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' These ideas went straight into the US Constitution of 1787, with its checks and balances, and into France's Declaration of the Rights of Man.

Some monarchs liked the new ideas, as long as they kept their own power. Frederick the Great of Prussia corresponded with Voltaire, allowed religious freedom and abolished most torture. Catherine the Great of Russia exchanged letters with Diderot and bought his library, yet serfdom grew harsher in her reign. Joseph II of Austria abolished serfdom in his lands and tolerated Protestants and Jews, but many of his reforms were reversed after his death. Historians call them 'enlightened absolutists': rulers who reformed from above but never shared power with their people.

The Enlightenment's promises were not meant for everyone. Thomas Jefferson, who wrote that 'all men are created equal', owned more than 600 enslaved people over his life. Most thinkers excluded women from politics, and Rousseau thought girls should be educated to please men. Critics soon turned the movement's logic against these limits. Olympe de Gouges published a Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791, and Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman followed in 1792. In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people led by Toussaint Louverture claimed the rights of man for themselves.

dd-nationalism.what: Nationalism is the idea that people who share a language, culture or history form a nation, and that each nation should govern itself in its own state. It took off with the French Revolution, which declared that sovereignty belonged to the nation rather than the king. In the 1800s it united Italy and Germany and helped Greeks, Serbs and others break away from the Ottoman Empire. After World War I it broke up the Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian empires, and after 1945 it powered independence movements across Asia and Africa. It also fuelled wars, ethnic cleansing and fascism.
dd-nationalism.why: Before 1800 most people's loyalty went to their village, religion or ruler. Mass schooling, newspapers, railways and conscript armies spread a shared national language and identity. Empires made many peoples feel like second-class subjects, and nationalism offered them dignity, self-rule and a reason to resist foreign domination.
dd-nationalism.after: Today almost the whole world is divided into nation-states, and the United Nations has 193 members. Nationalism still shapes politics: independence movements in Scotland, Catalonia and Kurdistan, wars over territory such as Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and populist parties that promise to put the nation first.

sections.t: In 1789 France's revolutionaries declared that power came from the nation, not the king. The new republic promoted one language, French, in its schools, though many citizens still spoke Breton, Occitan or other tongues, and in 1793 it raised a mass army of citizens. Napoleon's conquests then spread the idea, and stirred nationalism against him in Germany, Spain and Russia. Writers collected folk tales and songs to define their nations: the Brothers Grimm in Germany, and Elias Lönnrot, whose Kalevala epic of 1835 became Finland's national story.

In 1815 Italy and Germany were both patchworks of states. Italy was united between 1859 and 1870 under the King of Piedmont-Sardinia, through the diplomacy of Count Cavour and the volunteer army of Giuseppe Garibaldi, who conquered Sicily and Naples in 1860. German unity came through 'blood and iron'. Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's chief minister, fought wars against Denmark, Austria and France, and in January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Both new nations soon sought colonies and great-power status.

Nationalism was deadly for empires that ruled many peoples. The Ottoman Empire lost Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria in the 1800s, and in 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist's assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand helped trigger World War I. In 1918 US President Woodrow Wilson called for self-determination, and new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia rose from the ruins of the Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires. After World War II, nationalist leaders such as Gandhi, Sukarno and Kwame Nkrumah won independence from European empires across Asia and Africa.

Nationalism could unite people, but it could also turn them against outsiders and minorities. Extreme nationalism fed fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany, which claimed the nation needed racial purity and 'living space'. Creating nation-states often meant moving or expelling minorities. In 1923 Greece and Turkey exchanged about 1.6 million people, and the partition of India in 1947 uprooted about 15 million. In the 1990s the breakup of Yugoslavia brought 'ethnic cleansing' back to Europe, and rival nationalisms still drive conflicts from the Caucasus to the Middle East.

dd-women.what: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women were not naturally inferior to men, only less educated. In 1848 American campaigners met at Seneca Falls and demanded equal rights, including the vote. Over the next century movements in dozens of countries won women entry to universities, control of their own property and wages, and the vote, first in New Zealand in 1893. After 1945 the fight moved to work, family law and the body: equal pay laws, the contraceptive pill, divorce reform and laws against violence. Today women vote almost everywhere and lead governments, but they still earn less, hold under a third of parliamentary seats, and in Afghanistan are barred from school.
dd-women.why: Industrialisation, mass schooling and cities drew women into paid work and public life, and Enlightenment ideas of equal rights were hard to limit to men. Women organised petitions, marches and, in Britain, militant protest. Two world wars, when women filled factories and offices, made the case harder to refuse. Later, safer contraception, higher education and service-sector jobs let women plan careers, and international agreements put pressure on governments.
dd-women.after: Women's rights changed daily life more than almost any other movement: in most countries girls now go to school as long as boys, and women make up about four in ten workers. Gaps remain. The World Economic Forum estimated in 2026 that at current rates full equality is about 120 years away. Debates continue over pay, care work, abortion, violence, and religious and cultural rules on dress and family.

sections.t: In Britain the vote was fought for in two ways. From 1897 Millicent Fawcett's suffragists lobbied politely through petitions and meetings. From 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst's suffragettes chose 'deeds, not words': they chained themselves to railings, smashed shop windows and set fire to empty buildings. Jailed suffragettes went on hunger strike and were force-fed through tubes. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison ran onto the track at the Derby and was fatally struck by the King's horse. Historians still debate whether militancy helped or hurt. War work by millions of women from 1914 shifted opinion, and in 1918 women over 30 won the vote.

For much of history married women had few legal rights of their own: in English common law a wife's property and earnings belonged to her husband until the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882. After 1945 more women took paid work, and campaigners turned to equal pay. The US passed an Equal Pay Act in 1963 and Britain in 1970, after women machinists at Ford's Dagenham factory went on strike in 1968. The contraceptive pill, approved in the US in 1960, let women plan families and careers. In many countries women now outnumber men at university, but they still earn less, partly because they do most unpaid care work.

After 1945 women's rights became an international cause. In 1979 the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), which 189 countries have ratified; the United States has signed but not ratified it. In 1995, at the Beijing conference, 189 governments agreed a plan for action on education, health, work and violence. Movements took local forms: Indian campaigners fought dowry deaths, Latin Americans won quotas for women in parliament, and in 2017 the #MeToo campaign against sexual harassment spread worldwide from the United States. In Iran the 2022 protests after Mahsa Amini's death in police custody took the slogan 'Woman, life, freedom'.

By the World Economic Forum's 2026 measure, the world has closed about 69% of the gap between men and women in health, education, work and politics. Health and education gaps are nearly closed in most countries; the largest gaps are in politics and the economy. Women hold about 27.5% of seats in parliaments, and the International Labour Organization estimates they earn roughly a fifth less than men worldwide. Iceland, Finland and Norway come closest to equality. The widest gaps are in parts of South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, and Afghanistan under the Taliban is the only country that bars girls from secondary school.

dd-communism.what: In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto, predicting that workers would overthrow capitalism. The first communist revolution came in Russia in 1917, where Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power and founded the Soviet Union. Under Stalin it industrialised at enormous human cost, and after World War II the Red Army installed communist governments across Eastern Europe. Mao Zedong won China's civil war in 1949, and communists later took power in North Korea, Vietnam, Cuba and parts of Africa. By the 1980s these states held about a third of humanity, but in 1989 Eastern Europe's regimes fell, and in 1991 the Soviet Union itself dissolved.
dd-communism.why: Industrialisation brought great wealth alongside harsh poverty, and Marx's promise of a classless society of equals inspired millions. Communists won power mostly where wars had shattered old regimes, as in Russia in 1917 and China in the 1940s, or where they led struggles against colonial rule. The systems later failed because planned economies stagnated, people resented the lack of freedom, and Gorbachev's reforms loosened control.
dd-communism.after: Five states, China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and North Korea, are still ruled by communist parties, though China and Vietnam now run market economies. Former Soviet bloc countries in Central Europe joined NATO and the EU. The era left deep scars: famines, purges and labour camps killed millions, and historians still debate the totals. Many former communist states remain under authoritarian rule.

sections.t: Marx argued that history is driven by struggle between classes. Under capitalism, he said, factory owners, the bourgeoisie, grew rich by paying workers, the proletariat, less than the value they produced. Competition would squeeze wages and concentrate wealth until workers rose up, took over the means of production and built a classless society in which the state would eventually 'wither away'. He expected this in advanced industrial countries such as Britain and Germany. Instead, revolutions succeeded in largely peasant countries, Russia and China, and the state grew more powerful rather than withering. Marx gave few details of how a communist society would actually work, leaving Lenin and others to invent it.

From 1928 the Soviet Union ran its economy by five-year plans: officials, not markets, decided what to make and at what price. This built steel mills, dams and a huge arms industry quickly, and brought near-universal literacy, free health care and guaranteed jobs. But consumer goods were scarce and often poor. People queued for meat, shoes and toilet paper, and in East Germany buyers could wait more than ten years for a Trabant car. Housing was cheap but cramped, and many families shared flats. Criticism could cost a job or worse, and travel abroad was tightly restricted. Jokes and black markets became part of everyday survival.

Communist states caused some of the 20th century's worst disasters, though death tolls are debated. In 1932–33 famine caused by Soviet collectivisation killed millions, including an estimated 3.5 to 5 million in Ukraine, where it is known as the Holodomor. In Stalin's Great Terror of 1937–38 about 680,000 people were shot, according to Soviet records, and millions passed through the Gulag labour camps. China's Great Leap Forward caused a famine in 1959–61 with estimates ranging from about 15 million to over 40 million deaths. In Cambodia the Khmer Rouge's rule in 1975–79 left an estimated 1.5 to 2 million dead.

By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating and the war in Afghanistan was draining it. Mikhail Gorbachev, leader from 1985, tried to revive it with perestroika, restructuring, and glasnost, openness, and made clear he would not send tanks to save Eastern Europe's regimes. In 1989 they fell one after another: Poland's Solidarity won elections in June, the Berlin Wall opened on 9 November, and Czechoslovakia's 'Velvet Revolution' followed. That same June, China's leaders chose force instead, crushing protests in Tiananmen Square. After a failed hardline coup in August 1991, the Soviet republics declared independence, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned.

dd-climate.what: From the 1800s, burning coal, then oil and gas, powered industry, transport and electricity, first in Europe and North America and later across Asia. Scientists showed as early as the 1850s that carbon dioxide traps heat, and from 1958 measurements in Hawaii tracked its steady rise. By the 1980s many scientists were warning that the planet was warming, and governments set up the IPCC in 1988 to assess the evidence. Treaties followed in Rio in 1992, Kyoto in 1997 and Paris in 2015, but global emissions kept rising and reached a record in 2025. That year the world was about 1.4°C warmer than before industrialisation.
dd-climate.why: Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide that has been locked underground for millions of years, and it stays in the air for centuries, so warming builds up as emissions accumulate. Cutting emissions has been hard because fossil fuels were cheap and reliable and underpin modern economies, the benefits of cutting are shared globally while the costs are local, and countries disagree over who should cut first and pay.
dd-climate.after: The IPCC concludes that human activity has unequivocally warmed the planet, bringing more intense heatwaves, heavier rain, melting ice and rising seas, with the poorest countries often hit hardest. At the same time solar and wind power have become the cheapest new electricity in most places, and in 2025 renewables overtook coal worldwide. Debates continue over the speed of change, its costs, and who pays.

sections.t: In 1856 the American scientist Eunice Foote put jars of different gases in the sun and found that the one filled with carbon dioxide grew hottest. In 1859 John Tyndall in London measured how carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb heat. In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius estimated that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the world by about 5–6°C, though he expected it to take thousands of years. In 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring the air on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, at about 315 parts per million. His 'Keeling Curve' rose every year, passing 425 in 2025, about 50% above pre-industrial levels.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, founded in 1988, reviews thousands of studies and has its summaries approved line by line by governments. Its 2021–2023 assessment concluded that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, by about 1.1°C in 2011–2020 compared with 1850–1900. Warming has since continued: the World Meteorological Organization says 2015–2025 were the eleven warmest years on record. The IPCC finds that each extra fraction of a degree brings more heat extremes, heavier downpours, droughts in some regions and rising seas, and that limiting warming to 1.5°C would require global emissions to fall steeply and reach net zero around 2050.

Most governments accept the mainstream science, though the US government under Trump rejects much of it, and countries disagree about what to do and how fast. Developing countries such as India argue that rich nations, which emitted most of the carbon already in the air, should cut first and pay for poorer ones to adapt; rich countries point out that most emissions now come from developing economies, led by China. Some favour carbon taxes or trading schemes, others subsidies, regulation or nuclear power. Critics of rapid change, including the Trump administration, argue that it raises energy prices, threatens jobs and hurts competitiveness; supporters argue that clean energy is now often cheaper and that delay makes the damage costlier.

In the 1970s scientists found that chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, used in spray cans and fridges, were destroying the ozone layer that shields life from ultraviolet light, and in 1985 British researchers reported a 'hole' over Antarctica. In 1987 the Montreal Protocol agreed to phase out these chemicals, and every UN member eventually ratified it. The ozone layer is now slowly recovering, and UN scientists expect it to return to 1980 levels over most of the world by about 2040, and over Antarctica by about 2066. It is often cited as proof that global environmental agreements can work, though cutting CFCs was far easier than replacing fossil fuels.

dd-oil.what: In 1859 Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial oil well in Pennsylvania, and kerosene lamps soon lit homes worldwide. Cars, ships and aircraft then made oil the fuel of the 20th century, and both world wars were fought partly over access to it. Huge finds in Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia shifted the centre of the oil world to the Gulf. Producers founded OPEC in 1960, and in 1973 an Arab embargo quadrupled prices and stunned the West. Since then oil has shaped wars from Kuwait in 1990 to the Strait of Hormuz in 2026, while the US shale boom made America the top producer again.
dd-oil.why: Oil packs a lot of energy into a liquid that is easy to move and store, so it beat coal for transport and became the base of plastics and chemicals. But the cheapest oil lies in a few places, often far from the countries that use the most. That mismatch made oil a source of wealth, power and conflict: governments fought for supplies, and producers fought foreign companies for control of their own resources.
dd-oil.after: Oil wealth built the modern Gulf states and funds governments from Norway to Nigeria, though many producers struggle with corruption and dependence on one product. Price shocks still ripple through the world economy, as in 2026. Burning oil also releases about a third of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels, so the shift to electric cars and clean energy is now reshaping the industry's future.

sections.t: On 6 October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. When the US rushed weapons to Israel, Arab producers led by Saudi Arabia cut output and banned sales to the United States and the Netherlands. The price of a barrel of Saudi crude went from about $3 to almost $12 within months. Americans waited in long queues for petrol, some stations ran dry, and Congress set a national speed limit of 55 mph. The Netherlands and West Germany banned most Sunday driving, and people cycled and skated on empty motorways. The embargo ended in March 1974, but the shock pushed the West into recession and started the search for new oil in the North Sea and Alaska.

In 1950 Dubai and Doha were small towns of traders, fishermen and pearl divers. Oil changed everything. At first Western companies controlled the fields and paid the rulers royalties. From the 1970s producers took over: Saudi Arabia bought full ownership of Aramco by 1980, and Kuwait, Iraq and others nationalised their oil. The money paid for cities, airports, free health care and education, and generous state jobs for citizens, while millions of foreign workers came to build it all. Today Gulf states use their oil income to diversify into finance, tourism and airlines, and their sovereign wealth funds are among the largest investors in the world.

In 1912 Britain's navy began switching from coal to oil, and two years later the government bought control of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company to secure supplies. In World War II oil shaped strategy: Japan attacked the US and the oil-rich Dutch East Indies after America cut off its oil in 1941, and Germany drove towards the Caucasus oilfields in 1942. In 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait, and a US-led coalition drove it out in 1991, as retreating troops set over 600 wells on fire. In 2026 war between the US, Israel and Iran choked shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow outlet for about a fifth of the world's oil.

Burning oil releases carbon dioxide, the main gas driving climate change. Oil accounts for roughly a third of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels, coming mostly from cars, lorries, ships and planes. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement nearly every country promised to cut emissions, and at the 2023 COP28 climate summit in Dubai countries agreed for the first time to 'transition away from fossil fuels'. Electric cars are spreading fast, especially in China and Europe. Producers argue the world will still need oil for decades, while critics say new fields are incompatible with climate goals. World demand was still rising slowly in the mid-2020s.

dd-fascism.what: In March 1919 Benito Mussolini, a former socialist journalist and war veteran, founded the Fascist movement in Milan. His blackshirt squads beat and killed socialists, and in October 1922, after the March on Rome, the king made him prime minister. By 1926 Italy was a one-party state. In Germany Adolf Hitler's Nazi party failed in a coup in 1923 but grew in the Depression, winning 37% of the vote in July 1932. Appointed chancellor in January 1933, Hitler crushed all opposition within months. Both regimes rearmed and expanded: Italy took Ethiopia and Albania, Germany took Austria and Czechoslovakia, and in 1939 the invasion of Poland began World War II.
dd-fascism.why: World War I left millions of bitter veterans, economies in ruins and fear of a communist revolution like Russia's. Italians felt cheated of the land they had been promised; Germans resented defeat and the Treaty of Versailles. Fascists offered order, national pride and a strong leader. Conservative elites, hoping to use them against the left, helped both men into office, and the Depression's mass unemployment gave the Nazis their voters.
dd-fascism.after: Fascism's wars killed tens of millions and led to the Holocaust. Mussolini and Hitler both died in April 1945, and the Nuremberg trials judged leading Nazis. Germany and Italy rebuilt as democracies whose laws ban reviving the old parties, and Spain and Portugal stayed dictatorships until the 1970s. Small neo-fascist groups survived, and 'fascist' became the strongest insult in politics, though historians use the word much more precisely.

sections.t: The word comes from the fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe carried before magistrates in ancient Rome, a symbol of strength through unity. Fascists put the nation above the individual and wanted one party, one leader and one will. They despised liberal democracy, parliaments and Marxism, and they glorified youth, violence and war as signs of national health. Mussolini defined the idea as 'everything within the state, nothing outside the state'. Nazism added an obsession with race: Hitler taught that Germans were a superior 'Aryan' people and that Jews were their enemy. Historians such as Robert Paxton stress that fascism was defined less by a fixed doctrine than by what it did.

sections.h: Into power through the front door
sections.t: Neither dictator seized power by a successful coup. Mussolini's March on Rome was largely a bluff: the army could have stopped it, but King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign an order of martial law and appointed him prime minister instead. Hitler, after his failed Munich putsch of 1923, chose the ballot box. The Nazis were Germany's largest party by July 1932, but never won a majority in a free election. Conservative politicians around President Hindenburg made Hitler chancellor, believing they could control him. Within weeks the Reichstag fire gave him an excuse to suspend civil rights, and the Enabling Act of March 1933 let him rule by decree.

Both regimes tried to shape every part of life. Children joined youth groups such as the Hitler Youth and the Opera Nazionale Balilla, and schools taught loyalty to the leader. Radio, newsreels and giant rallies spread propaganda, and books by Jewish and left-wing authors were burned in German cities in May 1933. Trade unions were abolished and replaced by state-run organisations that also organised cheap holidays. Opponents were jailed, exiled to islands in Italy or sent to concentration camps in Germany, the first opening at Dachau in March 1933. Many people went along out of belief, fear or career, while full employment from rearmament won the Nazis support.

dd-internet.what: In 1936 Alan Turing imagined a universal computing machine, and the Second World War produced the first real ones, from Zuse's Z3 in Berlin to Colossus at Bletchley Park and ENIAC in Philadelphia. The transistor (1947) and the microchip (1958–59) made computers ever smaller, cheaper and faster. Personal computers spread from the late 1970s. ARPANET, a US research network, sent its first message in 1969 and grew into the internet, and in 1991 Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web made it easy to use. Smartphones put it in billions of pockets after 2007, and from 2022 AI chatbots such as ChatGPT reached hundreds of millions of people.
dd-internet.why: War and the Cold War paid for the first computers, to break codes, aim artillery and design nuclear weapons, and US defence money funded early networks. After that, the steady shrinking of chips, roughly doubling their power every two years, made each new device cheaper than the last. Open standards such as TCP/IP and the free web let anyone build on the network, and businesses raced to profit from it.
dd-internet.after: About 6 billion people were online in 2025, according to the ITU, though 2.2 billion still were not. Computing transformed work, shopping, banking, news, friendship and politics, and made a few tech firms among the world's most valuable companies. It also brought new problems: surveillance, online misinformation, cybercrime and worries about screen time. Today rivalry over AI and advanced chips, centred on the US, China and Taiwan, shapes world politics.

sections.t: At Bletchley Park, a country house north of London, about 9,000 people at the 1945 peak, roughly three-quarters of them women, worked to read German codes. Building on Polish work, Alan Turing helped design the 'Bombe' machines that cracked daily Enigma settings. For the even harder Lorenz cipher, used by Hitler's high command, the Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers built Colossus, with about 1,600 to 2,400 vacuum tubes. After the war most Colossus machines were destroyed and the work stayed secret until the 1970s, so the Americans' ENIAC long got the credit as the first electronic computer. Turing was prosecuted for homosexuality in 1952, died in 1954 and received a royal pardon in 2013.

In 1965 Gordon Moore, later a co-founder of Intel, predicted that the number of components on a chip would keep doubling, a pace he revised in 1975 to about every two years. The prediction held for half a century, and it explains much of modern history. Intel's first microprocessor, the 4004 of 1971, had about 2,300 transistors; a top smartphone chip today has tens of billions, each far smaller than a virus. The guidance computer that helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon in 1969 had a tiny fraction of the power of a modern phone. Progress is now slowing as transistors near the size of atoms.

A common story says the internet was built to survive a nuclear war. In fact ARPANET's main purpose was to let researchers share scarce, expensive computers, though the idea of breaking messages into small 'packets', developed separately by Paul Baran in the US and Donald Davies in Britain, did come partly from thinking about networks that could survive damage. Another confusion: the internet and the web are not the same. The internet is the global network of connected computers, running since the 1970s and 1980s; the web, from 1991, is one service on top of it, a system of linked pages, alongside email, video calls and apps.

dd-nuclear.what: In December 1938 scientists in Berlin discovered that uranium atoms could be split, releasing huge energy. The United States, fearing a Nazi bomb, built the first atomic weapons, and in August 1945 destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The Soviet Union tested its own bomb in 1949, and an arms race followed: hydrogen bombs, intercontinental missiles and, by the mid-1980s, about 70,000 warheads worldwide. In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world close to nuclear war. Treaties then banned most tests, limited the spread of weapons and, after the Cold War, cut arsenals by over 80%, though nine countries still have them.
dd-nuclear.why: Physics made the bomb possible, and World War II made it urgent: scientists feared Hitler would build one first. After 1945 the Cold War rivals each believed only their own arsenal could deter the other, which led to 'mutually assured destruction'. Other countries built bombs for security against rivals, such as China against the superpowers, India against China and Pakistan against India, or for prestige and independence, as Britain and France did.
dd-nuclear.after: No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945, which many credit to deterrence and luck. The 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty, joined by almost every country, has kept the number of nuclear-armed states to nine. But arsenals are growing again, China is expanding fast, and the last US–Russian arms control treaty expired in February 2026. Nuclear power, born of the same science, still supplies about a tenth of the world's electricity.

sections.t: When a neutron hits the nucleus of a uranium-235 or plutonium-239 atom, the nucleus can split, releasing energy and two or three more neutrons. Those split more atoms, a chain reaction that, in a bomb, runs away in less than a millionth of a second. The Hiroshima bomb released energy equal to about 15,000 tonnes of TNT. Hydrogen bombs, first tested by the US in 1952, use a fission explosion to fuse hydrogen atoms, and can be hundreds or thousands of times stronger. The largest ever, the Soviet 'Tsar Bomba' of 1961, released about 50 million tonnes. The hard part is making the fuel: enriching uranium or producing plutonium takes huge industrial plants.

The Cuban Missile Crisis was more dangerous than people knew at the time. Kennedy's advisers did not know that Soviet forces in Cuba also had about 100 short-range nuclear weapons. On 27 October 1962, the worst day, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing its pilot. The same day US ships dropped practice depth charges to force a Soviet submarine to surface. Its crew had lost contact with Moscow, and the submarine carried a nuclear torpedo; according to later accounts, officer Vasily Arkhipov refused to agree to launch it. Afterwards the two sides set up a direct hotline, and in 1963 signed a treaty banning tests in the air, sea and space.

During the Cold War, schoolchildren in the United States practised 'duck and cover' drills, and some families built fallout shelters. Both superpowers kept bombers and missiles ready to strike within minutes. That brought close calls: in September 1983 a Soviet early-warning system reported US missiles heading for the Soviet Union, and the duty officer, Stanislav Petrov, judged it a false alarm, which it was. Over 2,000 nuclear tests have been carried out since 1945, many in the open air before 1963, spreading fallout and harming people near test sites from Nevada to Kazakhstan and the Pacific islands.

dd-globalization.what: After World War II the United States and its allies built new institutions, the IMF, the World Bank and the GATT, to keep trade open and currencies stable. Tariffs fell round after round, Western Europe formed a common market, and from 1956 the shipping container slashed the cost of moving goods. Japan, then South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grew rich by exporting. After the Cold War almost the whole world joined in: China opened from 1978 and entered the World Trade Organization in 2001, becoming the world's factory. From 2008, and especially after 2016, a backlash grew, and in 2025 the United States raised tariffs to their highest level since the 1930s.
dd-globalization.why: The Allies blamed the tariff wars of the 1930s for deepening the Depression and helping cause war, so they wanted rules for open trade. Cheaper shipping, jet travel, computers and the internet made it easy to split production across continents. Companies chased lower costs, consumers wanted cheaper goods, and poorer countries saw exports as the fastest route out of poverty. The end of communism opened huge new markets and workforces.
dd-globalization.after: Trade grew from about a quarter of world output in 1960 to around 60% by 2008. Hundreds of millions escaped extreme poverty, above all in China and the rest of East Asia, and goods became cheaper everywhere. But factory towns in rich countries lost jobs, inequality rose, and long supply chains proved fragile in the pandemic. Governments now use tariffs and subsidies to protect industries and national security, and trade is splitting into rival blocs.

sections.h: The box that changed the world
sections.t: Until the 1950s ships were loaded by gangs of dockworkers carrying sacks, barrels and crates, and a ship could spend as long in port as at sea. In 1956 the American trucking owner Malcom McLean sent a converted tanker, the Ideal X, from Newark to Houston with 58 metal boxes on deck. Standard containers could be lifted straight from ship to truck or train, cutting the cost of loading, by one estimate, from almost $6 a ton to about 16 cents. Theft and breakage fell, and ports moved to vast new terminals. Today ships carrying over 20,000 containers link Asia, Europe and the Americas, and shipping a T-shirt across the world costs only a few cents.

In 1978 China was poor and largely closed. Deng Xiaoping's reforms let farmers sell surplus crops, and from 1980 special economic zones such as Shenzhen welcomed foreign factories. Cheap labour, good ports and huge investment in roads and power made China the place to make almost anything. After it joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 its exports grew about sevenfold in a decade. The World Bank estimates that around 800 million Chinese people escaped extreme poverty over four decades. By 2025 China made nearly a third of the world's manufactured goods and ran a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion.

Economists broadly agree that trade made the world richer overall, but the gains were uneven. Consumers got cheaper goods and exporters boomed, while factory towns in the US and Europe lost jobs: one well-known study estimated that Chinese import competition cost the US about 2–2.4 million jobs in 1999–2011. Protesters disrupted the WTO's 1999 meeting in Seattle, and after the 2008 financial crisis anger grew. Britain voted to leave the EU in 2016, and the US began a trade war with China in 2018. Supporters of tariffs argue they protect jobs and security; critics say they raise prices and invite retaliation.

In April 2025 President Trump announced tariffs on imports from almost every country, calling the day 'Liberation Day'. Tariffs between the US and China briefly passed 100% before truces in Geneva and Busan. Many partners, including the EU, Japan and Britain, agreed deals accepting US tariffs of about 10–15%. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled that the emergency law used for most of these tariffs did not allow them, and companies began claiming refunds. The administration replaced them with tariffs under other laws, while other countries signed new deals with each other, such as the EU's agreement with Mercosur.

dd-humanrights.what: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, whatever their nationality, sex, religion or race. The idea had roots in religious teachings and the Enlightenment, but it became a global standard only after World War II and the Holocaust. In 1945, 51 countries founded the United Nations to keep the peace, and in 1948 its General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. Later treaties banned genocide, torture and racial discrimination, and courts such as the European Court of Human Rights and the International Criminal Court tried to enforce them.
dd-humanrights.why: The horrors of World War II, including the Holocaust and the deaths of tens of millions, convinced world leaders that how a state treats its own people is everyone's concern. They hoped that agreed rules, and a forum where countries could talk, would prevent another world war.
dd-humanrights.after: The UN has grown to 193 members and runs peacekeeping, refugee and food agencies around the world. Human rights became a shared language for activists, from the anti-apartheid movement to campaigns for women's and gay rights. But enforcement is weak: the Security Council's five permanent members can veto action, and many governments sign treaties they then ignore.

sections.t: The United Nations replaced the failed League of Nations. Its Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and took effect on 24 October, now celebrated as UN Day. Every member has a vote in the General Assembly, but real power lies with the Security Council, where five victors of World War II, the United States, the Soviet Union (now Russia), Britain, France and China, hold permanent seats and a veto. The UN's headquarters in New York opened in the early 1950s, and agencies such as UNICEF and the World Health Organization were set up alongside it.

Drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of President Franklin Roosevelt, with Lebanon's Charles Malik, China's P. C. Chang and France's René Cassin among its authors, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948. Its 30 articles begin: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.' They include freedom from torture and slavery, freedom of speech and religion, the right to a fair trial, and rights to education and work. Forty-eight countries voted in favour, none against, and eight abstained.

The Declaration was not a binding law, so later treaties tried to make rights enforceable. The Genocide Convention of 1948 made genocide an international crime, using a word coined by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin. In 1950 members of the Council of Europe signed the European Convention on Human Rights, whose court in Strasbourg can rule against governments. After the wars in Yugoslavia and the Rwandan genocide, UN tribunals tried those responsible, and in 2002 a permanent International Criminal Court opened in The Hague, though the United States, Russia, China and India have not joined it.

Human rights often collide with power politics. During the Cold War each side accused the other of abuses while backing friendly dictators, and the Security Council veto has blocked action in crises from Syria to Ukraine. Yet the idea of universal rights has also brought real change: international pressure helped end apartheid in South Africa, and courts have held some leaders to account, such as Liberia's Charles Taylor, convicted of war crimes in 2012. Some governments argue that 'universal' rights reflect Western values; supporters reply that they were drafted by people from many cultures and traditions.

dd-space.what: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beeping metal ball, into orbit. Americans were stunned, and the US answered with Explorer 1 in 1958 and a new agency, NASA. The Soviets kept winning firsts: Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space on 12 April 1961, Valentina Tereshkova the first woman in 1963, and Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965. President Kennedy set the US the goal of reaching the Moon. Apollo 8 circled it at Christmas 1968, and on 20 July 1969 Apollo 11 landed. By 1972 twelve Americans had walked on the Moon, and in 1975 an Apollo and a Soyuz docked in orbit.
dd-space.why: The race grew out of the Cold War. Both superpowers were building long-range missiles to carry nuclear warheads, and a rocket that can put a satellite in orbit can also hit a city across the world. Firsts in space were also propaganda: each side wanted to show the world that its system, communist or capitalist, was the more advanced.
dd-space.after: The race made satellites part of daily life: weather forecasts, global television and phone links, spy satellites and, later, GPS. It poured money into science and computing. After the Moon landings both sides turned to space stations, and the 1975 handshake in orbit led, decades later, to the International Space Station, built from 1998 by Russia, the US and partners. Today China, India and private companies are the new players.

sections.t: Both sides' rockets descended from Nazi Germany's V-2, the first long-range ballistic missile, fired at London and Antwerp from 1944. It was built partly by concentration camp prisoners, and more people died making it than were killed by it. After the war its chief designer, Wernher von Braun, surrendered to the Americans and later led the team that built the Saturn V Moon rocket. The Soviets took German engineers and V-2 parts too, but their programme was led by Sergei Korolev, a designer who had survived years in Stalin's prison camps. His R-7, the world's first intercontinental missile, launched Sputnik and Gagarin. Korolev's name was kept secret until he died in 1966.

Apollo 11 lifted off from Florida on 16 July 1969 on a Saturn V, still among the most powerful rockets ever flown. Four days later Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin flew the lunar module Eagle down to the Sea of Tranquillity while Michael Collins stayed in orbit. Computer alarms flashed during the descent, and Armstrong steered past a boulder field by hand, landing with little fuel left. Hundreds of millions of people watched him step out and say, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' The two men spent about two and a half hours outside, collected about 22 kg of rock and splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July.

The biggest gifts are in orbit. Weather satellites, starting with TIROS-1 in 1960, transformed forecasting. Communication satellites such as Telstar in 1962 carried live television across oceans. The US military's GPS, opened to civilians and fully working by 1995, now guides phones, planes, farm machines and bank timing, alongside Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo and China's BeiDou. Space also changed how people saw Earth: the 1968 'Earthrise' photo from Apollo 8 became an emblem of the environmental movement. Some famous 'spin-offs' are myths, though: NASA did not invent Tang, Velcro or Teflon, it only made them famous.

dd-polynesia.what: The ancestors of the Polynesians spoke Austronesian languages that spread from Taiwan through Island South-East Asia. By about 1350 BC their descendants, makers of stamped Lapita pottery, lived in the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea. Sailing east into islands no one had ever reached, they settled Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and by about 850 BC Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture took shape. Then came a long pause. Around 1000 AD voyagers reached the Society Islands, and within about three centuries they found Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally New Zealand, around 1250–1300, completing the last great human migration to empty lands.
dd-polynesia.why: The voyagers had superb double-hulled and outrigger canoes and a deep knowledge of stars, swells, winds and birds, passed down by trained navigators. They sailed deliberately, often against the prevailing easterly winds so they could ride home if they found nothing. Why they set out is debated: growing populations, quarrels between chiefs, younger sons seeking land, and shifts in wind patterns that opened eastward routes may all have played a part.
dd-polynesia.after: Polynesians spread one family of closely related languages, gods and customs across a triangle of ocean from Hawaiʻi to New Zealand to Rapa Nui. On isolated islands they built distinct societies, from the moai of Rapa Nui to Hawaiʻi's kingdoms. From the 1760s European contact brought disease, missionaries and colonial rule. Since the 1970s a revival of voyaging, languages and culture, led by Hōkūleʻa and Māori and Hawaiian schools, has restored pride in that heritage.

sections.t: Polynesian navigators carried a map of the sky in their heads. They knew where dozens of stars rose and set on the horizon, and steered by them through the night, holding the canoe's angle to the ocean swells by feel when clouds hid the sky. Islands could be sensed long before they were seen: a fixed cloud over a peak, a green tint on clouds above a lagoon, swells bent and reflected by land. Birds such as terns and noddies fly out to fish by day and return to land at dusk, pointing the way. In 1769 the Raiatean navigator Tupaia, sailing with Captain Cook, drew a chart showing dozens of islands across the Pacific.

Voyaging canoes were usually double-hulled, two hulls lashed together under a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves, and could be 15–20 metres long or more. A settling party carried everything it needed to start life on an empty island: taro, breadfruit, bananas, yams and coconuts as plants or cuttings, paper mulberry for making bark cloth, and pigs, dogs and chickens. The Pacific rat came too, perhaps as a stowaway, perhaps as food, and its DNA now helps scientists trace the voyages. Not every island got everything: New Zealand's settlers arrived without pigs or chickens, and its colder climate could not grow most tropical crops, so they turned to sweet potato, birds and seafood.

The sweet potato, a South American plant, was growing in Polynesia before Columbus; burnt remains from the Cook Islands date to around 1200–1400, and Polynesian kumara resembles the Quechua word kumar. Most scholars think Polynesians, or less likely South Americans, made the crossing, though some botanists have argued the plant drifted on its own. In 2020 a genetic study of modern Polynesians found traces of Native American ancestry, pointing to a contact around 1200 with people most closely related to Indigenous groups of today's Colombia. In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl's raft Kon-Tiki drifted from Peru to the Tuamotus to argue that Polynesia was settled from America; language, archaeology and DNA show it was settled from Asia.

dd-brazil.what: Portugal claimed Brazil in 1500 and built a colony of sugar plantations and, from the 1690s, gold mines, worked by millions of enslaved Africans. In 1808 the Portuguese royal family fled Napoleon to Rio, and in 1822 Prince Pedro declared independence and made Brazil an empire. It stayed united, fought Paraguay in 1864–70, and in 1888 became the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery. A coup made it a republic in 1889. Getúlio Vargas dominated the mid-1900s, the capital moved to Brasília in 1960, and the military ruled from 1964 to 1985. Since then Brazil has been a democracy, led by figures as different as Lula and Jair Bolsonaro.
dd-brazil.why: Portugal's monarchy, which ruled from Rio and then through its own heir, held Brazil's regions together while Spanish America split into many republics. Sugar, gold, coffee and slavery shaped a deeply unequal society, with land and power concentrated among a small elite. That inequality, and the Cold War fear of communism, helped bring the 1964 coup. Since 1985 Brazilians have argued over how to share the wealth of a resource-rich country and how to fight corruption and crime.
dd-brazil.after: Brazil has about 213 million people, Latin America's largest economy and the largest share of the Amazon rainforest. It is a farming superpower and a voice for the Global South in the BRICS group. Its politics are sharply split: in 2025 its Supreme Court sentenced former president Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years for plotting a coup, and in October 2026 Lula narrowly beat his son Flávio in a presidential runoff to win a fourth term.

sections.t: Brazil took in more enslaved Africans than any other country: nearly 5 million, by the SlaveVoyages database's estimate, against about 400,000 brought to North America. On sugar estates in Bahia and Pernambuco, and later in gold mines and coffee farms, many died within a few years, so planters kept buying new captives. People resisted by escaping to free settlements called quilombos; the largest, Palmares, held out for most of the 1600s, and its last leader, Zumbi, is honoured on 20 November, now a national holiday. Slavery was abolished only in 1888, with no land or compensation for the freed. Today over half of Brazilians identify as Black or mixed race.

In 1964 the army overthrew President João Goulart, whose land reform plans alarmed landowners, business and Washington, which backed the coup. The generals ruled for 21 years, picking presidents, censoring the press and banning most opposition. From 1968 they tortured and killed opponents: a National Truth Commission in 2014 named 434 people killed or disappeared. The years 1968–73 brought a growth 'miracle', with roads, dams and factories, but also huge foreign debts and widening inequality. Mass protests demanding direct elections in 1984 helped end military rule in 1985, and a new constitution followed in 1988. A 1979 amnesty law has shielded officers from prosecution for these crimes.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a former metalworker and union leader, was president from 2003 to 2010, when a commodity boom and cash transfers such as Bolsa Família lifted millions out of poverty. A huge corruption scandal, Car Wash, later engulfed his party, and he spent 580 days in prison from 2018 before the Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021. The far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro won in 2018. Lula beat him narrowly in 2022, and on 8 January 2023 Bolsonaro supporters stormed Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace. In 2025 Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years for plotting a coup, and in October 2026 Lula narrowly beat his son Flávio to win a fourth term.

The Amazon is the world's largest rainforest, and about 60% of it lies in Brazil. Since the 1970s highways, cattle ranches, soy farms and illegal mining have cleared roughly a fifth of Brazil's share. Scientists warn that if too much is lost, parts of the forest could dry out and turn into savanna, releasing vast amounts of carbon. Clearing rose under Bolsonaro and fell sharply after Lula returned in 2023, dropping for a fourth year in a row in 2025, according to the space agency INPE. The forest is also home to hundreds of Indigenous peoples, and in 2025 Brazil hosted the COP30 climate summit at Belém.

dd-japan.what: In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the battle of Sekigahara, and from 1603 his family ruled Japan as shoguns from Edo for over 250 years, while the emperor stayed in Kyoto with little power. Fearing Christian missionaries and foreign meddling, the shoguns banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and confined Dutch traders to the island of Dejima. Japan enjoyed long peace, growing cities and a rich urban culture. In 1853 Commodore Perry's American warships arrived at Uraga and forced treaties on the shogun. Rebel samurai overthrew him in 1868 in the name of Emperor Meiji, and the new government rebuilt Japan on Western lines so fast that by 1905 it had defeated Russia.
dd-japan.why: Seclusion grew from the shoguns' fear that Christianity and European powers could split the country, as rival lords had done in the century of civil war before 1600. Japan opened because it had no answer to steam-powered warships, and China's defeat in the Opium War showed what resisting could cost. The shogun's surrender to foreign demands discredited him, and samurai from Satsuma and Choshu concluded that only a strong, modern state under the emperor could keep Japan independent.
dd-japan.after: Japan became the first non-Western country to industrialise and the first Asian great power of modern times. It won Taiwan in 1895, defeated Russia in 1905 and annexed Korea in 1910, and its victory inspired nationalists across Asia even as its own colonial rule was harsh. The same drive for empire later carried Japan into China and the Pacific War. The Meiji model of state-led catch-up influenced later Asian economies.

sections.t: Under the Tokugawa, the emperor reigned in Kyoto while the shogun ruled from Edo. About 260 lords, the daimyo, governed their own domains but were tightly watched: under the system of 'alternate attendance' they had to spend every other year in Edo and leave their wives and heirs there as virtual hostages. The samurai were a hereditary warrior class who alone could wear two swords, but with no wars to fight for over two centuries most became salaried officials and clerks. Society was ranked into samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, yet merchants often grew rich while many samurai fell into debt.

The word sakoku, 'closed country', was only coined in 1801, and Japan was never fully sealed. It traded through four gateways: Nagasaki, where the Dutch lived on Dejima, a fan-shaped artificial island about 120 metres long, and Chinese merchants in their own quarter; Tsushima for Korea; Satsuma for the Ryukyu kingdom; and Matsumae for the Ainu of Hokkaido. What was banned was Christianity, Portuguese and Spanish ships, and Japanese travel abroad, on pain of death. Through Dutch books, Japanese scholars studied European medicine and astronomy, a field called 'Dutch learning' (rangaku).

The Meiji leaders worked under the slogan 'rich country, strong army'. In 1871 they abolished the domains and replaced them with prefectures, and in 1871–73 the Iwakura Mission toured the US and Europe to study how modern states worked. The government ended samurai privileges, created a conscript army, built the first railway from Tokyo to Yokohama in 1872, set up state factories and made schooling compulsory. Not everyone agreed: in 1877 discontented samurai under Saigo Takamori rose in the Satsuma Rebellion and were crushed by the new army. The 1889 constitution created a parliament but left great power with the emperor and the military.

dd-australia.what: In January 1788 the First Fleet landed convicts and marines at Sydney Cove, founding a British penal colony on land Aboriginal peoples had lived on for at least 50,000 years. Over the next century Britain set up six colonies around the continent and sent about 160,000 convicts until 1868. Free settlers, sheep farming and the gold rushes of the 1850s drew far more people, as frontier violence and disease devastated Aboriginal communities. In New Zealand, Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with Britain in 1840, but wars and land confiscations followed. Australia federated in 1901 and New Zealand became a dominion in 1907. Both fought at Gallipoli in 1915 and grew into prosperous, independent democracies.
dd-australia.why: Britain needed a new dumping ground for convicts after losing America, and wanted a foothold in the Pacific. Its law treated Australia as terra nullius, land belonging to no one, so no treaty was made there, while in New Zealand the strength of Māori and missionary pressure led to a treaty. Cheap land, wool and gold then pulled in settlers, whose demand for land drove conflict with Indigenous peoples.
dd-australia.after: Both countries became stable democracies and early pioneers of votes for women. For decades Australia kept a White Australia immigration policy, removed many Aboriginal children from their families and denied Indigenous land rights. Since the 1960s both have tried to reckon with that past, through land rights, the Waitangi Tribunal and official apologies, and today both are diverse countries drawing many migrants from Asia and the Pacific.

sections.t: Most convicts were transported for theft, often petty, usually for seven or fourteen years. The first years at Sydney were hungry: crops failed and the colony waited anxiously for supply ships. Convicts were assigned to work for the government or free settlers, building roads and clearing land, and harsh punishments, from flogging to remote prisons such as Port Arthur in Tasmania, awaited those who broke the rules. Many who served their time, called emancipists, stayed on, farmed and prospered. Transportation to New South Wales ended in 1840 and to Western Australia in 1868. For the Eora people of Sydney, the colony's arrival brought a smallpox epidemic in 1789 that killed many.

On 6 February 1840 dozens of Māori chiefs signed a treaty with the British Crown at Waitangi, and over 500 signed in the months that followed. The English text says the chiefs ceded sovereignty. The Māori text uses 'kāwanatanga', governance, and promises chiefs 'tino rangatiratanga', full authority over their lands and treasures. That gap has shaped New Zealand ever since. Disputes over land led to the New Zealand Wars of 1845–1872 and huge confiscations. Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated breaches, leading to settlements with many iwi. In April 2025 Parliament voted down a bill to redefine the treaty's principles, by 112 votes to 11, after large Māori-led protests.

In a 1967 referendum about 91% of Australians voted to let the federal government make laws for Aboriginal people and count them in the census. In 1992 the High Court's Mabo decision rejected terra nullius and recognised native title. A 1997 inquiry found that between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children had been taken from their families between about 1910 and 1970, the Stolen Generations, and in 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised in Parliament. In October 2023 about 60% of voters rejected a proposal to give Indigenous Australians a constitutional Voice to Parliament. Supporters saw a lost chance at recognition; many opponents said it would divide Australians by race.

dd-frenchrev.what: In May 1789 a bankrupt Louis XVI called the Estates-General for the first time since 1614. The commoners' deputies proclaimed a National Assembly, Parisians stormed the Bastille on 14 July, and in August the Assembly abolished noble privileges and declared the Rights of Man. In 1791 the king tried to flee, and in 1792, with Austria and Prussia invading, crowds overthrew the monarchy and a republic was declared. Louis was guillotined in January 1793. Under Robespierre's Committee of Public Safety, the Terror executed thousands of suspected enemies until his own fall in July 1794. A weak Directory followed, until General Bonaparte seized power in November 1799.
dd-frenchrev.why: France's crown was deep in debt after costly wars, including its help for the American revolutionaries, and the nobles and clergy were largely exempt from tax. Bad harvests in 1788 sent bread prices soaring. Enlightenment writers had taught educated people to question privilege and divine-right monarchy. Once the old order cracked, war, fear of counter-revolution and hunger pushed politics to extremes. Historians still debate how far the revolution was driven by class, ideas or chance.
dd-frenchrev.after: The revolution ended absolute monarchy and feudal privilege in France and made equal citizenship, written constitutions and national sovereignty central to modern politics. Its wars, continued by Napoleon, spread these ideas across Europe. It gave the world the words 'left' and 'right', the metric system and the model of the nation in arms. Its motto, 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity', is still France's, and the storming of the Bastille is celebrated every 14 July.

sections.t: In September 1793, with France invaded and in revolt, the Convention passed the Law of Suspects, allowing the arrest of anyone thought hostile to the revolution. According to Britannica, at least 300,000 people were arrested, about 17,000 were officially executed, and perhaps 10,000 more died in prison or without trial. Most victims were not nobles but peasants and townspeople, many from rebel regions such as the Vendée. The guillotine, adopted in 1792 as a humane and equal method, became its symbol. The revolution's leaders turned on each other: Danton was executed in April 1794, and Robespierre himself on 28 July, the day after his arrest.

The revolutionaries set out to rebuild daily life on reason. A new calendar started at Year I, from the republic's founding in September 1792. It had twelve months of 30 days with names drawn from nature, such as Thermidor, the month of heat, and ten-day weeks with only one day of rest. It was used until the end of 1805. Decimal clocks, with ten-hour days, were tried for only about 17 months. The metric system was a lasting success: the metre was defined in 1791 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and it is now used almost everywhere.

Women were central to the revolution's great days. In October 1789 thousands of Parisian market women marched to Versailles over the price of bread and brought the royal family back to Paris. In 1791 the playwright Olympe de Gouges published a 'Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen', arguing that women should share every right men had won. The republic legalised divorce in 1792, but it never gave women the vote. In 1793 it closed women's political clubs, and de Gouges was guillotined that November. French women won the vote only in 1944.

dd-latam.what: In 1791 enslaved people in French Saint-Domingue rose up, and in 1804 they founded Haiti. When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808 and deposed its king, Spain's colonies set up their own governing councils, and many soon declared independence. Years of brutal war followed. Simón Bolívar fought from Venezuela across the Andes to Bogotá and Quito, while José de San Martín led an army from Argentina over the Andes into Chile and then by sea to Peru. Victory at Ayacucho in 1824 ended Spanish power in South America. Mexico won independence in 1821, and Brazil broke from Portugal in 1822 under a Portuguese prince. Only Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish, until 1898.
dd-latam.why: American-born creoles resented rule by officials sent from Spain, trade limits and new taxes from the Bourbon reforms. The ideas of the Enlightenment and the American and French revolutions offered a model, while Haiti's revolution both inspired and frightened them. The real trigger was Napoleon's conquest of Spain, which left the colonies without a legitimate king. Elites also feared revolts from below, so many sought independence on their own terms.
dd-latam.after: About twenty new countries emerged, but Bolívar's dream of unity failed: Gran Colombia and the Central American federation broke apart. Military strongmen, border wars and foreign debt marked much of the century, and Mexico lost about half its land to the US. Slavery ended slowly, last in Brazil in 1888, and creole elites, not Indigenous or Black majorities, held power. Spanish and Portuguese remain the shared languages of the region today.

sections.h: Haiti, the first to break free
sections.t: Saint-Domingue produced more sugar and coffee than any other colony in the world, worked by about half a million enslaved Africans. In August 1791 they rose up. A formerly enslaved man, Toussaint Louverture, became the revolution's leader and France abolished slavery in 1794. When Napoleon sent a large army in 1802 to restore French control, Toussaint was captured and died in a French prison, but his successor Jean-Jacques Dessalines, helped by yellow fever, defeated the French. Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804. It later armed Bolívar on condition that he free enslaved people. France forced Haiti to pay a huge indemnity from 1825, a burden that weighed on it for generations.

Simón Bolívar, a rich creole from Caracas, lost two early attempts to free Venezuela. In 1819 he led a small army through flooded plains and over a freezing Andes pass to surprise the Spanish at Boyacá. Over the next five years he and his general Antonio José de Sucre freed what are now five countries, and Bolivia took his name. José de San Martín, a career officer born in Argentina, trained the Army of the Andes and led it across mountain passes in 1817, freeing Chile and then Lima. After meeting Bolívar in Guayaquil in 1822 he stepped aside and died in France in 1850. Bolívar died in 1830, his dream of a united South America in ruins.

Independence was led mostly by creole elites, and for many people it changed less than its speeches promised. Enslaved people often won freedom by fighting, and Chile abolished slavery in 1823 and Mexico in 1829, but it lasted into the 1850s in Venezuela, Peru and Argentina, until 1886 in Spanish Cuba and until 1888 in Brazil. Indigenous communities lost some colonial protections, and their lands were often taken by new landowners. Generals who had won the wars, the caudillos, ruled many countries for decades. Still, the new republics abolished noble titles and, on paper at least, made all free men equal citizens.

dd-ireland.what: The 1801 Act of Union made all of Ireland part of the United Kingdom. From 1845 potato blight brought the Great Famine: about a million people died and millions emigrated. Campaigns for home rule failed until 1914, and in 1916 republicans staged the Easter Rising in Dublin. After a war of independence, the island was partitioned: 26 counties became the Irish Free State, later the Republic of Ireland, while six north-eastern counties stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland. There, from the late 1960s, three decades of conflict known as the Troubles killed about 3,500 people, until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998.
dd-ireland.why: Centuries of English and then British rule had left most land in the hands of a mainly Protestant elite, while the Catholic majority were mostly poor tenants. The Famine deepened bitterness towards British government. In the north-east, however, Protestants descended largely from 17th-century settlers formed a majority and wanted to remain British. These two identities, nationalist and unionist, could not both be satisfied, and partition, then disputes over equality and power in Northern Ireland, followed.
dd-ireland.after: Ireland became a sovereign republic, joined the European Community with the UK in 1973 and grew into one of Europe's richest economies. Under the Good Friday Agreement, Northern Ireland is governed by power sharing between unionists and nationalists, and its status can change only if a majority there votes for it. Since February 2024 Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill has served as the first nationalist First Minister. Brexit made the Irish border a delicate question again.

sections.t: The blight, a mould from the Americas, destroyed about three-quarters of the potato harvest in 1846, and 1847 became 'Black '47'. The government in London set up public works, then soup kitchens, but officials such as Charles Trevelyan believed the market should not be disturbed and that the Irish poor had to help themselves. Grain and cattle were still shipped out of Ireland in the worst years, though food imports in 1847 were larger. Evicted families crowded into workhouses where fever spread. Most historians blame callous policy and ideology rather than a plan to kill, but the Famine left a lasting grievance. In 1847 the Choctaw Nation in America, itself recently expelled from its lands, sent $170 in aid.

Nationalists, mostly Catholic, saw Ireland as one nation with a right to rule itself. Unionists, mostly Protestant and concentrated in Ulster, saw themselves as British and feared a Dublin parliament dominated by Catholics. When Home Rule seemed certain in 1912, about 470,000 unionists signed the Ulster Covenant or its women's Declaration, and both sides formed armed volunteer forces. Partition left a Catholic minority of about a third in Northern Ireland, where unionist governments held power from 1921 to 1972; Catholics complained of discrimination in jobs, housing and voting boundaries. The Irish Free State, in turn, became overwhelmingly Catholic. Symbols still divide: many nationalists say Derry, many unionists Londonderry.

Secret contacts in the early 1990s led to IRA and loyalist ceasefires in 1994. The Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998 rested on compromise. Northern Ireland stays in the UK as long as a majority there wishes, and Ireland dropped its constitutional claim to the whole island. A power-sharing government must include both unionists and nationalists, and new bodies link North and South. Paramilitary prisoners were released early, and the IRA declared an end to its armed campaign in 2005. Voters approved the deal by 71% in Northern Ireland and 94% in the Republic. John Hume and David Trimble shared the 1998 Nobel Peace Prize. The power-sharing government has often been suspended, but large-scale violence has not returned.

dd-mexico.what: Mexico's war of independence began with Miguel Hidalgo's revolt in 1810 and ended in 1821. Decades of coups followed, Texas broke away, and after the US–Mexican War of 1846–48 Mexico lost about half its territory. Benito Juárez defeated a French-installed emperor in the 1860s, and Porfirio Díaz then ruled for over 30 years. The revolution of 1910–1920 toppled him and killed hundreds of thousands. Its heirs formed a party, later called the PRI, that ruled for 71 years, nationalised oil in 1938 and redistributed land. NAFTA bound Mexico to the US economy from 1994, the PRI lost power in 2000, and from 2006 a war against drug cartels brought soaring violence.
dd-mexico.why: Independent Mexico inherited deep inequality from Spanish rule and a huge, thinly settled north that it could not defend against an expanding United States. Díaz's rapid growth enriched foreign investors and large landowners while most villagers lost their land, which fuelled the revolution. Afterwards the ruling party kept peace by absorbing unions, farmers and rivals and by managing elections. Its economic crises in the 1980s and 1990s pushed Mexico towards free trade and, in time, real democracy.
dd-mexico.after: Mexico is now deeply tied to the US: it is the largest US trading partner, tens of millions of Americans have Mexican roots, and migrants send home about $60 billion a year. Cartel violence, fed by US demand for drugs and by guns from the US, remains its gravest problem. Since 2018 Morena, the movement of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, has dominated politics, and in 2024 Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first woman president.

sections.t: From 1929 the revolution's party, renamed the PRI in 1946, won every presidential election for 71 years. Presidents served a single six-year term and then picked their successor, a ritual called the 'dedazo', the tap of the finger. The party gave jobs, land and favours to unions and peasant leagues in return for votes, and rigged results when needed. It also repressed dissent: on 2 October 1968, days before the Mexico City Olympics, troops fired on student protesters at Tlatelolco, killing dozens and possibly hundreds. In 1990 the Peruvian writer Mario Vargas Llosa called the system 'the perfect dictatorship'. It ended peacefully when Vicente Fox of the opposition PAN won the presidency in 2000.

The 1917 constitution promised land to the villages and made the nation the owner of everything under the soil. President Lázaro Cárdenas (1934–40) carried it out: he handed out about 18 million hectares to peasant communities, and on 18 March 1938 he expropriated the foreign oil companies, creating the state firm Pemex. Mexicans queued to donate money, jewellery and even chickens to help pay compensation.
