Eco-tourism, medical devices and nearly 100% renewable electricity define modern Costa Rica; 'pura vida' is the national motto.

cards.s: Costa Rica has no army.

cards.p: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, 150 km from Florida. Havana's harbour made it the key port of Spain's empire, where treasure fleets gathered before crossing the Atlantic.

Columbus landed in 1492. The native Taíno were almost wiped out within decades. From the late 1700s Cuba became the world's largest sugar producer, worked by about 800,000 enslaved Africans; slavery lasted until 1886. African religions, such as Santería, and rhythms shaped Cuban culture and music.

Cubans fought Spain for decades; the poet José Martí died in the 1895 war. In 1898 the US intervened after its battleship Maine exploded in Havana, defeated Spain and occupied Cuba. Cuba became independent in 1902, but the US kept the right to intervene and the naval base at Guantánamo.

cards.q: What was the main crop of colonial Cuba?

cards.p: Fulgencio Batista, a US-backed dictator, ran a corrupt regime where American mobsters ran Havana's casinos. Fidel Castro, his brother Raúl and Che Guevara led a guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra mountains and took power on 1 January 1959.

Castro nationalised US businesses and allied with the Soviet Union. A CIA-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs failed in 1961, and in 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world to the edge of nuclear war. The US embargo began and largely remains. The revolution gave free health care and near-universal literacy but no free elections or press; over a million Cubans left, many to Miami.

When the Soviet Union collapsed, Cuba plunged into the 'Special Period' of hunger. Fidel died in 2016; the Communist Party still rules alone. Today Cuba faces blackouts, shortages and the largest emigration in its history.
Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean; legend says Aphrodite rose from the sea here. Copper was mined here so early that the metal may be named after it.
Greeks, Phoenicians, Persians, Romans, Byzantines, Crusaders, Venice, the Ottomans (1571) and Britain (1878) ruled it. Greek and Turkish Cypriots lived side by side.

cards.q: Why is Cyprus divided?

cards.p: Cyprus became independent in 1960. Violence between communities followed, and after a Greek-backed coup in 1974 Turkey invaded and occupied the north. A UN 'Green Line' still divides the island and Nicosia.
The Republic of Cyprus joined the EU in 2004; the north, recognised only by Turkey, remains separate. Reunification talks have repeatedly failed.

cards.s: Cyprus joined the EU in 2004.

cards.p: Czechia (the Czech Republic) is a landlocked country in central Europe made up of Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia. Prague, with its castle and Charles Bridge, is one of Europe's best-preserved old cities. Czechs are among Europe's least religious people, and famous brewers: pilsner beer was invented in Plzeň.

The Kingdom of Bohemia was a major power; under Emperor Charles IV in the 1300s Prague was capital of the Holy Roman Empire, with central Europe's first university. Reformer Jan Hus was burned in 1415, a century before Luther, and his followers fought the Hussite wars. In 1620 the Habsburgs crushed the Czech nobles at White Mountain and ruled for 300 years.

cards.q: Which Czech reformer was burned a century before Luther?

cards.p: Czechoslovakia was founded in 1918 under Tomáš Masaryk, central Europe's only lasting democracy between the wars. Britain and France let Hitler take the Sudetenland at Munich in 1938; Germany occupied the rest in 1939. Communists took power in 1948. The 1968 'Prague Spring' reforms were crushed by Soviet tanks.

In 1989 the peaceful Velvet Revolution ended communism, and the dissident playwright Václav Havel became president. In 1993 Czechs and Slovaks split peacefully in the 'Velvet Divorce'. Czechia joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.

cards.s: Czechoslovakia split into two countries peacefully in 1993.

units.title: Tribes, Holy Roman Empire and Reformation

cards.p: Germany lies in the middle of Europe, with no natural borders to the east or west. That made it a crossroads and a battlefield, and for most of its history it was not one country but hundreds of states.

Romans called the peoples beyond the Rhine 'Germani'. In AD 9 Germanic tribes destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest, and Rome never conquered the land east of the Rhine. Those tribes later overran the Western Roman Empire.

From 962 German kings were crowned Holy Roman Emperors, claiming Charlemagne's mantle. But the empire was a patchwork of hundreds of princedoms, bishoprics and free cities, and the emperor was usually weak. As Voltaire joked, it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.

cards.h: Luther and the Thirty Years War
cards.p: In 1517 Martin Luther, in Wittenberg, launched the Protestant Reformation. Germany split between Catholic south and Protestant north. The Thirty Years War (1618–48) devastated Germany: perhaps a third of its people died. The peace left it more divided than ever.

cards.q: Who began the Protestant Reformation in Germany?

cards.p: In the north-east, Prussia, ruled from Berlin by the Hohenzollerns, built a powerful army and efficient bureaucracy. Frederick the Great (1740–86) made it a great power. Napoleon crushed the German states, but resistance to him stirred German nationalism: the idea that all Germans belonged in one nation.

Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's chancellor, united Germany through 'blood and iron': wars against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870–71). In January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the Prussian king was proclaimed German emperor.

The new empire, industrial and militarist, became Europe's strongest power. Bismarck also created the first state pensions and health insurance.

Under Kaiser Wilhelm II Germany challenged Britain's navy and backed Austria-Hungary in 1914. After four years of war and a British blockade that starved its people, Germany collapsed in 1918; the Kaiser fled, and the Treaty of Versailles took land, colonies and money, and blamed Germany for the war.

The Weimar Republic was Germany's first democracy, and a brilliant cultural age. But it was hit by hyperinflation in 1923, when money became worthless, and by the Depression from 1929, when six million were jobless. Many blamed democracy and the Versailles treaty.

Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party promised jobs, national revival and revenge, and blamed Jews and communists. He became chancellor in January 1933 and within months was a dictator. Opponents were jailed in concentration camps, Jews were stripped of rights, and Germany rearmed.

His invasion of Poland in 1939 began World War II, in which Germany conquered most of Europe.

The Nazis murdered about six million European Jews, as well as Roma, disabled people and millions of others, in mass shootings and death camps. Germany was utterly defeated in 1945, its cities in ruins.

Modern Germany has made remembering these crimes central to its identity: denying the Holocaust is a crime, and memorials stand at the heart of Berlin.

pins: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe

cards.q: What helped Hitler come to power?
a: The Depression and anger at the Versailles treaty

cards.p:
Germany was split by the winners. In 1949 the western zones became the democratic Federal Republic (West Germany), the Soviet zone the communist German Democratic Republic (East Germany). Berlin, inside the East, was divided too.

West Germany had an 'economic miracle' and joined NATO and the European Community; East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop its people fleeing.

On 9 November 1989 the Berlin Wall opened, and on 3 October 1990 Germany reunited. Rebuilding the East cost trillions, and differences between east and west remain.

Under Angela Merkel (2005–21) Germany led Europe through the euro crisis and welcomed about a million refugees in 2015.

Germany is Europe's largest economy, built on cars, machines and exports. Russia's invasion of Ukraine ended its reliance on Russian gas and its post-war reluctance about the military: it is now rearming. In 2025 Friedrich Merz became chancellor; the far-right AfD has grown, especially in the east.

items: "Coming to terms with the past" shapes politics and education.
Power spread out, a legacy of centuries of division.

cards.s: Germany reunited in 1990.
cards.why: On 3 October 1990, a year after the Wall opened.

cards.p: Djibouti is a tiny, hot, desert country at the mouth of the Red Sea, on one of the world's busiest shipping routes. Lake Assal is Africa's lowest point. Its people are mainly Somali (Issa) and Afar.
France bought the port in 1862 and built a railway to Addis Ababa; it was French Somaliland.

cards.q: Why is Djibouti strategically important?
a: It guards the entrance to the Red Sea

cards.p: Djibouti became independent in 1977; Ismaïl Omar Guelleh has ruled since 1999.
Its ports serve landlocked Ethiopia, and the US, France, China, Japan and Italy all have military bases here.

cards.s: China has a military base in Djibouti.

cards.p: Dominica is a mountainous, rainforested volcanic island with a boiling lake, the 'nature island of the Caribbean'.
The Kalinago (Caribs) held out here longer than anywhere else; their territory still exists. France and Britain fought over it; Britain took it in 1763.

cards.q: Which indigenous people still have a territory in Dominica?

cards.p: Dominica became independent in 1978. Eugenia Charles became the Caribbean's first woman prime minister in 1980.
Hurricane Maria devastated it in 2017; it aims to be the first climate-resilient nation.

cards.s: Hurricane Maria devastated Dominica in 2017.

cards.p: Denmark is a flat country of the Jutland peninsula and hundreds of islands between the North Sea and the Baltic. It also includes the Faroe Islands and Greenland, the world's largest island.

Danish Vikings raided and settled England; King Cnut ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the 1000s. Harald Bluetooth's runestone at Jelling records Denmark's conversion to Christianity (Bluetooth technology is named after him). The Kalmar Union (1397) united Scandinavia under Denmark; it ruled Norway until 1814 and lost southern Sweden in 1658 and Schleswig to Prussia in 1864.

cards.q: Which modern technology is named after a Danish king?

cards.p: Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849 and has the world's oldest continuous monarchy. Germany occupied it in 1940; in 1943 Danes smuggled almost all their 7,000 Jews to safety in Sweden.

Denmark built one of the world's most generous welfare states, joined NATO (1949) and the EU (1973), and leads in wind power. Danes regularly rank among the happiest people; hygge, cosiness, is a national ideal. US interest in buying Greenland caused tension in 2025.

cards.s: Danes rescued most of their Jews in 1943.

cards.p: The Dominican Republic covers the eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola. Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, is the oldest European city in the Americas, with the first cathedral and university.

Spain's first American colony became a backwater after richer lands were found. Haiti ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844; the Dominican Republic dates its independence from breaking away from Haiti in 1844.

cards.q: What is the oldest European city in the Americas?

cards.p: After instability and a US occupation (1916–24), Rafael Trujillo ruled as dictator from 1930 until his assassination in 1961; in 1937 his troops massacred thousands of Haitians.
The Dominican Republic is now one of the fastest-growing economies in Latin America, a top Caribbean tourist destination, and a powerhouse of baseball and merengue and bachata music.

cards.s: The Dominican Republic broke away from Haiti, not Spain, in 1844.

cards.p: Algeria is the largest country in Africa; over four-fifths is Sahara desert, and most of its 46 million people live along the Mediterranean coast. It is a major oil and gas producer.

The Amazigh (Berber) kingdom of Numidia fought Rome; later the region was Roman, and Saint Augustine was born here. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s. From the 1500s Algiers was a self-ruling Ottoman province and a base for Barbary corsairs.

cards.q: What covers most of Algeria?

cards.p: France invaded in 1830 and, unlike its other colonies, made Algeria part of France itself. About a million European settlers, the pieds-noirs, took the best land, while Muslim Algerians had few rights.

In 1954 the FLN launched a war of independence. It lasted eight years, with terror, torture and massacres on both sides; perhaps hundreds of thousands of Algerians died. It toppled France's Fourth Republic. Algeria won independence in 1962, and almost all the settlers left.

The FLN ruled as a single party, backed by the army and oil. When Islamists were about to win elections in 1991, the army cancelled them; a civil war in the 1990s killed about 150,000. The peaceful Hirak protests of 2019 forced out the long-time president Bouteflika, but the army-backed system remains.
Ecuador is named after the equator, which crosses it. It has Andean volcanoes like Chimborazo, the Amazon, and the Galápagos Islands, whose unique animals inspired Darwin's theory of evolution.
The Inca conquered the region in the late 1400s; Quito was a northern capital. Spain conquered it in 1534. Ecuador gained independence as part of Gran Colombia in 1822 and became separate in 1830.

cards.q: Whose theory was inspired by the Galápagos Islands?

cards.p: Ecuador has had frequent coups and political turmoil. Oil, bananas and shrimp are the main exports; it adopted the US dollar in 2000 after a financial crisis.
Once peaceful, Ecuador has been hit since 2020 by drug-gang violence as cartels use its ports; President Daniel Noboa declared war on the gangs in 2024.

cards.s: Ecuador uses the US dollar.

cards.p: Egypt is almost all desert. Ninety-five percent of its people live along the Nile and its delta, a green ribbon through the sand. Every summer, until the Aswan Dam, the river flooded and left fertile black silt. The Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile'.

Around 3100 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were united under one king, the pharaoh, seen as a living god. Egypt lasted as a civilisation for 3,000 years. The Old Kingdom built the pyramids of Giza around 2560 BC; the New Kingdom, from Thebes (Luxor), ruled an empire and buried kings such as Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings.

Egyptians worshipped many gods, such as Ra the sun god and Osiris, lord of the dead. They believed the soul could live forever if the body was preserved, so they mummified the dead and filled tombs with goods for the afterlife. Hieroglyphs, deciphered only in 1822 thanks to the Rosetta Stone, recorded it all.

Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BC and founded Alexandria, whose library was the greatest of the ancient world. His general's descendants, the Ptolemies, ruled until Cleopatra, who lost to Rome in 30 BC. Egypt became Rome's breadbasket, and later a centre of early Christianity: the Coptic church.

cards.q: Why did Egyptians mummify their dead?
a: They believed the soul needed the body to live forever
To keep them for medical study
cards.why: Tombs were filled with goods for the afterlife.

cards.p: Arab armies took Egypt in 641. Over centuries most Egyptians became Muslim and Arabic-speaking; about 10% remain Coptic Christians. The Fatimids founded Cairo in 969 and al-Azhar, one of the world's oldest universities. Saladin ruled from Cairo, and the Mamluks, slave-soldiers turned sultans, stopped the Mongols in 1260.

The Ottomans ruled from 1517. Napoleon invaded in 1798. Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer, then modernised Egypt and ruled it almost independently. The Suez Canal opened in 1869, but debts let Britain take control in 1882.

Egypt became formally independent in 1922. In 1952 army officers overthrew the king, and Gamal Abdel Nasser became the hero of the Arab world. He nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956, defeating an Anglo-French-Israeli invasion politically, and built the Aswan High Dam, which ended the Nile floods.

But Israel crushed Egypt in the Six-Day War of 1967.

Anwar Sadat fought Israel in 1973, then made peace in 1979 and got Sinai back; Islamists assassinated him in 1981. Hosni Mubarak ruled for 30 years until the Arab Spring protests in Tahrir Square forced him out in 2011. The Muslim Brotherhood won elections, but in 2013 General Abdel Fattah el-Sisi took power and has ruled with an iron hand since.

items: Now worried by Ethiopia’s new dam upstream.
Runs politics and much of the economy.
A source of pride and tourist income.

cards.p: Eritrea lies on the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa. Its name comes from the Greek for 'red'. Its highland capital, Asmara, is full of Italian modernist buildings and is a World Heritage site.
The coast was part of the Aksumite kingdom and later contested by the Ottomans and Ethiopia. Italy made Eritrea its first colony in 1890 and used it to invade Ethiopia. Britain took over in 1941.

cards.q: Which European country colonised Eritrea?

cards.p: Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia in 1952 and annexed in 1962, sparking a 30-year war of independence. Eritrea won and became independent in 1993. A border war with Ethiopia (1998–2000) killed about 80,000.
Isaias Afwerki has ruled since independence with no elections, no free press and indefinite military service, driving hundreds of thousands to flee. Peace with Ethiopia came in 2018.

cards.s: Eritrea has never held a national election since independence.

cards.p: Spain covers most of the Iberian Peninsula, cut off from France by the Pyrenees and only 14 km from Africa at the Strait of Gibraltar. It has been a bridge between Europe and Africa, and between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic.

Phoenicians, Greeks and Carthaginians traded on the coasts; Rome conquered Hispania by 19 BC and made it one of its richest provinces: emperors Trajan and Hadrian were born there, and Spanish grew from Latin. After Rome, the Germanic Visigoths ruled a Christian kingdom.

In 711 Muslim armies from North Africa crossed at Gibraltar and conquered most of the peninsula. For centuries Muslim al-Andalus was one of the most advanced societies in Europe: Córdoba had perhaps the largest library in the West, and Muslims, Christians and Jews lived side by side, if not as equals.

The Alhambra palace in Granada and the Great Mosque of Córdoba are its masterpieces.

Christian kingdoms in the north slowly pushed south over 700 years, the Reconquista. In 1469 Isabella of Castile married Ferdinand of Aragon, uniting the two biggest. In January 1492 they took Granada, the last Muslim state.

That same year they expelled all Jews who would not convert, and the Inquisition hunted those suspected of secretly keeping their faith.

cards.q: What was al-Andalus?
cards.why: Córdoba and Granada were its great cities.

cards.p:
Also in 1492 Isabella and Ferdinand sent Columbus west. Spain conquered the Aztecs (1521) and the Inca (1533) and built an empire from California to Chile, plus the Philippines.

Silver from Potosí and Mexico made Spain Europe's richest power. Spanish became the language of most of the Americas, and Catholicism its faith.

Under the Habsburg kings Charles V and Philip II, Spain was the leading power of Europe, champion of the Counter-Reformation. It was a Golden Age of art and letters: Cervantes wrote Don Quixote, and Velázquez and El Greco painted.

But endless wars, the defeat of the Armada in 1588 and inflation from American silver drained it, and Spain slowly declined.

cards.q: What made Spain the richest power in Europe in the 1500s?
cards.why: Above all from Potosí in Bolivia.

cards.p:
Napoleon invaded in 1808, provoking a brutal guerrilla war, a Spanish word. Meanwhile most of Spanish America won independence by 1825. Spain lost its last colonies, Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines, to the US in 1898.

The 1800s brought coups, civil wars and a short-lived republic.

In 1931 Spain became a republic again, but it was bitterly divided between left and right. In 1936 General Francisco Franco led a military uprising. The Civil War (1936–39) killed about 500,000 people; Hitler and Mussolini helped Franco, the Soviet Union the Republic, and German bombers destroyed Guernica, painted by Picasso.

Franco won and ruled as a dictator until his death in 1975.

After Franco died, King Juan Carlos led a peaceful transition to democracy; a 1978 constitution created a parliamentary monarchy with strong regions. Spain joined the European Community in 1986 and boomed. ETA, a Basque terrorist group, gave up arms in 2011.

Spain is a country of strong regions, some with their own languages: Catalan, Basque, Galician. In 2017 Catalonia held an illegal independence referendum and declared independence; Madrid suspended its autonomy and its leaders were jailed or fled. The question still divides Spain.

items: Still debated: graves, monuments, Franco’s legacy.
Now one of Europe’s most secular societies.

cards.p: Estonia is the northernmost Baltic state, with forests, islands and a medieval capital, Tallinn. Estonian is related to Finnish, not to Latvian or Lithuanian.
Danes and German knights conquered it in the 1200s; Sweden and then Russia (from 1710) ruled it. German barons dominated until the 1900s.

cards.q: Which language is Estonian related to?

cards.p: Estonia was independent 1918–40, then occupied by the Soviets and Nazis, with mass deportations. In the 'Singing Revolution' of 1987–91, Estonians sang their way to independence.
Estonia is now the world's most digital society: voting online, e-residency, and the birthplace of Skype. It joined NATO and the EU in 2004.

cards.s: Estonians can vote online.

cards.p: Ethiopia is a vast highland plateau in the Horn of Africa, 'the roof of Africa', where the Blue Nile begins. It is Africa's second most populous country, about 130 million, and one of the oldest homes of humankind: 'Lucy', a 3.2-million-year-old human ancestor, was found here.

From about AD 100 the kingdom of Aksum traded across the Red Sea, minted its own coins and raised giant stone obelisks. Around 330 King Ezana adopted Christianity, making Aksum one of the first Christian states in the world. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, with its own scripts and calendar, is still central to national life.

Ethiopian tradition holds that its kings descended from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and that the Ark of the Covenant rests in Aksum. In the 1100s–1200s King Lalibela had 11 churches carved down into solid rock. Ethiopia also welcomed early Muslims fleeing persecution in Mecca, and has a large Muslim population.

cards.q: Why is Ethiopia remarkable in African Christian history?
a: It became Christian around 330, one of the first Christian states
It was converted by Portuguese missionaries

cards.p: Emperor Tewodros II and his successors reunified the empire. When Italy invaded, Emperor Menelik II crushed its army at Adwa in 1896, the greatest African victory over a colonial power. Ethiopia stayed independent while almost all of Africa was colonised, and its colours, green, gold and red, became the symbol of pan-Africanism.

Haile Selassie, crowned in 1930, modernised the state. Mussolini's Italy invaded in 1935 using poison gas; the emperor appealed in vain to the League of Nations and returned with British help in 1941. He became a global figure, revered by Rastafarians as a messiah.

cards.q: Where did Ethiopia defeat Italy in 1896?

cards.p: A Marxist military junta, the Derg, overthrew Haile Selassie in 1974 and killed tens of thousands in the 'Red Terror'. War and drought caused the 1983–85 famine that killed perhaps a million and inspired Live Aid. Rebels overthrew the Derg in 1991, and Eritrea became independent in 1993.

Ethiopia became one of the world's fastest-growing economies and built the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, alarming Egypt. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 for peace with Eritrea, but a war in Tigray (2020–22) killed hundreds of thousands, and conflicts continue.
Finland is a northern land of forests and about 188,000 lakes. Finnish is related to Estonian and Hungarian, not to its Scandinavian neighbours' languages. There are more saunas than cars.
Sweden ruled Finland for about 600 years, bringing Lutheranism and law. In 1809 Russia took it as an autonomous Grand Duchy. The epic Kalevala and Sibelius's music inspired Finnish nationalism.

cards.q: Which language is Finnish related to?

cards.p: Finland declared independence in 1917. In the Winter War of 1939–40 it fought off a far bigger Soviet invasion, though it lost land; then it fought again in 1941–44. It stayed independent and neutral, carefully balancing between East and West.

Finland built an excellent education system and welfare state, joined the EU in 1995 and, after Russia invaded Ukraine, NATO in 2023. It is regularly ranked the happiest country in the world. Nokia, saunas and the Northern Lights are national symbols.

cards.s: Finland joined NATO in 2023.

cards.p: Fiji is a South Pacific nation of over 300 islands. iTaukei (indigenous Fijians) and Indo-Fijians make up most of the people.
Lapita voyagers arrived about 3,000 years ago. Chief Cakobau ceded Fiji to Britain in 1874, which brought Indian indentured labourers for sugar plantations.

cards.q: Who brought Indian workers to Fiji?

cards.p: Fiji became independent in 1970. Tension between iTaukei and Indo-Fijians led to coups in 1987, 2000 and 2006.
Democratic elections resumed in 2014. Fiji is a hub of the Pacific, a rugby powerhouse and threatened by rising seas.

cards.s: Fiji has had several coups.

cards.p:
France sits at the crossroads of western Europe, with coasts on the Channel, the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, and natural borders in the Pyrenees, the Alps and the Rhine. Its rich farmland made it Europe's most populous country for centuries, and so its most powerful.

Paris grew on an island in the Seine and has been the centre of everything for a thousand years.

In ancient times the land was Gaul, home to Celtic tribes. Julius Caesar conquered it in 58–50 BC, defeating the chieftain Vercingetorix at Alesia. For five centuries Gaul was Roman: Latin became the language that grew into French, and Roman cities, roads and arenas still stand at Nîmes and Arles.

As Rome fell, a Germanic people, the Franks, took over; France is named after them. Their king Clovis converted to Catholicism around 496, tying the French monarchy to the Church for 1,300 years.

Charlemagne, king of the Franks, built an empire across western Europe and was crowned emperor in 800. When it was split in 843, the western part became France.

cards.q: Which language did French grow out of?

cards.p: From 987 the Capetian kings slowly built royal power outward from Paris. Great cathedrals rose: Notre-Dame de Paris, Chartres, Reims, where kings were crowned. French knights led the Crusades, and French became the language of Europe's nobility.

cards.h: The Hundred Years' War and Joan of Arc
cards.p:
English kings, who held much of western France, claimed the French throne. The war lasted from 1337 to 1453. When France was close to defeat, a peasant girl, Joan of Arc, who said saints told her to save France, lifted the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw the king crowned at Reims. The English burned her in 1431, but France won the war.

She is still France's great national heroine.

In the 1500s France split between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots. On St Bartholomew's Day in 1572 thousands of Huguenots were massacred. In 1598 King Henry IV, a former Protestant ('Paris is worth a Mass'), ended the wars with the Edict of Nantes, granting toleration.

Louis XIV ruled for 72 years (1643–1715), the longest reign in European history. He made himself an absolute monarch ('I am the state', he supposedly said), built the vast palace of Versailles to keep the nobles under his eye, and fought endless wars.

French art, manners and language set the standard for all Europe. But the wars and Versailles left huge debts.

By 1789 the state was bankrupt, bread prices were soaring, and the nobles and clergy paid almost no tax. Enlightenment writers such as Voltaire and Rousseau had questioned the old order. When Louis XVI called the Estates-General to raise money, the commoners declared themselves the National Assembly.

On 14 July a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille fortress, now France's national day. The Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaimed liberty, equality and the sovereignty of the nation.

steps: Bastille stormed; privileges of nobles abolished; Rights of Man.
France at war with Austria and Prussia; monarchy abolished; a republic.
Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette guillotined.
The Terror under Robespierre: about 17,000 officially executed.

cards.p:
Napoleon made himself emperor in 1804 and conquered most of Europe. At home he built institutions that still run France: the Napoleonic Code of law, the lycées, the prefects who run each département, the Bank of France.

His invasion of Russia in 1812 destroyed his army, and in 1815 he was finally beaten at Waterloo.

cards.q: What does 14 July, Bastille Day, celebrate?
a: The storming of the Bastille in 1789
The end of World War I
cards.why: It became the symbol of the Revolution.

units.title: Republics, empire and two world wars

cards.p:
After Napoleon, France swung between kings, revolutions (1830, 1848), a second Napoleonic empire under Napoleon III, and republics. Defeat by Prussia in 1871 cost it Alsace and Lorraine and created a united Germany next door.

The Third Republic (1870–1940) made schools free, compulsory and secular, and in 1905 separated Church and state: the root of laïcité, strict secularism.

France built the world's second-largest colonial empire: Algeria from 1830, much of West and North Africa, Madagascar, Indochina and Pacific islands. It called its mission 'civilising', while ruling by force.

France was the main battlefield of the Western Front. At Verdun in 1916 the French held out ('They shall not pass'), at a cost of hundreds of thousands of lives. About 1.4 million French soldiers died, a scar on every village war memorial.

In 1940 Germany defeated France in six weeks. Marshal Pétain's Vichy regime collaborated with the Nazis and helped deport about 75,000 Jews. General Charles de Gaulle, from London, led the Free French, and a Resistance fought at home.

After the 1944 Normandy landings and liberation, de Gaulle walked down the Champs-Élysées in triumph.

pins: De Gaulle and the Free French

cards.s: Vichy France collaborated with Nazi Germany.
cards.why: Pétain’s regime ruled the south and helped deport about 75,000 Jews.

cards.h: Europe and the end of empire
cards.p:
After 1945 France chose reconciliation with Germany: the two became the core of what became the European Union. Thirty years of boom, the 'Trente Glorieuses', modernised the country.

The empire fell painfully: defeat in Indochina in 1954, then a brutal war in Algeria (1954–62), home to a million French settlers. The Algerian crisis brought de Gaulle back to found the Fifth Republic in 1958, with a powerful president.

In May 1968 students and workers rose in a vast revolt: the largest general strike in French history. It changed social attitudes for good. Since then France has alternated between left and right, and protest, from strikes to the 'yellow vests' of 2018, remains a national habit.

Emmanuel Macron, president since 2017, lost his majority in 2024; parliament is split between the left, his centrists and Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, and prime ministers keep falling. Debt, immigration and living costs dominate politics.

items: Equal citizens, no privileges, a strong state.
Religion kept out of public life; debates over the headscarf.

cards.q: What is laïcité?
a: The French principle of strict secularism in public life
cards.why: It grew from the 1905 separation of Church and state.

cards.p: The Federated States of Micronesia is 607 islands in the western Pacific, spread over 2,700 km, in four states.

Nan Madol, a city of basalt-log islets built from about 1180, was the seat of the Saudeleur dynasty. Spain, Germany and Japan ruled the islands; after World War II the US ran them as a UN trust territory.

cards.q: What is Nan Madol?
a: An ancient city built on artificial islets

cards.p: Micronesia became independent in 1986 in 'free association' with the US: the US provides defence and money, and Micronesians can live and work in the US.
It depends on US aid and fishing licences and is threatened by rising seas.

cards.s: Micronesia is in free association with the US.

cards.p: Gabon, on the equator on Africa's Atlantic coast, is almost 90% rainforest, with forest elephants and gorillas. Its small population and oil make it one of Africa's wealthier countries per person.
Portuguese sailors arrived in 1472. Libreville was founded by freed slaves in 1849. France ruled it as part of French Equatorial Africa; Albert Schweitzer ran a famous hospital at Lambaréné.

cards.q: How much of Gabon is rainforest?
cards.why: One of the most forested countries.

cards.p: Gabon became independent in 1960. Omar Bongo ruled from 1967 to 2009, one of the world's longest rulers, with close French ties; his son Ali succeeded him.
In 2023 the army overthrew Ali Bongo after a disputed election; General Brice Oligui Nguema was elected president in 2025.

cards.s: The Bongo family ruled Gabon for over 50 years.

cards.p: The United Kingdom joins four nations, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, on the islands of Great Britain and part of Ireland. The sea protected it from invasion after 1066 and pushed it to become a seafaring, trading power.

Farmers raised Stonehenge around 3000–2000 BC. Celtic Britons lived here when Rome invaded in AD 43. For nearly 400 years most of Britain was a Roman province; Hadrian's Wall marked the frontier with the unconquered north. London began as Roman Londinium.

After Rome left, Germanic Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled; 'England' means land of the Angles, and English grew from their language. Missionaries converted them to Christianity from 597.

Vikings raided from 793 and settled the north and east, the Danelaw, until Alfred the Great of Wessex fought back. His successors united England in the 900s.

In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, invaded and killed King Harold at the Battle of Hastings. The Normans took the land, built castles everywhere, recorded it all in the Domesday Book, and made French the language of the ruling class for 300 years, which is why English has so many French words.

cards.q: Where does the name England come from?

cards.p: In 1215 barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta: even the king was under the law. Through the 1200s kings began calling Parliament, nobles and later elected commoners, to approve taxes. Over centuries, Parliament's power to control money became its power to rule.
English kings conquered Wales by 1283 and invaded Ireland from 1169. Scotland, under William Wallace and Robert the Bruce, won its independence at Bannockburn in 1314 and stayed a separate kingdom.

Henry VIII broke with the Pope in 1534 to end his marriage, making himself head of the Church of England and closing the monasteries. His daughter Elizabeth I (1558–1603) settled a Protestant church, defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588, and presided over a golden age: Shakespeare wrote his plays, and English sailors began to cross the oceans.

cards.q: Why did Henry VIII break with the Pope?
a: The Pope would not end his marriage
He wanted to join the Ottomans
cards.why: He made himself head of the Church of England in 1534.

units.title: Civil war and a constitutional monarchy

cards.h: Union of crowns and civil war
cards.p: In 1603 James VI of Scotland also became James I of England, joining the crowns. His son Charles I tried to rule without Parliament. Civil war broke out in 1642; Parliament's New Model Army under Oliver Cromwell won, and in 1649 Charles was beheaded. For 11 years England was a republic, then the monarchy returned in 1660.

In 1688 Parliament replaced the Catholic James II with the Protestant William of Orange and Mary. The 1689 Bill of Rights made Parliament supreme: the monarch could not raise taxes or an army without it. Britain became a constitutional monarchy, the model for many others.

In 1707 England and Scotland united as Great Britain.

From the 1760s Britain became the first industrial nation: cotton mills, steam engines, coal mines, canals and then railways. Cities such as Manchester and Birmingham exploded in size, with terrible slums. By 1851, when the Great Exhibition showed off its machines, Britain was 'the workshop of the world'.

Britain lost its American colonies in 1783 but built a bigger empire: India, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, much of Africa, and islands on every ocean, guarded by the Royal Navy. By 1914 it ruled about a quarter of the world's land and people.

The empire spread English, parliamentary government and sport; it also brought conquest, famine and racism. Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833, after having been the biggest slave-trading nation.

Queen Victoria reigned 1837–1901. Reforms slowly widened the vote, ended child labour in mines and built sewers and schools. Ireland's Great Famine (1845–52), worsened by British policy, killed a million and drove another million abroad, fuelling the demand for Irish independence.

cards.q: What made Britain "the workshop of the world"?
a: It was the first country to industrialise
It was the largest country in Europe
cards.why: Steam, coal and cotton from the 1760s.

cards.p:
About 880,000 British soldiers died in World War I. In 1940, after France fell, Britain under Winston Churchill fought on alone, won the Battle of Britain in the air and survived the Blitz. 'We shall never surrender' became a defining national memory.

Most of Ireland had won independence in 1922; the north stayed British.

cards.h: Welfare state and the end of empire
cards.p:
In 1945 voters chose Labour, which built the welfare state: the National Health Service (1948), free at the point of use, and social security. India became independent in 1947, and most of the empire followed by the 1960s, many joining the Commonwealth.

Migrants from the Caribbean, South Asia and Africa made Britain far more diverse.

Conflict in Northern Ireland, 'the Troubles', killed about 3,500 people from 1968 until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998. Margaret Thatcher (1979–90) shrank the state, privatised industry and broke the miners' unions.

Britain joined the European Community in 1973 and voted narrowly to leave in 2016; Brexit took effect in 2020. Scotland and Wales got their own parliaments in 1999, and Scotland voted to stay in the UK in 2014.

items: Built up over centuries, never in one document.
And debates over how to remember it.

cards.q: What did the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 do?
a: It largely ended the Troubles in Northern Ireland
It took Britain out of the EU

cards.s: The NHS, free at the point of use, was created in 1948.
cards.why: Part of the welfare state built after World War II.

cards.p: Georgia lies in the Caucasus between the Black Sea and the Caspian, with high mountains in the north. It has its own unique alphabet and claims to be the birthplace of wine, made here for 8,000 years in clay jars.

Ancient Colchis was the land of the Golden Fleece in Greek myth. Georgia became Christian around 337, one of the first nations. Under King David the Builder and Queen Tamar (1100s–1200s) it had a golden age. Then Mongols, Persians and Ottomans invaded.

cards.q: What does Georgia claim to be the birthplace of?

cards.p: Russia annexed Georgia in 1801. Georgia was independent 1918–21, then Soviet; Stalin was Georgian.

Independent in 1991, Georgia lost control of Abkhazia and South Ossetia in wars; Russia fought a short war with Georgia in 2008 and recognised them. The 2003 Rose Revolution brought reforms. Since 2024 mass protests have opposed the ruling party's turn away from the EU.

cards.s: Stalin was born in Georgia.

cards.p: Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa. It is a leading producer of gold and cocoa. Its name honours the medieval Ghana Empire, which was actually further north-west.

cards.h: The Ashanti and the slave castles
cards.p: The Ashanti (Asante) Empire, centred on Kumasi and symbolised by its sacred Golden Stool, grew rich on gold and trade. Europeans built forts along the coast; castles such as Elmina and Cape Coast held enslaved people before the Atlantic crossing. Britain conquered the Ashanti in 1901.

cards.q: What is the sacred symbol of the Ashanti?
cards.why: Believed to hold the nation’s soul.

cards.p: In 1957 the Gold Coast became Ghana, the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence, led by Kwame Nkrumah, a champion of pan-Africanism. He became authoritarian and was overthrown in 1966. Coups followed until Jerry Rawlings restored democracy in the 1990s.

Since 1992 Ghana has held peaceful elections with power changing hands several times, one of Africa's most stable democracies. Kofi Annan, UN Secretary-General, was Ghanaian. Cocoa, gold and oil drive the economy.

cards.s: Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence.

cards.p: Guinea, on West Africa's Atlantic coast, has the Fouta Djallon highlands where the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers rise. It holds about a quarter of the world's bauxite (aluminium ore) and huge iron deposits at Simandou.
Fulani Muslims founded the Imamate of Futa Jallon in the 1700s. In the 1880s–90s Samory Touré built an empire and fought the French for 16 years before capture. France ruled Guinea until 1958.

cards.q: Which mineral is Guinea a leading source of?
cards.why: About a quarter of world reserves.

cards.p: In 1958 Guinea alone voted 'No' to staying in a French community and became independent at once; France withdrew everything. Sékou Touré ruled a harsh socialist dictatorship until 1984.
Military rule, the Ebola epidemic of 2014–16 and coups have marked recent decades; General Mamadi Doumbouya seized power in 2021.

cards.s: Guinea was the only French colony to vote for immediate independence in 1958.
cards.why: It voted 'No' to the French community.

cards.p: The Gambia is mainland Africa's smallest country, a thin strip along the Gambia River, almost surrounded by Senegal. Its borders follow the river because Britain controlled the river trade.
Portuguese, then British traders took enslaved people from forts such as James (Kunta Kinteh) Island. Alex Haley's 'Roots' traced his ancestor Kunta Kinteh here. Britain ruled it as a colony.

cards.q: Why is The Gambia shaped as it is?
a: It follows the Gambia River, which Britain controlled
It was drawn along a railway

cards.p: The Gambia became independent in 1965. Yahya Jammeh seized power in 1994 and ruled harshly for 22 years.
In 2016 Jammeh lost an election and, after West African troops intervened, left; democracy has held since. Tourism and remittances matter most.

cards.s: The Gambia is mainland Africa’s smallest country.

cards.p: Guinea-Bissau is a small West African country of mangrove coasts and the Bijagós islands. Cashew nuts are its main export.
Portuguese traders arrived in 1446 and used it for the slave trade. Portugal ruled until a long liberation war led by Amílcar Cabral.

cards.q: Who led Guinea-Bissau’s independence struggle?

cards.p: Guinea-Bissau declared independence in 1973, recognised in 1974. Cabral was assassinated just before.
It has seen many coups and has been a transit point for cocaine to Europe; another coup struck in 2025.

cards.s: Guinea-Bissau was a Portuguese colony.

cards.p: Equatorial Guinea has the island of Bioko (with the capital Malabo) and mainland Río Muni. It is the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa.
Portugal traded the territory to Spain in 1778. Spain grew cocoa on Bioko using forced labour.

cards.q: What language is spoken in Equatorial Guinea?
cards.why: The only Spanish-speaking country in Africa.

cards.p: Independent in 1968, it suffered under Francisco Macías, whose terror killed or drove out a third of the population.
His nephew Teodoro Obiang overthrew him in 1979 and still rules, one of the world's longest. Oil found in the 1990s made a few very rich while most stayed poor.

cards.s: Teodoro Obiang has ruled since 1979.
cards.why: One of the world’s longest rulers.

cards.p: Greece is mountainous, with thousands of islands, and no point is far from the sea. Mountains split the land into small valleys, which is why ancient Greece was a world of independent city-states, and the sea made Greeks traders and colonists across the Mediterranean.

On Crete the Minoans built the palace of Knossos around 2000 BC. On the mainland the Mycenaeans, the Greeks of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, fought, by legend, the Trojan War. Their world collapsed around 1200 BC.

From the 700s BC city-states (poleis) flourished. Athens created democracy in 508 BC; Sparta trained every man as a soldier. United, the Greeks beat the Persian invasions at Marathon (490) and Salamis (480). Athens' golden age followed: the Parthenon, theatre, history and philosophy from Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. The Olympic Games began in 776 BC.

Philip of Macedon conquered the city-states, and his son Alexander the Great spread Greek culture from Egypt to India. Rome conquered Greece in 146 BC but, as the poet Horace said, 'captive Greece took its captor captive': Roman culture was soaked in Greek art and ideas.

items: Reasoning about ethics, politics and nature.

cards.q: Which Greek city created democracy?

cards.p: When the Roman Empire moved its capital to Constantinople, the eastern empire became Greek-speaking and Orthodox Christian. For a thousand years Byzantium carried Greek culture; the Orthodox Church remains central to Greek identity.
After Constantinople fell in 1453, Greece was ruled by the Ottomans for nearly 400 years. The Orthodox Church held Greek communities together, and Greek merchants prospered across the empire.

cards.q: Which church is central to Greek identity?
cards.why: It held Greek communities together under Ottoman rule.

cards.p: In 1821 the Greeks rose against the Ottomans; European volunteers such as Lord Byron joined them, and Britain, France and Russia destroyed the Ottoman fleet at Navarino in 1827. Greece became independent in 1830, much smaller than today. Over a century it grew north and into the islands, dreaming of 'the Great Idea' of reuniting all Greeks.

In 1919 Greece invaded Turkey and was routed in 1922; Greek Smyrna burned, and a population exchange sent over a million Greeks from Turkey to Greece. In World War II Greece resisted Italy, then suffered a brutal German occupation and famine, followed by a civil war (1946–49) between communists and royalists.

A military junta ruled from 1967 to 1974; democracy returned in 1974, and Greece joined the European Community in 1981.

After the 2008 crash Greece revealed its debts were far larger than reported. Three international bailouts (2010–18) came with harsh austerity: the economy shrank by a quarter and unemployment hit 27%. It recovered, and tourism, with about 30 million visitors a year, is its lifeline.
Grenada is a small Caribbean island known as the 'spice isle' for its nutmeg, which appears on its flag.
Carib and Arawak peoples lived here before Europeans; most were killed or driven out. France and then Britain ruled, with sugar and later nutmeg plantations.

cards.q: Which spice is on Grenada’s flag?

cards.p: Grenada became independent in 1974. In 1979 Maurice Bishop's leftist revolution took power; in 1983 he was killed by rivals in his own party.
Days later the US invaded, ending the revolutionary government. Democracy was restored. Hurricane Beryl hit hard in 2024.

cards.s: The US invaded Grenada in 1983.

cards.p: Guatemala, in Central America, was the heart of the Maya world; over 40% of its people are Maya today, speaking more than 20 Mayan languages. It has volcanoes, highland lakes and jungle.

Tikal was one of the greatest Maya cities, with temples rising above the jungle around 250–900. Spain conquered the highlands from 1524; Antigua was the colonial capital until earthquakes. Independence came in 1821.

cards.q: Which civilisation built Tikal?

cards.p: A democratic revolution in 1944 brought land reform, which threatened the US United Fruit Company; in 1954 a CIA-backed coup overthrew President Árbenz. A civil war (1960–96) followed in which about 200,000 died, most of them Maya killed by the army, acts later ruled genocide.

Peace came in 1996. Maya activist Rigoberta Menchú won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992. Poverty, corruption and gangs drive many to migrate north. Bernardo Arévalo, an anti-corruption reformer, became president in 2024.

cards.s: The US backed a coup in Guatemala in 1954.

cards.p: Guyana, on South America's north coast, is mostly rainforest; Kaieteur Falls is one of the world's most powerful waterfalls. It is the only English-speaking country in South America and culturally Caribbean.

The Dutch founded plantations; Britain took over in 1814 as British Guiana. After slavery ended in 1834, indentured workers came from India; today Indo-Guyanese and Afro-Guyanese are the two largest groups.

cards.q: Which is the only English-speaking country in South America?

cards.p: Guyana became independent in 1966. Politics have long divided along ethnic lines. In 1978 over 900 people died at the Jonestown cult in its jungle.
Huge offshore oil discoveries from 2015 made Guyana's economy the fastest-growing in the world. Venezuela claims two-thirds of its territory.

cards.s: Venezuela claims a large part of Guyana.

cards.p: Honduras is a mountainous country in Central America with coasts on the Caribbean and the Pacific. The ruins of Copán were one of the great Maya cities, famous for its sculpture.
Spain conquered Honduras from 1524; silver mines drew settlers. Independence came in 1821, then as part of the Central American federation until 1838.

cards.q: Which Maya city is in Honduras?

cards.p: In the early 1900s US fruit companies dominated Honduras so completely that the term 'banana republic' was coined for it. Coups were frequent; in the 1980s the US used it as a base against Nicaragua's Sandinistas.

Hurricane Mitch in 1998 killed about 7,000. A 2009 coup ousted the president. Poverty and gang violence have made it a major source of migrants to the US; Xiomara Castro became the first woman president in 2022.

cards.s: The phrase 'banana republic' was coined about Honduras.

cards.p: Croatia curves along the Adriatic coast with over a thousand islands and the walled city of Dubrovnik, plus the Pannonian plain inland. It is mostly Catholic.

Croatia became a kingdom in 925, then joined Hungary in 1102. Dubrovnik (Ragusa) was a rich independent republic for centuries. Venice held the coast, the Ottomans took much of the interior, and the Habsburgs ruled the rest.

cards.q: Which walled city was an independent republic for centuries?

cards.p: Croatia joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918. In World War II the fascist Ustaša regime murdered hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews and Roma. Then it was part of Tito's Yugoslavia.

Croatia declared independence in 1991; a war with Serb forces lasted until 1995. It joined NATO (2009), the EU (2013) and the euro (2023). Tourism booms, and its football team reached the 2018 World Cup final.

cards.s: Croatia joined the EU in 2013.

cards.p: Haiti shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic. Columbus landed in 1492; the native Taíno were wiped out.

As the French colony of Saint-Domingue it became the richest colony in the world, producing sugar and coffee with about 500,000 enslaved Africans under horrific conditions. In 1791 they rose up, led by Toussaint Louverture and later Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeating France, Spain and Britain. In 1804 Haiti became the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people.

cards.q: What made the Haitian Revolution unique?
a: It created the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people

cards.p: In 1825 France forced Haiti to pay a huge 'indemnity' for its own freedom, crippling it for over a century. The US occupied it from 1915 to 1934; the Duvalier dictators ('Papa Doc' and 'Baby Doc') ruled with terror from 1957 to 1986.
A 2010 earthquake killed over 200,000. Since the president's assassination in 2021, armed gangs have taken over most of Port-au-Prince, and millions face hunger.

cards.s: Haiti was forced to pay France compensation for its independence.

cards.p: Hungary lies on the great plain of the Danube in central Europe. Hungarians, or Magyars, speak a language unrelated to their neighbours', related distantly to Finnish. Budapest, split by the Danube, is one of Europe's grandest capitals.

Magyar horsemen arrived from the east in 895. King Stephen was crowned in 1000 and made Hungary Christian. In 1526 the Ottomans crushed Hungary at Mohács and ruled much of it for 150 years; then the Habsburgs. Hungarians rose against Austria in 1848.

cards.q: Which language is Hungarian related to?

cards.p: In 1867 Hungary became an equal partner in Austria-Hungary. After defeat in World War I, the 1920 Treaty of Trianon took two-thirds of its land, leaving millions of Hungarians in neighbouring countries, a wound still felt.

Hungary fought with Germany in World War II; about 550,000 Hungarian Jews were murdered. In 1956 Hungarians revolted against Soviet rule; Soviet tanks crushed them. Hungary opened its border in 1989, helping bring down the Iron Curtain, and joined the EU in 2004. Viktor Orbán, prime minister since 2010, has built what he calls an 'illiberal democracy'.

cards.s: Hungary lost about two-thirds of its land after World War I.

cards.p: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelago, with over 17,000 islands stretching 5,000 km along the equator, more than 270 million people, and hundreds of ethnic groups and languages. It sits on the 'Ring of Fire', with about 130 active volcanoes. It has the largest Muslim population of any country.

Indian traders brought Hinduism and Buddhism. Srivijaya, on Sumatra, controlled the sea trade of the Malacca Strait. On Java, the Sailendra built Borobudur, the world's largest Buddhist temple, around 800, and the Majapahit empire (from 1293) ruled much of the archipelago. Bali is still mostly Hindu.
From the 1200s Muslim traders and Sufi preachers spread Islam peacefully along the trade routes; by 1600 most of Java and Sumatra was Muslim. Indonesian Islam blended with older traditions.

cards.q: What is Borobudur?

cards.p: Europeans came for spices: nutmeg, cloves and pepper grew here and almost nowhere else. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) took control from 1602, ruling from Batavia (Jakarta), sometimes brutally: on the Banda Islands it massacred the people to monopolise nutmeg. The Dutch state later forced farmers to grow export crops.

Japan occupied the islands in 1942–45. Two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno declared independence on 17 August 1945. The Dutch fought for four years to return before recognising Indonesia in 1949. Bahasa Indonesia, a form of Malay, was chosen as a shared national language.

cards.q: What brought Europeans to Indonesia?
a: Spices such as nutmeg and cloves

cards.p: Sukarno led the new nation with a philosophy of unity, Pancasila. In 1965–66, after a murky coup attempt blamed on communists, the army and militias killed perhaps 500,000 or more suspected communists. General Suharto took power.

Suharto ruled for 32 years, bringing growth and corruption and brutally occupying East Timor. The 1997 Asian financial crisis brought him down in 1998. Indonesia became the world's third-largest democracy, East Timor became independent, and a peace deal ended war in Aceh after the 2004 tsunami killed about 170,000 people there.

items: Alongside Christian, Hindu and Buddhist minorities.
Earthquakes and eruptions are part of life.
Nickel, palm oil, a new capital

units.title: From the Indus to the Guptas

cards.p: India is a subcontinent, walled off by the Himalayas to the north. The great river plains of the Indus and the Ganges fed huge populations, and the monsoon rains, arriving each summer, decide whether harvests succeed. Today about 1.4 billion people live here, speaking hundreds of languages.

The Indus civilisation built planned cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro around 2600–1900 BC. Later, Indo-Aryan peoples composed the Vedas, sacred hymns, from about 1500 BC, the roots of Hinduism and of the caste (varna) system that ranked society into priests, warriors, merchants and labourers.

items: End suffering by ending craving: the Eightfold Path.
Absolute non-violence to every living being.
One God, equality, service; centred on Punjab.
cards.p: About 80% of Indians are Hindu and 14% Muslim; India also has large Christian, Sikh, Buddhist and Jain communities.

The Maurya Empire (from 322 BC) united most of India; Ashoka, after a bloody war, embraced Buddhism and non-violence. Under the Guptas (about 320–550) India had a golden age: mathematicians developed the decimal system and zero.

cards.q: Which number concept came from ancient India?
a: Zero as a number, with decimal place value
cards.why: It spread to the world through Arab scholars.

cards.p:
From the 1000s Muslim armies raided from Afghanistan; the Delhi Sultanate ruled the north from 1206. In 1526 Babur, from Central Asia, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire.

Akbar (1556–1605) won over Hindus with tolerance and debate. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for his wife. Aurangzeb (1658–1707) expanded the empire to its widest but ruled as a strict Muslim, and it broke up after him.

cards.q: Who built the Taj Mahal?
cards.why: As a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.

cards.p: The English East India Company came to trade cotton, spices and tea. As the Mughals weakened it used its private army: it won Bengal at Plassey in 1757 and over a century took most of India. After a great rebellion in 1857, the British government took over: the Raj.

Britain built railways, universities and a civil service, and made English the elite language. But it drained wealth, destroyed India's cotton industry to favour Lancashire's, and famines killed millions. Indians were second-class in their own country.

The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, demanded self-rule. Mohandas Gandhi led mass non-violent resistance: boycotts, strikes and the 1930 Salt March. After World War II a weakened Britain agreed to go.

But the Muslim League feared Hindu rule and demanded Pakistan. In August 1947 British India was partitioned; about a million died in the violence and some 15 million fled across the new borders. Gandhi was murdered by a Hindu extremist in 1948.

cards.q: What happened at Partition in 1947?
a: British India split into India and Pakistan amid mass violence

cards.p:
Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister, built a secular democratic republic with a constitution (1950) that outlawed caste discrimination. India stayed non-aligned in the Cold War. It fought wars with Pakistan, largely over Kashmir, and with China in 1962.

Indira Gandhi suspended democracy in an emergency in 1975–77 and was assassinated in 1984.

After reforms in 1991 opened the economy, India grew fast, with an IT industry centred on Bengaluru. Hindu nationalism rose: Narendra Modi's BJP has governed since 2014. In 2023 India passed China as the most populous country and landed a probe near the Moon's south pole. It is expected to become the third-largest economy.

items: Hundreds of languages and many faiths
Tension over Hindu nationalism and minorities.

cards.s: India is the world’s most populous country.

cards.p: Ireland is an island of green, rain-fed farmland on the western edge of Europe. Newgrange, a great passage tomb older than the pyramids, aligns with the winter sunrise. Celtic languages arrived in the Iron Age; Irish (Gaelic) is still an official language.

Saint Patrick, a Briton, brought Christianity in the 400s. While much of Europe was in turmoil, Irish monasteries preserved learning and produced masterpieces such as the Book of Kells, and Irish monks re-founded monasteries across Europe. Vikings raided from 795 and founded Dublin.

cards.q: Who brought Christianity to Ireland?

cards.p: Anglo-Normans invaded in 1169, and English kings claimed Ireland. After the Reformation, Protestant England tightened its grip on Catholic Ireland. In the 1600s land was confiscated and given to English and Scottish Protestant settlers, especially in Ulster: the Plantation. Cromwell's campaign (1649–50) was brutal, and Penal Laws barred Catholics from owning land or voting.

In 1801 Ireland was united with Britain. From 1845 potato blight destroyed the crop most poor families lived on. Food was still exported while about a million people died and another million emigrated. Emigration continued for a century, and today about 70 million people worldwide claim Irish descent, as many as 30 million in the US.
From about 8.5 million to about 4.5 million, through famine and emigration. It still has not fully recovered.

cards.q: What caused the Great Famine?
a: Potato blight, made worse by British policy

cards.p: At Easter 1916 Irish republicans seized Dublin; the rising was crushed and its leaders executed, which turned opinion toward independence. A war of independence (1919–21) led to a treaty: 26 counties became the Irish Free State in 1922, while six Protestant-majority counties in the north stayed in the UK as Northern Ireland. A civil war over the treaty followed. Ireland became a republic in 1949.

hl: Northern Ireland stays in the UK

cards.p: In Northern Ireland, Catholic nationalists faced discrimination; from 1968 conflict between republicans, unionists and British forces, 'the Troubles', killed about 3,500 people. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 brought peace and shared government.

Ireland joined the European Community in 1973 and, with low taxes, attracted tech and pharma giants (Apple, Google, Meta), becoming one of the richest countries in Europe: the 'Celtic Tiger'. Once deeply Catholic, it voted to legalise same-sex marriage in 2015 and abortion in 2018.

Iran is a high plateau ringed by mountains, between the Middle East, Central Asia and South Asia. Its people mostly speak Persian (Farsi), an Indo-European language, not Arabic, and its sense of being an ancient, distinct civilisation is very strong.

Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 550s BC, the largest the world had yet seen, from Egypt to India. It was known for tolerating conquered peoples' religions; Cyrus let the exiled Jews return home. Darius I built the ceremonial capital Persepolis. Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC.

Ancient Persia's religion, Zoroastrianism, taught a cosmic struggle between good and evil, with judgement after death, ideas that may have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The Parthians and then the Sasanians (224–651) ruled great empires that rivalled Rome and Byzantium. Nowruz, the Persian new year, comes from this era.

cards.q: What language do most Iranians speak?

units.title: Islamic Iran and the Shia faith

cards.p: Arab armies conquered Persia in 651, and Iranians gradually became Muslim, but kept their language and culture; Persian poetry by Ferdowsi, Rumi, Hafez and Omar Khayyam is still loved and recited.

In 1501 the Safavid dynasty made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, setting Iran apart from its Sunni Ottoman neighbours. Today about 90% of Iranians are Shia, and the mourning for Imam Hussein, killed at Karbala in 680, is central to its religious life. Shah Abbas made Isfahan one of the most beautiful cities in the world.
In the 1800s weak Qajar shahs lost the Caucasus to Russia, and Britain and Russia competed for influence. Oil was found in 1908, and a British company, later BP, controlled it.

cards.q: Which branch of Islam do most Iranians follow?
cards.why: Made the state religion by the Safavids in 1501.

units.title: Shahs, revolution and the Islamic Republic

cards.p: Reza Shah Pahlavi modernised Iran from 1925. In 1951 Prime Minister Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry; in 1953 a coup organised by the CIA and Britain overthrew him and strengthened Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who ruled with US backing and a feared secret police. Many Iranians never forgot it.

In 1979 mass protests drove out the shah. Ayatollah Khomeini returned from exile and created an Islamic Republic, ruled by Shia clerics under a Supreme Leader. Students seized the US embassy and held 52 hostages for 444 days. Iraq invaded in 1980; the war lasted eight years and killed hundreds of thousands.

Iran backs allies across the region, such as Hezbollah and the Houthis, and its nuclear programme has brought sanctions. Protests, such as 'Woman, Life, Freedom' in 2022, have been crushed. In February 2026 US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Khamenei, and war since has disrupted oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

pins: A fifth of the world’s oil passes here

items: Nowruz, poetry, a sense of greatness.
Often at odds with its rulers.

cards.p: Iraq is ancient Mesopotamia, 'the land between the rivers', the Tigris and the Euphrates. Here, in Sumer, the first cities, writing and law codes appeared over 5,000 years ago. Today it is a mainly Arab, Shia-majority country with a Kurdish north and huge oil reserves.

Sumer invented writing around 3200 BC. Babylon's King Hammurabi wrote one of the first law codes (c. 1750 BC). The Assyrians built a feared empire from Nineveh, and Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, with its legendary Hanging Gardens, destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC.

Arabs brought Islam in the 630s; the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala grew around the shrines of Ali and Husayn. The Abbasid caliphs founded Baghdad in 762, and it became the world's centre of learning, until the Mongols sacked it in 1258.

cards.q: What does 'Mesopotamia' mean?

cards.p: After World War I Britain created Iraq from three Ottoman provinces with different peoples, Shia Arabs, Sunni Arabs and Kurds, and installed a king. A 1958 revolution ended the monarchy. In 1979 Saddam Hussein of the Baath party took power.

Saddam attacked Iran in 1980 (an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands), gassed Kurds at Halabja in 1988, and invaded Kuwait in 1990, provoking the Gulf War. In 2003 a US-led invasion toppled him; insurgency and Sunni–Shia civil war followed, and in 2014 the Islamic State seized Mosul before being defeated in 2017.

items: Much damaged by war and looting.

cards.p: Iceland is a volcanic island in the North Atlantic, with glaciers, geysers and hot springs; almost all its electricity and heating come from geothermal and hydro power.

Norse settlers arrived from 874. In 930 they founded the Althing, one of the oldest parliaments in the world, at Þingvellir. Medieval Icelanders wrote the great sagas. Norway and then Denmark ruled from 1262.

cards.q: What did Icelanders found in 930?
a: The Althing, one of the oldest parliaments

cards.p: Iceland gained home rule in 1918 and became a fully independent republic in 1944. It won 'Cod Wars' against Britain over fishing waters.
Its banks collapsed in 2008, but tourism helped it recover. It has no army, high equality, and elected the world's first woman president, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, in 1980.

cards.s: Iceland elected the world’s first woman president.

units.title: Ancient Israel and the Jewish people

cards.p: Israel is a small country, about the size of New Jersey, on the eastern Mediterranean, between the sea and the Jordan River. Jerusalem is holy to three religions: Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Few places have been fought over so long.

Around 1000 BC, by biblical tradition, King David made Jerusalem his capital, and his son Solomon built the First Temple. The Israelites developed monotheism, the belief in one God, and the Hebrew Bible. Babylon destroyed the Temple in 586 BC and exiled many; they returned and built a Second Temple.

Rome conquered the land. After revolts, the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in AD 70 (its Western Wall survives) and in 135 expelled Jews from Jerusalem, renaming the province Palaestina. For almost 2,000 years most Jews lived in the diaspora, scattered across the world, often persecuted, praying 'next year in Jerusalem'.

cards.q: What is the Western Wall?
a: A surviving part of the Second Temple

cards.p: Arab Muslims took the land in 636; the Dome of the Rock was built in Jerusalem in 691, on the site of the Temple. Crusaders held it for a time. From 1517 it was part of the Ottoman Empire, with a mostly Arab Muslim population and Christian and Jewish minorities.

In the late 1800s, amid pogroms in Russia and antisemitism in Europe, Theodor Herzl founded Zionism: a movement for a Jewish homeland in the ancient land. Jewish settlers began arriving. In 1917 Britain's Balfour Declaration supported 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine, which Britain ruled from 1920; it had also made promises to the Arabs.

After the Holocaust, support for a Jewish state grew. In 1947 the UN proposed partition; Jewish leaders accepted, Arab leaders rejected it. On 14 May 1948 Israel declared independence, and its Arab neighbours attacked. Israel won. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled: the Nakba, 'catastrophe'. Over the next years about 800,000 Jews left or were driven from Arab countries, many to Israel.

cards.q: What did the Balfour Declaration of 1917 do?
a: Supported a Jewish national home in Palestine

cards.p: In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel took the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, the Golan Heights and Sinai. Egypt and Syria attacked in 1973. Egypt made peace in 1979 and got Sinai back; Jordan made peace in 1994. Israeli settlements have grown in the occupied West Bank.

Palestinian uprisings (intifadas) began in 1987 and 2000. The 1993 Oslo Accords created limited Palestinian self-rule but no state. Hamas took over Gaza in 2007. On 7 October 2023 Hamas attacked Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking hostages; Israel's war in Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and devastated the territory.

items: Any Jew can become a citizen.
The unresolved question at the centre.

cards.p: Italy is a long peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean, with the Alps sealing it off in the north and the Apennine mountains running down its spine. That position made it the natural centre of the Mediterranean world, and the heart of an empire.

Rome began as a small town on the Tiber, traditionally founded in 753 BC. It became a republic around 509 BC, conquered Italy, destroyed Carthage, and ruled the whole Mediterranean. After Julius Caesar's murder in 44 BC, Augustus became the first emperor.

At its height under Trajan in AD 117 the empire ran from Britain to Iraq.

Rome left Latin, the root of Italian, French and Spanish; Roman law; roads, aqueducts and the Colosseum; and Christianity, which became the empire's religion in 380. The Pope, bishop of Rome, made the city the centre of Catholic Christianity, as it still is: Vatican City is a tiny independent state inside Rome.

cards.q: What happened to the Western Roman Empire in 476?
a: The last western emperor was deposed
It moved its capital to Paris
cards.why: The East, the Byzantine Empire, survived until 1453.

cards.p: After Rome fell, Italy stayed divided for 1,400 years: among Lombards, Byzantines, the Papal States, Normans in the south, and later Spain, France and Austria. Rich trading city-states grew: Venice and Genoa ruled the sea trade with the East; Florence and Milan grew rich on banking and cloth.

From about 1400, Italy led the Renaissance, the 'rebirth' of ancient learning and art. Florence, under the Medici bankers, was its heart: Brunelleschi's dome, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael. Machiavelli wrote The Prince. Galileo later turned a telescope on the heavens.

Italy's cities are still full of this art, the reason millions visit.

Once the Atlantic route to Asia opened, Mediterranean trade declined, and Italy's states became prizes fought over by Spain, France and Austria. Napoleon conquered the peninsula around 1800; afterwards Austria dominated the north.

cards.q: Which city was the heart of the Italian Renaissance?
cards.why: Paid for by the Medici bankers.

cards.p:
In the 1800s the Risorgimento, 'resurgence', sought to unite Italy. The statesman Cavour of Piedmont used diplomacy and war with Austria; the soldier Garibaldi led 1,000 volunteer 'Red Shirts' to conquer Sicily and Naples in 1860. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, and Rome became its capital in 1871.

'We have made Italy; now we must make Italians,' said one politician: most people still spoke local dialects.

Unification left a deep gap between the industrial north and the poor, rural south, the Mezzogiorno. Millions emigrated, mostly from the south, to the Americas: today tens of millions of Americans, Argentines and Brazilians have Italian roots. The Mafia grew in Sicily where the state was weak.

After World War I, Benito Mussolini's Fascists seized power in 1922: the world's first fascist regime. He crushed opposition, invaded Ethiopia, and allied with Hitler. Defeats in World War II brought his overthrow in 1943; partisans shot him in 1945.

In 1946 Italians voted to abolish the monarchy and became a republic.

Postwar Italy was a founding member of the European Community and had an 'economic miracle', becoming famous for design, fashion and cars such as Fiat and Ferrari. Politics were unstable, with dozens of governments, and the 1970s brought terrorism.

In the 1990s corruption scandals swept away the old parties; the billionaire Silvio Berlusconi then dominated politics for two decades.
Italy has the oldest population in Europe after Japan's, slow growth and high debt. Since 2022 Giorgia Meloni, from a party with roots in post-fascism, has led a right-wing government.

items: Loyalty to your town and region, its food and dialect.
Catholic tradition is woven into life, even for the non-religious.
Family ties and businesses run society.

cards.q: What divides Italy's economy?
a: A rich industrial north and a poorer south
cards.why: The gap dates back to unification.

cards.p: Jamaica is a mountainous Caribbean island south of Cuba, its motto 'Out of many, one people'. Most Jamaicans are of African descent.

The Taíno called it Xaymaca, 'land of wood and water'. Spain took it in 1494, Britain in 1655. It became Britain's richest sugar colony, worked by enslaved Africans who outnumbered whites ten to one. Escaped slaves, the Maroons, fought Britain to a treaty in 1739. Slavery ended in 1838.

cards.q: Who were the Maroons?
a: Escaped enslaved people who won freedom in the mountains

cards.p: After the 1865 Morant Bay rebellion was brutally suppressed, Britain ruled directly. Labour protests in the 1930s led to self-government, and Jamaica became independent in 1962.

Jamaica gave the world reggae, Bob Marley, ska and dancehall, Rastafari, and the fastest sprinters, such as Usain Bolt. Marcus Garvey inspired Black pride worldwide. Gang violence and debt are challenges.

cards.s: Bob Marley was Jamaican.

cards.p: Jordan is a mostly desert country east of the Jordan River, with the Dead Sea, the lowest point on land, and the red sandstone city of Petra. It has few resources, not even much water, but a key location.

The Nabataeans carved Petra into rock cliffs and grew rich on the incense trade; Rome annexed it in 106. Jesus was baptised in the Jordan River, by tradition at Bethany. Muslim Arabs ruled from the 630s; then the Ottomans.

cards.q: Who carved the city of Petra?

cards.p: After World War I Britain created Transjordan for Abdullah, of the Hashemite family that claims descent from the Prophet. Independent in 1946, it took the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 1948 and lost them to Israel in 1967.

Jordan has absorbed waves of refugees, Palestinians (over half of Jordanians have Palestinian roots), Iraqis and Syrians, and stayed stable under King Hussein and, since 1999, King Abdullah II. It made peace with Israel in 1994.

cards.s: Jordan made peace with Israel in 1994.
cards.why: The second Arab state to do so.

units.title: Islands, gods and the first emperors

cards.p:
Japan is a chain of mountainous islands off the coast of Asia: four main ones (Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku) and thousands of smaller ones. Mountains cover about three-quarters of the land, so people crowded onto narrow coastal plains, as they still do: Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya sit on the few big flat areas.

The sea protected Japan. It was invaded seriously only twice before 1945, and both attempts failed. That isolation let it borrow from China and Korea on its own terms.

For over 10,000 years the Jōmon people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, and made some of the world's oldest pottery.

From about 300 BC, newcomers from Korea and China, the Yayoi, brought wet-rice farming, bronze and iron. Rice became the base of Japanese life, wealth and even taxes for 2,000 years.

cards.h: Shinto: the way of the gods
cards.p:
Japan's native religion is Shinto. It has no founder or holy book. Its followers honour kami: spirits found in mountains, rivers, trees, ancestors and great people. Shrines, marked by red torii gates, are places to meet the kami; purity, gratitude and harmony with nature matter more than doctrine.

According to myth, the emperors descend from the sun goddess Amaterasu. Japan's imperial family claims an unbroken line from the 6th century or earlier, the oldest monarchy in the world.

From the 500s Japan's Yamato rulers looked to China, then the most advanced state in the world. Buddhism arrived from Korea around 538 and was championed by Prince Shōtoku. Japan adopted Chinese characters for writing, Confucian ideas about government and Chinese-style law.

In 710 a planned capital was built at Nara, copying the Chinese capital Chang'an.

r: From India via China and Korea
cards.p: Most Japanese mix the two without seeing a conflict: 'born Shinto, die Buddhist', as the saying goes.

cards.q: What are kami in Shinto?
a: Spirits in nature, ancestors and great people

cards.s: Japan's imperial family is the oldest continuing monarchy in the world.
cards.why: It claims an unbroken line going back at least to the 6th century.

cards.p:
In 794 the court moved to Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto, which stayed the imperial capital for over a thousand years.

In the Heian period Japan stopped copying China so closely and developed its own culture. A Japanese phonetic script, kana, made writing in Japanese easier.

Around 1000, Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at court, wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel. Court life prized poetry, beauty and refined manners.

Real power slipped from the emperors to the Fujiwara family, who ruled as regents by marrying their daughters to emperors. In the provinces, landowners hired armed men to protect their estates: the first samurai.

cards.q: What is The Tale of Genji?
a: A novel of court life written around 1000
A history of Japan written by Chinese monks
cards.why: Murasaki Shikibu wrote it at the Heian court.

cards.p:
